He never attempted a literal reproduction of any Greek building.
Schinkel’s best-known work is the museum in Berlin now known as Das Altes Museum (Old Museum, 1824–30).
The façade is a simple portico of eighteen Ionic columns that stretch across the entire width of the building, supporting an entablature band.
A simple attic block rises above at the center of the building.
In this building, Schinkel faced a basic problem of the Greek Revival: the interiors of Greek temples, the only ancient Greek interior spaces of any importance, were relatively small and dark spaces not suited to any modern use.
The Greek Revivalist had to invent a Greek approach to interior design and was thus driven to originality.
This was, at the time, often criticized as unauthentic, but it now appears creative and interesting.
In the Altes Museum behind the façade portico, an outdoor stair-hall loggia gives access to a great central domed rotunda, the dome of which is fitted into the attic story and so is invisible externally.
Stairs lead to an upper-level gallery (11.6) in the rotunda, where exhibition galleries are placed in a rectangle with two inner light courts.
The interiors are full of rich detail, paintings, sculpture, and Neoclassical architectural motifs arranged with great skill.
Karl Friedrich Schinkel, Upper Stair Gallery, Altes Museum, Berlin, 1824–30.
The engraving shows how the Greek revival in Germany was advanced by Schinkel’s skillful adaptation of Greek architectural elements for this monumental building.
In this engraving, based on Schinkel’s own drawing, the many Ionic columns that surround the building externally can be seen through the four-columned entrance opening.
The stair railings, floor, and ceiling designs are Schinkel’s effort to extrapolate Greek practice into the forms of a nineteenthcentury building.

## England
In England, the Neoclassicism of Regency design slipped easily into the more specifically neo-Greek of a revival.
The British Museum, begun in 1823 by Sir Robert Smirke (1780–1867), has a pedimented, eight-columned portico using the Ionic order of the Erechtheum in Athens, which continues as a colonnade wrapped around the two side wings that project forward to form an entrance court—there are forty-four columns in all.
The Greek Doric order was also put to use in Britain in ways that now seem surprising.
The London terminal of the London and Birmingham Railway, Euston Station (1835–7), was approached through a pedimented Doric pavilion designed by Philip Hardwick (1792–1870).
The station behind the entrance screen was an arrangement of outdoor sheds, destined to be replaced by a more monumental station in 1846–9, also by Hardwick.
It included a vast Great Hall (11.7) with stairs leading up to a screen of Ionic columns —a glorious space, but scarcely Greek in spirit.
The difficulty of devising Greek interiors appropriate to Greek exterior architecture may have been a factor in bringing the Greek Revival to an early end in England.
Philip Hardwick and Philip Charles Hardwick, Great Hall, Euston Station, London, 1846–9.
A new building type, the railroad station, brought forth many monumental projects.
This dignified hall (now demolished), which is lit by high windows, makes use of the Greek Ionic order at the far end, where stairs rise to give access to the doors and surrounding balcony.

## United
States In the United States, Greek Revivalism was supported by an element of ideology.
The newly independent nation was the first modern country to declare itself a democracy (actually a republic), just as ancient Athens had been.
Towns were given Greek names—Syracuse, Utica, Schenectady, and Ithaca—in a flurry of enthusiasm for Greek art, literature, architecture, and governmental system.
The aim was to recreate the glory of the Periclean age on the North American continent.
In architecture and design, the Federal style, already inclined toward the use of Greek detail, moved into a Revival phase in which the aim was to create whole buildings that would appear to be Greek.
The Second Bank of the United States in Philadelphia (1818–24), by William Strickland (1788– 1854), is the first American building to be designed in the form of a Greek temple; it has an eightcolumned pedimented portico on the model of the Parthenon at front and rear.
Windows were introduced along all four walls to make the interior spaces functional.
In the interest of fire safety as well as monumentality, the building is entirely of stone, and all interior spaces are vaulted in a manner unknown to ancient Greece.
The main banking room that occupies the center of the building is a handsome chamber with six columns along each side, supporting an entablature below the simple barrel-vaulted ceiling.
The new federal government encouraged Greek Revivalism by commissioning a number of official buildings in the increasingly popular style.
In New York, the firm of Town and Davis (Ithiel Town, 1784–1844, and Alexander Jackson Davis, 1803–92) produced another Parthenonlike temple to be the U.S.
Customs House (1833–42; now called the Federal Hall).
It is also an allstone building with Doric porticos front and back and windows along the sides alternating with pilasters.
The interiors were largely the work of John Frazee (1790–1852), who was the designer of the main public room, a rotunda with a circle of Corinthian columns and pilasters supporting a coffered dome fitted under the main gable roof (11.8).
This totally non-Greek interior space is another reflection of the continuing problem of dealing with interiors of what appear externally to be Greek temples.

## 11.8 Town and Davis with John Frazee, U.S. Customs House (now Federal Hall), New York, 183
3–42.
A large public hall was required within a Greek Revival, temple-like exterior, something not developed in ancient Greece.
Frazee approached the problem by inserting a round domed hall with an oculus skylight.
Although surrounded by Greek Corinthian columns, the effect is more Roman than Greek.
Greek Revival buildings that made freer adaptations of Greek precedents were often functionally successful as well as dignified and impressive.
Robert Mills (1781–1855), best known for his 1836 design for the Washington Monument, was the architect for a number of government buildings including the Old Patent Office (now the National Portrait Gallery) with its Doric portico, and the Treasury Building (1836–42) with its seemingly endless Ionic colonnade.
The Patent Office has many simple and dignified stairways and vaulted spaces, with only restrained efforts at Greek detail.
William Strickland worked in a freer and more creative version of the Greek idiom after his temple bank in Philadelphia.
In Philadelphia, his Exchange building (1832–4) uses the Corinthian order for a semicircular portico that is topped by a tower imitative of the ancient Choragic Monument of Lysicrates in Athens.
A similar tower motif tops the building usually considered to be Strickland’s masterpiece, the Tennessee State Capitol in Nashville (1845–59).
It is a simple, rectangular block with eight-columned pedimented Ionic porticos at each end and six-columned porticos without pediments at the center of each side.
The monument-topped tower makes this one of the few American state capitol buildings that does not have a dome.
Internally, lobbies and stairs and the legislative chambers all use Greek details in ways that are restrained and handsome.
The Greek Revival quickly became a favored style for residential building, with results that spread from the northeast states into the south, and into the Midwest as far as the Mississippi River.
The Lee Mansion in Arlington, Virginia (1802–26), largely the design of its original owner, G.
W.
P.
Custis (1781–1857), in simple Federal style, was transformed by the addition of a massive Doric portico and pediment by George Hadfield (c.
1764–1826).
The wooden paneling, fireplace, and window and door trim are typical of Federal style, although there are arched openings and a triple-arch separation between parlor and dining room that give these rooms a special character.
The Greek portico gives the building the form that became known as a temple house.
Hundreds of such houses were built, often with designs developed by local carpenter–builders who found their Greek details in books.
One such was the Modern Builder’s Guide (1833), by Minard Lafever (1798– 1854), a successful professional practitioner in the Greek vocabulary.
Small houses were generally built entirely of wood, and the skill with which the stone detail of Greek temples was reproduced in that material is remarkable.
Temple houses often exhibit strange compromises in the effort to fit reasonable dwelling plans—complete with windows and chimneys where needed—into Greek temple forms.
Row houses in the large cities could not be made into temple houses, but they were often fitted with small doorway porticos such as those surviving on the handsome row along Washington Square North in New York.
Within such houses, major rooms were made Greek with woodwork and plaster details, egg and dart or Greek key moldings, and even pilasters or columns using one of the orders—Ionic was a special favorite.
There is a fine rendering of such a room, thought to be designed by Town and Davis for a New York town house, showing two pairs of Ionic columns separating front and back parlors in a town house.
Greek-inspired furniture, klismos chairs, and a sofa with upholstery embroidered in Greek motifs are set beneath Greek cornice moldings and a plaster ceiling rosette.
Even the wall-to-wall carpeting of the floor uses a vaguely Greek pattern.
The modest row house that was built in New York for Joseph Brewster in 1832 (now called the Merchant’s House Museum), is remarkable for having quite well-preserved interiors of this style (11.9 and 11.10).
Dining room and principal parlor, Tredwell Row House, New York, 1832.
The typical town house in Greek revival style is now called the Merchant’s House Museum.
The dining room and front parlor are separated by an opening with sliding doors.
Greek Ionic columns flank the opening, and plaster detail uses Greek-inspired elements.
The furniture seen here is by Duncan Phyfe, and the patterned carpet is typical of the period.
The elaborate window drapery would be usual in the home of wealthy people.
The hanging gaslight fixtures are of a somewhat later date than the house.
Bedroom, Tredwell Row House, New York, 1832.
In 1834 the house was bought, and lived in until 1933, by the Tredwell family.
This shows the bedroom of Eliza Tredwell, the matriarch of the family.
It was customary at the time for husbands and wives in wealthy families to have separate bedrooms and Eliza’s also served as her private parlor.
Compared to the dining room and principal parlor, it is an austere room, but the bed with its drapes forms an impressive focus.
A small washstand and wall mirror offer a modest alternative to the plumbed bathrooms that would emerge at the end of the nineteenth century.
The dressing table and mirror by the side of the bed doubled as a writing desk.
From about 1820 until the 1850s, Greek Revival design was applied to almost every kind of building.
Greek churches were built in great numbers.
Some, such as St.
Paul’s in Richmond, Virginia (1845), add a quite un-Greek tower to a temple plan with, in this case, Corinthian columns in a semicircle behind the altar.
Others, like the 13th Street Presbyterian Church in New York (1847), are simple brick meeting houses made Greek by the addition of a Doric portico, well executed here in wood.
There are Greek college buildings (Amherst, Washington, and Lee), Greek asylums (Raleigh, North Carolina), Greek courthouses, and Greek hotels.
In the south, Greek porticos turned out to be genuinely functional for the great mansions built on plantations, where their shade helped keep interiors comfortably cool.
The Hermitage near Nashville (c.
1835), Oak Alley (also called Bon Sejour, 1839) and Madewood, an Ionic temple house of 1848—both near New Orleans in Louisiana—and D’Evereux (1840) near Natchez, Mississippi, are all examples of the many surviving great plantation houses of simple symmetrical plan with porticos rich in Greek detail.

## THE
INDUSTRIAL REVOLUTION The term “Industrial Revolution” is used to describe the complex developments that transformed Britain, then other Western European nations and the United States, into modern industrial nations.
It is helpful, in trying to grasp the extent of change in the last two centuries, to consider what technology was available in the eighteenth century.
The French encyclopedist Denis Diderot (1713–84) produced in his many-volume work documentation of the processes of manufacture in the eighteenth century.
The articles, illustrated with wonderfully detailed engraving, show the techniques of glass blowing, shipbuilding, cabinetmaking, and dozens of other trades.
Virtually all work is hand work—not, of course, without tools and equipment, but the tools are simple and the equipment is handmade.
There is no assembly line, no machinery.
The most advanced machinery shown by Diderot is the wooden gearing of a mill grinding hops for the making of beer.
The power is supplied by four horses walking in a circle in the basement of the mill.
A windmill is shown, entirely built of wood even to the wheels and gears.
The only sources of power are human, horse, water, and wind, all of the last three used only in limited ways.
Through human history from the stone age until the late eighteenth century, these had been the only ways in which things could be made.
A quick survey of the possessions of any modern family will reveal few, if any, handmade objects.
The plumbing fixtures, the lamps, the stove, and refrigerator, the telephone, radio, television, and computer, the furniture, the bedding, the clothing—not to speak of the automobile, the lawn mower, even the children’s toys—all are factory made, and most would be useless without the ready supply of pumped water, electric current, gasoline, and spare parts, which are in turn products of industrial processes.
The contrast is startling.

## Early
Industrialization and Inventions The first wave of industrialization was based on a few key inventions.
The steam engine, the first great “prime mover” to be turned to use as a source of power for pumping water and running the machinery of textile mills, was developed by a series of inventors, culminating with James Watt (1736–1819) of Glasgow.
His stationary engines of 1769 to 1788 offered the first practical alternative to hand, horse, wind, and water as a source of power.
Steam engines and the boilers that fed them required metals for their working parts.
Iron had been known, and steel made in small quantities for special purposes (armor, weapons, and knife blades), since ancient times, but the quantities needed for engines required mines and blast furnaces, foundries, and steel mills.
Transport of coal from mines, of iron from foundries, and of steel from mills to the shops where engines could be made called for something better than ox carts pulled along muddy roads.
Making a road of metal rails, a “rail road” with cars—no longer pulled by horses or oxen but by the special mobile version of the steam engine, the locomotive—made it easier to build more steam engines, to make more rails for more railroads, and to bring raw materials to factories and take their products to markets.
The building of iron ships powered by steam engines introduced similar improvements in sea travel and the intercontinental transport of goods.
The power loom of Joseph Cartwright (1785) and the steam engine together made possible a textile mill capable of producing cheap cloth in quantity.
The products of engine-powered factories required less manual labor and so could be inexpensive.
Profits earned by mills and factories could be used to build more factories, making their owners wealthy and, eventually, making the countries that turned to industrialization rich and powerful.
Britain became the dominant world power.
France, Germany, the United States, and, eventually, other countries rose in wealth and status as the process of industrialization progressed.
While all of this was happening, the world of design paid little attention, except to offer a few complaints about the noise and dirt associated with the new inventions.
The revivalists, Greek or Gothic, took little notice of the great changes taking place in their world.
But John Nash used iron columns in the Brighton Pavilion, Euston Station had a Greek entrance gate, Latrobe designed a steam-powered water pumping station with Greek detail.
Steam engines often incorporated structural parts of cast iron in the form of classical columns.
Locomotives sometimes had domes shaped like Roman temples or curiously squat versions of Greek columns.
Wealthy clients were less often titled aristocrats and more frequently self-made industrialists or the managers and professionals who served industry.
The segments of populations who would have been “peasants” working in agriculture and living in farm houses became the “mill-hands” who worked in factories and lived in cities, often in grim slums made up of squalid tenements.

## Industry
and Interiors The impact of the early phases of the Industrial Revolution on interior design was more technical than aesthetic.
First steps toward modern plumbing, lighting, and heating appeared, making some important elements of earlier interiors obsolescent.
Cast iron became an inexpensive and practical material for the making of stoves.
Stoves heated with wood, and then coal, had major advantages in terms of efficiency and convenience over the open fireplace (11.11).
Ready availability of coal resulted from improved mining and rail transport.
For cooking, the special form of stove called a kitchen range, also of cast iron, made kitchen fireplaces obsolete.
Kitchen ranges were developed with water reservoirs kept warm by the stove fire to provide hot water as needed.
In cities, central piped water systems began to appear, the pressure provided by steam pumps that could lift water to a high reservoir or water tower so that gravity would make water available to bathrooms on the upper floors of buildings.
Running water, flush toilets (11.12), and the drain trap that blocks the escape of sewer gases were all introduced into general use in the 1800s.
Bathtubs and showers were luxuries at first but eventually became standard in city houses and sometimes in rural houses as well.
Systems of central heating gradually replaced stoves.
Coalfired furnaces were placed in cellars to heat warm air which was circulated to living spaces through pipes and grilles called “registers.” The larger spaces of churches, theaters, schools, hospitals, and public buildings could also be heated by warm air systems.
Furnaces were also arranged to heat water so that piped hot water could be available in bathrooms.
Restored flat, tenement building, Glasgow, c.
1892.
The Industrial Revolution brought workers into parts of cities where living space was scarce and expensive.
Factory workers and their families often were crowded into tiny quarters, such as this room, where cooking stove, alcove bed, and clothes-drying lines share the same small space.
The restoration has probably made this room less squalid than it would have been in its original state.
The neat wall clock and small objects introduce a touch of elegance.
The radio is, of course, modern.
Sanitary-ware advertisement, England, mid nineteenth century.
The Doulton company, a leading sanitary-ware manufacturer, was founded in London in 1815 and, as sanitary provision improved throughout the century, it expanded dramatically.
The section offers technical information, since the sophistication of the new plumbing equipment was unfamiliar to customers.
Artificial lighting, confined to candles until the end of the eighteenth century, was improved through a series of inventions.
Oil lamps that burned a fuel called colza oil (made from a vegetable seed) were developed with wick holders and feed mechanisms that could be factory made in quantity and provided better light than candles, with less inconvenience (11.13).
Whale oil replaced colza oil as a fuel and was eventually replaced by “mineral oil,” that is, petroleum and its derivative, kerosene.
Various improved burners such as those using a mantle, a curtain of ash that produced a bright incandescent glow, gave better light than a direct flame.
The development of oil lamps with their functional advantages and varied appearance displaced candlesticks, sconces, and chandeliers in many applications.
The invention of illuminating gas, originally coal gas, made possible the gradual introduction of piped gas for lighting supplied by centralized city systems.
The same gas was also usable for cooking ranges and for various heating devices such as the gas grate, which could be placed in fireplaces to make an open fire unnecessary.
11.13 James S.
De Ville, bronze and ormolu chandelier, London, 1817.
De Ville (1777–1846) designed this six-branch chandelier for the dining room at Gawthorpe Hall, Lancashire, north England.
It was fueled by vegetable-derived colza oil.
The visible evidence of these technological developments remained minor in the early nineteenth century.
The bathroom emerged as a new kind of space, but it was usually given a minor place in house and other building plans and treated in a utilitarian way, perhaps with some marble trim or colorful tiles in luxury examples.
Kitchens, viewed as the workplaces of servants, were often early exercises in functional design by default, since they were not given any particular aesthetic attention.
In living spaces, the role of the fireplace and mantel diminished, giving way to a small coal grate, a “parlor stove,” and finally to a hot-air register inserted where the fireplace opening would have been.
The Regency and the Greek Revival style that followed it can be thought of as ending the sequence of stylistic developments dating back to antiquity.
The changes brought about by the Industrial Revolution upset this long continuity in design history.
Social and economic changes relating to the mechanization of so many aspects of production created new circumstances that designers struggled to deal with.
The Victorian era, the subject of the following chapter, is marked by the successes and failures of the efforts to come to terms with new realities.
The Victorian Era CHAPTER TWELVE A.
W.
N.
Pugin, St.
Giles Church, Cheadle, Staffordshire, England, 1846.
For pious Victorians—and most were—Gothic Revival church interiors became the inspiration for the decoration of their homes.
In 1815, Britain defeated Napoleonic France to end the Napoleonic Wars (1803–15) and became the dominant world power.
Naval supremacy secured trading links to its empire and to the raw materials that fed the factories that drew country dwellers to its booming cities and towns.
Factory work, however brutish, offered a fragile financial security that the uncertainties of country life could not.
Industrialized Britain gave the rest of the world a model for post-agrarian society and political power and social influence began to shift from land-owning aristocrats to self-made captains of industry.
With the rise of the middle class, the history of interior design, which had been about the aggrandizement of church, state and status quo, was shaped by individuals with aesthetic and social aspirations.
In growing industrial cities and towns, the new economic migrants needed housing.
Speculators seized the opportunity to build terraces or row houses and tenements appropriate to their occupants’ status and income.
Exteriors were simple in the Georgian manner but, apart from rudimentary moldings, the new dwellings were empty shells—it was left to their occupants to decorate and furnish them.
New wealth, however modest, meant that women who had worked long hours on family farms and in cottage industries became full-time housewives and responsible for the decoration of their homes.
Decorating options offered to country dwellers by local artisans and passing peddlers were few but in the new conurbations, shops specializing in household furnishings appeared.
Householders made their money in factories and, in a virtuous circle, spent it on factory products.
The philosophizing economist Adam Smith declared at the beginning of the industrializing of production methods that “consumption is the sole end and purpose of all production” and a symbiotic relationship between consumers and manufacturers began to change the nature of what was produced and what was bought.
Popular taste became prevailing taste.

## VICTORIAN
STYLE In 1837, the eighteen-year-old Princess Victoria of Kent became queen.
Her youth, gender, overt piety and enthusiasm for domesticity encouraged a reaction against Georgian decadence along with an enthusiasm for religious debate and practice.
It was presumed that the success of the country and its empire resulted from Christian values.
Indeed, The Secret of England’s Greatness (c.
1862–63), a painting by Thomas Jones Barker, depicts Queen Victoria presenting a kneeling African potentate with a Bible, which was deemed to be a handbook for civilized behavior and prosperity.

## Gothic
Revival in Britain As political self-confidence grew, Britain became doubtful about the pagan Neoclassical architectural traditions borrowed from continental Europe.
It wanted something indigenous to mark its supremacy.
Gothic architecture had begun in twelfth-century France but Britain had its own variations.
Extant examples were overwhelmingly of religious buildings and that further validated the change of style.
Creative ingenuity adapted Gothic principles for the new building types such as railway stations, and monumental municipal and commercial buildings.
The beginnings of Gothic Revival architecture and design had coincided with the beginnings of the Industrial Revolution.
Horace Walpole (1717–97), a writer and art historian, designed Strawberry Hill House in Twickenham, London.
Building began in 1749 and the exterior showed evidence of Gothic influences but they were most evident in the interior, particularly in the fan vaulting of the Long Gallery.
Walpole, increasingly fascinated by medieval history, published the first Gothic novel, The Castle of Otranto, in 1764.
It prompted a genre, including Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein in 1818 and Bram Stoker’s Dracula in 1897.
Edgar Allan Poe and Henry James wrote Gothic horror novels in the United States.
In 1796, William Beckford (1760–1844), another writer and the author of the Gothic novel Vathek (1786), commissioned James Wyatt (1746–1813) to design Fonthill Abbey, an enormous country house on Salisbury Plain in Wiltshire (12.2).
It was a fanciful assemblage of battlements, pinnacles and towers with vast Gothic halls and a 276-feet (84-m) high tower above an octagonal vaulted chamber, a stage set in which the romance and dramas of medieval life could be relished.
Built largely in wood and stucco, it collapsed in a windstorm in 1825 and appropriately became a romantic ruin.
12.2 James Wyatt, south end of St.
Michael’s Gallery, Fonthill Abbey, Wiltshire England, from 1795.
This engraving, of 1823, shows the richness of detail achieved in the wood and stucco construction, the plaster simulation of fan vaulting, the stained glass and the tracery.
However, the proportions, the windows with clear glass and transom, and the shallow arch suggest that there was no serious intention to replicate a Gothic interior.
A young architect and author, Augustus Welby Northmore Pugin (1812–52), took Gothic architecture more seriously and wrote Contrasts (1836), The True Principles of Pointed or Christian Architecture (1841), and further polemics in which illustrations made comparisons between classical and Gothic styles of architecture, always to the disadvantage of the former.
The intensity of Pugin’s attack and his moralistic tone set off the Battle of the Styles, in which Greek and Gothic revivalists vehemently aired their conflicting opinions.
Most architects and designers were happy to work in whatever style clients might request.
However, Pugin, the purist, argued against the trivial interpretations of Walpole and Beckford, for whom Gothic had been about romantic escapism, and made his case on moral and philosophical grounds.
Pugin and his camp prevailed.
Gothic Revival was confirmed as the new national style when a fire destroyed the Houses of Parliament in 1834 and Charles Barry (1795–1860) won a competition to design a replacement.
He was a Neoclassicist but was encouraged, it is said by Queen Victoria, to elevate in a Neo-Gothic style.
Pugin, who had made the drawings for Barry’s entry, was given responsibility for designing the interiors and comprehensively decorated every surface with color, pattern and carving, and topped every opening with a pointed arch (12.3 and 12.4).

## 12.3 A. W. N. Pugin, New Palace of Westminster (Houses of Parliament), House of Lords, Lon
don, 1836–60.
A richness of color and carving surpassed Gothic precedents and banished the comparative restraint of the Regency period.
It was an exuberant expression of Britain’s emergence as the dominant world power of the nineteenth century.
Charles Barry and A.
W.
N.
Pugin, New Palace of Westminster (Houses of Parliament), House of Lords, London, 1836–60.
A serious treatment of Gothic principles by the style’s greatest advocates.
The great chamber with its traceried stained glass, the arched windows and paneled ceiling are convincing replications of Gothic originals.
Pugin established his own practice and was prolific, as only a high-minded Victorian could be.
He brought an intensity of Gothic decoration to the forty churches (12.1) and six cathedrals he designed before he died at the age of forty.
He poured out Gothic Revival designs for furniture, metalwork, ceramics, stained glass, embroideries and wallpapers for his buildings and for manufacturers who recognized the growing popularity of all things Gothic.
He made time to address the social problems that were byproducts of industrialization and, in 1841, published Contrasted Residences of the Poor.
In a pair of drawings, he contrasted bleak, nineteenth-century workhouses, their meager food, harsh discipline, and paupers’ graves, with the glories of a medieval abbey.
He proposed that the latter provided accommodation and spiritual guidance, nourishing food, and the dignity of Christian burial.
Gothic values and Gothic style could, he asserted, solve the problems of industrialization.
When Gothic Revival churches were built precisely to architects’ instructions, they often lacked the vitality that came from slow building by generations of craftsworkers, each making their idiosyncratic contribution.
The work of William Butterfield (1814–1900) was not as stylistically correct as Pugin’s but its divergences make it interesting.
His church, All Saints (1849–59) in London, has patterned bands of differently hued red bricks, glazed brick tiles, and various marbles laid in geometric patterns.
It has something of the vigor of Victorian buildings in which Gothic devices are reinterpreted for secular purposes (12.5).
William Butterfield, All Saints, Margaret Street, London, 1849–59.
Butterfield’s work has an energy and originality that goes beyond mere conscientious replication.
The great arches and buttressing half arches have a raw strength that is counterpointed by the colorful wall and floor tiles typical of many Victorian interiors.
The British government was worried that revolution would incubate in factories and slums.
So, to strengthen the restraining hand of religion, it financed the building and refurbishment of 2,859 churches between 1841 and 1870.
Not attending church risked social exclusion at higher social levels and unemployment at the lowest.
Once food and shelter have been secured, human instinct has been to accumulate and decorate—to paint their caves.
If the restraint of the Regency interior had contrasted with the period’s social decadence then Victorians’ domestic overindulgences contrasted with their social restraints.
Gothic Revival church interiors sanctioned congregants’ natural impulse to decorate and the Victorian interior became synonymous with excess.
Inspired by the spectacles of church architecture and fired by an instinct to match and better the homes of their neighbors, Victorian householders went shopping.

## Shopping
Shopping took its first steps to becoming a leisure activity when retailers recognized the value of treating customers to spectacle.
It began in 1838 in Paris with the towering central hall of Le Bon Marché, which provided entertainments for children and a reading room for men content to leave their wives to enjoy the rigors of buying (12.6).
The Bon Marché name was subsequently borrowed by imitators offering varying degrees of splendor but the more ambitious borrowed the idea of spectacle.
In 1855, Robert Wylie and William Lochhead offered the citizens of Glasgow a hall, 200 feet (61 m) long and 70 feet (21 m) high, which was so popular that they issued free tickets to control the numbers of Saturday crowds.
Whiteleys in London had a central hall 300 feet (91.5 m) long.
In 1875, Liberty & Co., designed in Tudor style, grouped its sales areas around a five-story void (12.7).
The specialist London furniture store, Gillows carried a collection of historical furniture that, it claimed, offered an educational experience better than that of any museum.
Its workshop reproduced designs from the pattern books of the distinguished eighteenth-century designers, Chippendale, Hepplewhite and Sheraton.
It became a byword for good taste, mentioned in novels by Jane Austen and William Makepeace Thackeray, and an operetta by Gilbert and Sullivan.
Shopping could indeed be educational.
In the German writer Thomas Mann’s novel Confessions of Felix Krull (1954), the young Krull studied the windows of luxury stores to learn the details of taste that would ease his access to the layers of society on which he aimed to prey.
12.6 Louis-Charles Boileau and Gustave Eiffel, Le Bon Marché, Paris, 1876.
Grand stairways lead to the store’s upper level.
The slim iron structure allows views of the spectacul ar central aspace and supports the glass roof.
Customers found the store a source of entertainment.
Edwin T.
Hall and Edwin S.
Hall, Liberty & Co., London, 1875.
Liberty & Co. began by selling Japanese and Indian fabrics and objets d’art.
The timber structure of the central atrium suggested the medieval values of the Arts and Crafts movement.
Irish writer Oscar Wilde called it “the chosen resort of the artistic shopper.” As stores became more specialist, so the customers who were increasingly eager to take advice became “clients” but commercial prudence ensured that advice did not stray far from popular taste.
In 1873, the House Furnisher magazine suggested that the “true upholsterer” was “as trusted an agent in many homes as are the family lawyer and doctor.” Stores learned how to address their markets; even shoppers with a Victorian’s thirst for ornament seemed to sense that a sparse window display, with no indication of prices, denoted quality and good taste.
Stores at the cheap end of the market packed their windows and flaunted low prices.
In London, a secondhand furniture market had emerged in the eighteenth century and grown throughout the nineteenth.
Tudor pieces were popular; more readily available than genuine Gothic, they represented another part of England’s heritage.
Some stores opened antique sections.
Harrods had a gallery for antique, secondhand, and contemporary furniture.
Heal and Son, which would become a specialist in modern twentieth-century furniture, began by combining antique furniture and contemporary fabrics.
Since women were responsible for the decoration of their homes, it might be argued that the Victorian domestic interior is a feminine creation but The Gentleman’s House, a guide to the strategies and tactics of home decoration published in 1865, advised: the dining room should have an air of “masculine importance” and the drawing room should be “entirely ladylike.” The paterfamilias entertained his peers in the dining room and the materfamilias entertained hers in the drawing room (12.8).
Richard Norman Shaw, drawing room, Swan House, Chelsea Embankment, London, 1876.
A Victorian middle-class interior with antiquarian elements—Queen Anne chairs and a Georgian spinning wheel (left).
New pieces show early evidence of the emerging reaction against the decorative excesses of factory-made objects in favor of the handmade.

## A Great
Exhibition In 1851, Britain had chosen to demonstrate the superiority of its industries and the breadth and wealth of its empire with The Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations, or Great Exhibition.
It did so confident that its exhibits would surpass those of any other country rash enough to take part.
The exhibition building became known as the “Crystal Palace” (12.9) and was an enormous prefabricated cast-iron and glass structure designed by Joseph Paxton (1803– 65), a pioneering designer of greenhouses for aristocrats and municipalities.
With its barrelvaulted roof, it was evidently not Gothic Revival and, to Victorians, it seemed starkly utilitarian.
To modern eyes, drawings of its molded iron constructional details illustrate how far decoration was considered an integral component in any building, even a work of innovative engineering.
Joseph Paxton, Crystal Palace, London, 1851.
This prefabricated cast-iron framed, glazed building, seen in a contemporary lithograph, housed the Great Exhibition, the showcase of Victorian prosperity and taste.
The simplicity of the iron structure, glass walls and roof contrast with the elaborately decorated goods and classical statuary on display.
The large tree predated the building and remained after it was dismantled.
Pugin could not approve of the non-Gothic structure but consented to design the Medieval Court (12.10) exhibit and furnished it with objects in Gothic Revival style to his own design.
Although a philosophical medievalist, Pugin happily took advantage of manufacturing innovations.
Artifacts for his ecclesiastical interiors were assembled from generic components, produced to his design by his preferred metalworkers—Victorians were pragmatic.
A third of the British population visited the exhibition and were further convinced of their country’s supremacy by the audacity of Paxton’s building and the machinery it contained.
A.
W.
N.
Pugin, the Medieval Court, the Great Exhibition, Crystal Palace, London, 1851.
Whatever doubts he had about the Crystal Palace’s structure, Pugin overcame them to make his case for Gothic virtues at the Great Exhibition The importance for the economy of the burgeoning interiors market was recognized by government.
Design schools were established in industrial centers to support local manufacturers.
In 1856, the architect, designer, and theorist Owen Jones (1809–74) produced his The Grammar of Ornament (12.12), a compendium of decorative motifs from across the world adapted for the convenience of any manufacturers who cared to use them.
Critics and theorists, inevitably, considered that the glory of Gothic was being compromised as manufacturers competed to flood the market.
Owen Jones, The Grammar of Ornament, 1856.
One of the pages dealing with Egyptian ornament—original motifs are simplified and colored, made suitable for decorating industrial products, particularly fabrics and ceramics.
The acceptance that the practical should be overlaid by decoration was demonstrated in Queen Victoria’s private railroad car, which was opulently upholstered and trimmed with Neo- Gothic woodwork.
Fringed and tasseled curtains shut out evidence that Her Majesty was speeding along behind a locomotive that was designed for maximum operating efficiency and decorated by no more than a few painted stripes (12.11).
The dressing up of the utilitarian is often derided as a denial of reality but in 1979 Lance Wright, editor of the British magazine Designers Journal, wondered if it “might be possible ‘to accept the advantages of industrial production without feeling any need to express the thing as itself’ as the Victorians had done.” 12.11 Queen Victoria’s Royal Saloon (railroad car), 1869.
The major Victorian technological advance of the railroads came face to face with Victorian taste in interior design.
In the queen’s private railroad car, surfaces are padded and quilted, draperies are fringed, furniture is elaborately carved and sumptuously upholstered, and lamp shades are fringed.

## Aristocrats
and Plutocrats Aristocrats were not immune to Gothic Revival.
Despite the rise of the industrial barons, they still dominated politics, had, generally, lost none of their wealth, and embraced the style when building new.
The most enthusiastic was John Patrick Crichton-Stuart, 3rd Marquess of Bute, who was rich from owning the port of Cardiff that exported coal from the mines of South Wales, which he also owned.
He appointed the architect William Burgess (1827–81) to create Cardiff Castle and Castell Coch, a summer residence in a wooded landscape, a few miles outside the city.
Work began on the former in 1868 and the latter in 1875.
Both were built on and incorporated the remains of small Norman forts but were examples of Gothic Revival although details were filtered through nineteenth-century processes and perceptions.
Thomas Nicholls’s craved heraldic William Burgess, the summer smoking room, Cardiff Castle, Cardiff, Wales, 1873.
The Gothic spirit survived in a grand nineteenth-century house but the wall paintings and carvings are more nineteenthcentury Pre-Raphaelite than medieval Gothic.
When the Marquess’s principal home, Mount Stuart House, on the Isle of Bute, Scotland, burnt down in 1877, he employed Robert Rowand Anderson (1834–1921) to design a replacement (12.14).
Burgess designed the oratory.
Mount Stuart was on a grander scale than the Welsh buildings and incorporated the world’s first domestic heated swimming pool.
While detail remains Gothic-inspired, the massing, with its strong horizontal emphasis, was not.
In the colonnaded top-lit marble hall at the center of the house and the oratory polished marbles were used in place of the less decorative local stones that would have been used in medieval Gothic.
Robert Rowand Anderson, Mount Stuart House, Isle of Bute, Scotland, 1879–1900.
A late interpretation of Gothic Revival with plans, elevations, and materials evolving to meet contemporary domestic priorities.
In Ireland, Edward William Godwin (1833–86) made extensive examinations of Irish castles before designing Dromore Castle in County Limerick for the Earl of Limerick (12.15).
However, when completed in 1874, the finished building with its turrets, tall chimneys and gables bore more resemblance to castles on the Rhine than Ireland’s modest precedents.
Godwin designed all the furniture and fittings that, along with the wall paintings, are conspicuously nineteenth century.
Edward Godwin, Dromore Castle, County Limerick, Ireland, 1870–4.
A drawing for a dining-room sideboard and wall decoration in a free interpretation of Gothic form with wall painting that is unmistakably nineteenth century.
Not all aristocrats agreed on the merits of Gothic.
When building Castle Ward in Northern Ireland, between 1761 and 1767, Bernard Ward, Lord Bangor, had indulged the enthusiasm of his wife, Lady Anne Magill, by splitting the house along its long axis.
Half, on the pedimented entrance side, remained Palladian and the other was adapted to satisfy her yearning for the Gothic.

## Other
British Revivalist Styles Other revivalist styles found favor.
Wealthy industrials, merchants and bankers aspired to have houses that matched those of the nobility but they took the great, non-aristocratic Tudor, Jacobean, and Carolean houses as models.
Half-timbered gables, battlements, and clock towers were popular.
Ruins were sometimes incorporated into new structures to suggest pedigree.
Architects and decorators were knowledgeable about historical styles although, as with the murals and carvings in Cardiff Castle and Castel Coch, prevailing stylistic predilections asserted themselves and there were novel activities and social mechanisms to be accommodated.
The communal life of the medieval great halls was superseded by drawing rooms, dining rooms, libraries, batteries of guest bedrooms, and servants’ wings.
The most imposing example of the genre was Cragside near Rothbury, Northumberland, built for the industrialist William Armstrong, an armaments manufacturer and amateur scientist whose interests included hydraulics and electricity.
He had been seduced by a potential building site on the side of a moorland crag and had a house with eight bedrooms, a modest “shooting box,” designed by an unknown hand and completed in the mid-1860s.
It was well built, but Armstrong wanted something grander, a place to entertain the potentates and military men who were his customers, so he employed Richard Norman Shaw (1831–1912) to extend the box and begin its slow but spectacular evolution.
A narrow ledge was dynamited to accommodate successive additions that were stacked on the cliffside like an Italian hillside village but the architectural language is undeniably English and Tudor, a collage of half-timbered gables and towers.
Armstrong required that the shooting box be retained as the core of the extended house so the interior meandered as it became grander.
Most reception rooms and their accompanying service rooms were on the ground floor apart from the extension built for a visit by the Prince of Wales (later Edward VII) in 1884.
Royalty traditionally announced its intention to visit well in advance and hosts usually felt the obligation to impress.
The Cragside library of 1872, with oak half-height panels and packed with heavy dark wooden furniture, is generally considered to be Shaw’s finest interior (12.16).
Cragside was designed and built between 1869 and 1884.
Both client and architect, and the designers they engaged, were aware of the growing opposition in aesthetic circles to the decorative excesses of the Victorian interior.
The scale of the building militated against delicate domesticity.
As Armstrong’s art collection grew, so his museum became his gallery, remodeled as a processional route to the drawing room and its huge marble inglenook fireplace (12.17) designed by William Richard Lethaby (1857–1931), Shaw’s assistant, who would go on to pioneer the preservation of ancient buildings (12.18).
Armstrong introduced water-generated electricity to power lighting and early examples of household appliances such as a vacuum cleaner, a washing machine, and dishwasher.
Excess heat from the Turkish bath helped warm the house.
12.16 Richard Norman Shaw, Cragside, Rothbury, Northumberland, England, 1872.
The library, considered to be Shaw’s greatest interior, with half-height oak paneling and coffered ceiling.
Richard Norman Shaw, Cragside, Rothbury, Northumberland, England, 1884.
The great inglenook fireplace in the dining room.
12.18 Drawing of Cragside, c.
1883.
This drawing by W.
R.
Lethaby of Richard Norman Shaw’s proposal for a chimney breast indicates how Shaw used local vernacular details to create his own version of nineteenth-century English design, which projected a sense of the traditional without direct imitation.
In Cheshire, John Tollemache, 1st Baron Tollemache, employed Anthony Salvin (1799–1881) to build Peckforton Castle (1844–50) in a convincing interpretation of a medieval castle with a round tower, a stone-vaulted great hall and chapel, but with a billiard room, schoolroom and bathroom located next to the master’s chamber.
John Norton (1823–1904) remodeled Elveden in Suffolk around 1870 in a potpourri of styles.
It was owned by the Maharajah Duleep Singh, who had Norton replace the Georgian classical exterior with something more ornately Italianate and recreate the interiors in the Indian Mughal style.
It was bought in 1896 by Edward Guinness, 1st Earl of Iveagh, who appointed the director of London’s Victoria and Albert Museum, Caspar Purdon Clarke (1846–1911), and an architect, William Young (1843–1900), to transform what became known as the Indian Hall in Mughal style (12.19).
Indian Hall, Elveden Hall, Suffolk, England, c.
1896.
The room was remodeled in what was considered to be an Indian style, in tribute to its previous owner, an Indian maharajah.

## UNITED
STATES: VICTORIAN VARIATIONS Just as Britain moved on from Regency Neoclassicism, so there was reluctance in the United States to continue with the Greek Revivalism that had symbolized the country’s republican independence.
As in England, taste was swayed by romantic Gothic novels and reproductions of work by the English Pre-Raphaelite painters, who were themselves inspired by medieval values and techniques.
It is a reflection of Britain’s nineteenth-century pre-eminence and its totemic queen that architecture and design of the period in the United States is described as “Victorian.” The emancipated thirteen states continued to share British tastes in matters of interior decoration and items imported from Britain and Europe were particularly valued.
Where these were unobtainable or too expensive, Americans improvised.
Visiting Britons, perhaps still annoyed by their defeat in the American Revolutionary War (1775–83), were, like Fanny Trollope in her Domestic Manners of the Americas (1832), not always appreciative of their efforts.
Yet American energy and ambitions accelerated the development of homegrown industries.
In addition, a drift from country to town and city saw rural families become urban, farmers and farmers’ sons become business owners, managers and professionals.
Prosperous urbanites, like those in Britain, were able and willing to improve their homes and, as the market grew, the flow of imports from Europe increased.
In return, the New World provided fast-sailing Yankee Clipper ships to speed up ocean trade and McCormick reapers to replace farmhands who had gone to work in factories.

## Gothic
Revival Richard Upjohn (1802–78) was born and trained as a cabinetmaker in England and his Trinity Church (1839–46) on Wall Street in New York is a convincing version of an English Gothic parish church (12.20).
Its vaulted nave, stained glass, and decorative detail gave Americans their first serious experience of Gothic.
Other specialists in Gothic design emerged.
In 1843, James Renwick (1818–95) won a competition with a Gothic proposal to design Grace Church on Broadway in New York, a rival to Trinity Church, with another accurate recreation of an English Gothic church.
Renwick’s most important Gothic Revival work, St.
Patrick’s Cathedral in New York, was completed in 1878.
This was modeled on French Gothic examples, complete with cruciform-plan aisles and ambulatory, clerestory and stained glass.
The vaulting appears to be stone but is papiermâché and the flying buttresses needed to resist the thrust of stone vaulting were omitted.
Richard Upjohn, Trinity Church, New York, 1846.
A carefully detailed impression of an English medieval parish church.
Upjohn had wanted to design a church with a simple timber roof but his clients wanted vaulting and papier-mâché was used to imitate stone.
The window tracery and stained glass adds conviction to the illusion.
As in Britain, Gothic Revival quickly spread across architecture and interior design.
Renwick designed the main building of the Smithsonian Institute (1844–46) in Washington, D.C., which also takes inspiration from medieval examples, with a Romanesque and Norman exterior and a Gothic interior.
The firm of Town and Davis, alert to the shift in popular taste, abandoned Greek Revival and Alexander Jackson Davis became particularly enthusiastic about Gothic Revival.
In Lyndhurst, a large house in Tarrytown, New York overlooking the Hudson River (1838–65) he applied Gothic elements, including an impressive tower (12.21).
The plan was originally symmetrical but when he enlarged it in 1864 it became picturesquely asymmetric.
Most rooms are filled with Gothic details: plaster ceiling ribs that suggested vaulting, pointed windows with stone tracery and stained glass, and much carved ornamental detail.
The combined billiard room and art gallery had a wooden roof structure that suggested a baronial hall and Davis designed Gothicstyle furniture including wheelback chairs with carved backs that suggested the tracery of rose windows, a dining table with Gothic carving, and beds with massive, pointed arch heads and footboards.
Town and Davis, Lyndhurst, Tarrytown, New York, 1838–65.
The interiors add conviction to the Gothic Revival exterior.
Pointed arches, paneling, tracery and crockets, and the furniture, all executed in wood, complement the stained glass.
Ralph Adams Cram (1863–1942) was, as Pugin had been, a protagonist for the virtues of Gothic design and a skilled practitioner in the style.
In his book Church Building (1901), he argued for the virtues of medieval English Gothic, illustrated examples of excellence, and criticized what he considered to be poor work.
His design for All Saints (1891) in Dorchester, Massachusetts, is an accurate recreation of a typical English parish church.
Cram and his firm, Cram, Goodhue and Ferguson, became successful designers of Gothic churches and Tudor Gothic groupings for college campuses.
The term “Collegiate Gothic” came into use to describe such work.
They designed a number of buildings for Princeton University, including interiors for the refectory and chapel.
The firm’s large St.
Thomas Church (1906–13) in New York has an impressive interior, with stone vaulting, stained glass, and a tall sculptured reredos that combines details from many Gothic precedents.
The landscape gardener, Andrew Jackson Downing (1815–52) wrote Cottage Residences (1842) and The Architecture of Country Houses (1850) with engravings showing plans and perspectives of houses in a range of sizes and variety of styles, including a simplified version of Gothic suitable for wooden construction.
Carpenter Gothic was produced by local builders, who used a scroll saw to cut pointed arch forms in wood.
Exterior walls were given vertical emphasis with board and batten sidings, pointed arch windows often with leaded glass inserts, elaborately carved eaves, and pointed window heads dignified buildings of local importance such as churches and railway stations.
They became as evocative of small town, rural America as the dungarees and pitchfork in Grant Wood’s painting American Gothic (1930).
There were other indigenous variations.
Italianate drew on Northern Italian sources and was distinguished by shallow-hipped roofs, porches, loggias, and sometimes a small tower, often of wooden construction with wooden columns and carvings.
Mansardic, sometimes called “General Grant style,” was inspired by the almost vertical French Mansard roof, generally visible from the street, with cast iron or wooden decorative trim on the lower floors.
It was popular for public buildings in bigger towns.
Queen Anne or Queen Anne Revival was influenced by English Arts and Crafts developments and involved asymmetrical elements, such as bay windows.
Decoration was provided by different brick types, stained glass, and terracotta moldings.

## American
Homes The newly rich, manufacturers, entrepreneurs, and speculators, built big houses and packed them with objects, often in a random confection of styles.
Hard-earned wealth was considered worth flaunting.
Samuel Colt, inventor of the revolver, built a large house in a vaguely Italian manner and embellished it with Moorish domes.
The landscape painter Frederick E.
Church, assisted by the English architect and landscape designer Calvert Vaux (1824–95), designed his own house in what he considered to be a Persian style.
In 1857, Vaux published the Villas and Cottages pattern book, which offered illustrations of external and internal ornamental detail for thirty-nine houses, from modest cottages to enormous mansions.
The American farmhouse moved from symmetry and classical detail toward picturesque irregular plans and the plain homes of early settlers began to fill with the decorative indulgences of the affluent East Coast.
In industrial centers, houses for workers were arranged in rows: twinned or semidetached houses were for the better paid, while larger, single-family houses on their own plots in the manner of modern suburbia were for managers.
Such houses, whether for sale or rent, were built by speculators who understood the importance of decoration.
Books and manuals offered factory-made ornamental details to prettify interiors.
In comparatively modest houses, elaborately carved and upholstered furniture stood on boldly patterned carpets.
Factory-made objects—cast-iron stoves and harmoniums (12.22)—came ready-encrusted with ornament.
In expensive dwellings, elaborate paneling, mantelpieces, stair rails, and moldings were enriched further by strongly patterned wallpapers and fabrics.
Oil lamps, the primary source of artificial light, had intricate brass bases and colored glass shades.
For Victorians, empty spaces cried out to be filled and the “what-not,” an open-shelved display unit, provided extra space for ornaments.
Pictures and prints in intricately carved and gilded frames offered sentimental depictions of children and landscapes.
Small plaster figures by specialist modelers such as John Rogers (1829– 1904) depicted scenes of love and loss.
Mason and Hamlin, harmonium, 1876.
A Victorian harmonium (a reed organ) displayed at the Philadelphia Centennial Exhibition—ornamental details typical of Carpenter Gothic overwhelm functional necessity.
Even the convention of the rectangular room fell victim to gratuitous complication, which prompted a short-lived fad for octagonal houses.
The eight sides of the Armour-Stiner House (1860) in Irvington, New York, were skirted by a porch with florid cast-iron columns and railings and a dome topped by a cupola, topped by a spire.
Octagonal plans led inevitably to strange little triangular rooms, expediently designated as libraries and music rooms.
In the larger cities, even for the better off, row houses (12.23) replaced detached houses on their own plots.
The uniformity and monumentality of New York and Boston’s brownstones and Philadelphia and Baltimore’s brick rows established a civic structure that, when planted with trees, dignified urban living.
Houses began to benefit from technical innovations: central heating (usually by ducted warm air), gas lighting, bathrooms and kitchens with piped hot running water, coal, and later, gas cooking ranges, and iceboxes.
Storage cupboards and dressing spaces next to bedrooms, often with wash basins and running water, became staples.
Better houses had built-in marble surfaces and ornamental stairs climbed through three or four floors.
Servants moved unseen through narrow backstairs.
Doors and windows were tall and narrow to emphasize ceiling height but daylight was restricted by heavy drapes and permanently drawn net curtains.
Oil and gas lamps provided modest illumination but dark hues of browns, olive greens, and mauves 12.23 Blakeley Hall House, New York, 1896.
The hall of this typical row house on West 45th Street shows a characteristic late Victorian interior with dark woodwork, dull wallpapers and a profusion of draperies, carpets and upholstered furniture.
The elaborate newel post at the bottom of the stair sets the tone.

## A Centennial
Exhibition In Philadelphia, in 1876, with the Centennial Exhibition, the United States was ready to demonstrate what it had achieved in the hundred years since taking its independence.
Exhibits included a working example of a steam engine big enough to power a city’s pumping station and delicate decorative objects for the home.
A small organ, suitable for a Victorian parlor, was encrusted with inlays and carvings but described by a contemporary critic, Walter Smith, as “free from all the abortions in the shape of ornament with which many pretentious instruments are disfigured”.
Excess is in the eye of the beholder and determined at the time of the beholding.
The unpretentious organ and much of the furniture exhibited would have been classified as Eastlake, after Charles Locke Eastlake (1836–1906), an English architect influenced by the growing reaction in English aesthetes against what was seen as over-decorated factory-made products.
His book Hints on Household Taste in Furniture, Upholstery and Other Details (1868) influenced aspirational American householders and argued for simplicity but its illustrations showed Victorian excess (12.24).

## 12.24 Charles Locke Eastlake, dining-room sideboard, 1874. Eastlake, a journalist, nurture
d his readers’ taste and promoted his own designs.
An Arts and Crafts bias is evident in his work.
The sideboard shown is from Hints on Household Taste in Furniture, Upholstery and Other Details (1868), and is modified by the extensive display of ornamental ceramics.

## Later
American Indigenous Styles

## Shingle
While masonry or rubble might serve as ground-floor construction, exterior walls and roofs were generally timber framed and clad in cedarwood shingles that weathered to gray.
Exterior ornament was usually simple but building forms were often complex, with gables, projecting wings, porches, dormer windows, rounded bays, turrets, and towers.
Internally, wooden paneling, grand fireplaces, and nooks with built-in sofas replicated the cozy complexities of English Queen Anne style.
A few hotels, casinos and clubhouses used Shingle techniques, and acquired informal charm.

## Adirondack
As rail travel improved, mountainous landscape and cooler weather offered alternatives to summers in the city.
The Adirondacks were accessible from East Coast cities and a romantic pastiche of frontier living evolved with cabins and lodges as summer homes for hunters and fishers.
Toward the end of the century, the rusticity of the first simple dwellings evolved to become the Adirondack style.
Oversized, rough stone fireplaces dominated rooms, timber-clad walls were left to find their natural color, rugs and cloth wall hangings, oil lamps and hunting trophies added to the illusion (12.25).
Furniture often incorporated tree branches with bark intact for added rusticity.
12.25 Camp Cedars, Forked Lake, Adirondacks, New York, 1886.
The “camps” built for summer-vacation houses in the mountains were often luxurious but flaunted faux rusticity with rough stone fireplaces and furniture of rough-hewn timbers.
The lanterns, fans, and curios were more typical of Victorian taste.

## Shaker
Shakers emigrated from England in 1774 to escape religious persecution.
They founded agricultural communities and members shared property and work in a simple form of communism.
Large dwellings provided separate accommodation for males and females.
The communities chose to isolate themselves from neighboring settlements, constructed their own buildings and, as far as they could produced what they needed from agriculture and in their workshops.
Their religious beliefs forbade “worldly” ostentation and favored efficient application of human effort, which led them to produce objects of great simplicity and functional excellence.
By 1830, they had evolved their essentials and thereafter their dwellings and objects conformed to those meticulous standards.
Their interiors had white walls and dark wooden floors, benches, chairs, tables, cupboards and cabinets, were enriched by subtle proportions and detail (12.26).
Banks of built-in drawers provided storage and pegs on high wooden rails carried cloaks, hats and chairs, which made floor cleaning more efficient.
The regular and repetitious organization of drawers provided pattern that satisfied, at a fundamental level, the human need for decoration.
Shaker Village, Hancock, New York, c.
1820.
The bedroom of an elder or eldress in the communal residence contains a rope bed and wooden washstand.
The wood burning stove incorporates a Shaker invention, an upper smoke box that extracts extra heat from chimney gases.
The wooden trim is painted in a tone the Shakers called “Heavenly Blue.” Shakers advanced no aesthetic theory but achieved collective excellence, perhaps by subordinating the egos that drive designers who are less spiritual.
They offered some products for sale, ladderback chairs, rocking chairs and side chairs, all assembled from simple wooden components and these achieved surprising popularity given their divergence from the norms of Victorian taste, a popularity that contrasts with the failure of the later Arts and Crafts movement in England to find a substantial market.
Arts and Crafts artifacts were perhaps too much of an intellectual construct, too much the product of individual activists with individual perceptions, and Arts and Crafts designers handed over their designs to the craftsworkers who would make them.
It has been suggested that designers who did not make could not properly understand the potential of the materials they specified.
Shakers made and understood.
The contradictions and problems of the Victorian era did not go unnoticed, and eventually movements dedicated to reform emerged.
The most effective and interesting of these movements is the subject of the following chapter.

## INSIGHTS

## The
Shaker Philosophy The austerity of the Shaker lifestyle was expressed in a series of Millennial Laws governing everything from behavior, Ye shall have no talking, laughing, sneering, winking, blinking, hanging and lounging on the railings, hugging, fumbling and fawning over each other when going to the table1 to decorative finishes, Beadings, moldings and cornices which are merely for fancy may not be made by believers.2 Elder William Denning, a mid-nineteenth-century Shaker builder noted for his work on the Church Family Dwelling at Hancock, Massachusetts, commented on the Shaker habit of preserving neatness by suspending chairs and clothes from wooden pegs: we hang everything but people and that we leave for the world to do.3 The Shakers’ opinion of the furnishings of the outside world is captured by a report made by one member from Massachusetts on a visit to Harvard in 1850: I think they have gathered into their habitations too much furniture which belongs to Babylon!
Mother [Ann Lee] used to say “You may give such things to the moles and the bats.”4 1.
Millennial Laws of 1845, p.
33; 2.
Ibid, p.
92; 3.
Ibid, p.
168; 4.
Ibid, p.
168 CHAPTER THIRTEEN The Aesthetic Movements Philip Webb, Red House, Bexleyheath, Kent, England, 1859–60.
Webb designed the Red House for William Morris and this room contains typical Arts and Crafts details.
The white painted walls and a large bookcase and bench unit (called a settle) are Morris’s design.
The room incorporates a ladder (left) giving access to an attic.
The wall paintings are clearly Pre-Raphaelite.
The Shaker aesthetic evolved from interpretation of Christian doctrine dating to the eighteenth century and the renunciation of, what they considered to be, worldliness—the flaunting of unnecessary acquisitions.
Somehow, and collectively, they evolved artifacts that required no training in design or manufacture to appreciate them and to be moved by them.
The Victorians had their own interpretations of the same Christian doctrines, which they expressed through acquisition and display, but their artifacts found their roots in medieval ecclesiastical architecture.
Victorian taste was instinctive, ostentatious, and seen to be evidence of the fruits of honest labor.
Those fruits also supported a leisured class who had time to absorb elitist aesthetic sensibilities.
This leisured class was uncomfortable with popular taste and factory production, and gravitated to objects made by hand by skilled craftsworkers, usually to designs created by wealthy bohemians.
That work would come to be classified as Arts and Crafts.

## BRITAIN:
ARTS AND CRAFTS MOVEMENT The Victorian interior, bulging with artifacts, crossed barriers of class and income.
A description of a cottage parlor in a Welsh ironworks noted a “French-polished chest of drawers covered with a profusion of glass and other articles . . . a glass-fronted cupboard filled with china and glass and displaying ostentatiously silver sugar tongs and set of spoons . . . a mahogany table with a bright copper tea-kettle reposing on it.” In Britain, the children of early industrialists lived comfortably on the proceeds of their parents’ enterprise.
Some, disinclined or ill-equipped to join family businesses, declared themselves to be artistic.
They disparaged and despaired of popular taste and the factory-made objects designed to satisfy it.
These beneficiaries of nineteenth-century prosperity imagined that they could see virtues in living a simpler life, surrounded by handmade objects crafted by contented artisans.
Factories could make facsimiles of medieval objects but they thought mass production responding to popular taste was distorting Gothic purity, while handmade artifacts were easy to like because they eschewed excessive decoration, and hand crafting meant that they bore the physical marks of their production, which added an aura of authenticity.

## Arbiters
of Taste and Virtue Artistic gentlemen and social reformers, such as John Ruskin (1819–1900), remained enthusiasts for medievalism and a return to craft production by the nineteenth-century equivalents of medieval craft guilds that would hand down skills and safeguard aesthetic standards.
Ruskin was an independently wealthy patriarch able to pay for craft skills and could afford to believe that good design could not be produced by a machine.
He and like-minded reformers also presumed that by improving living and working conditions they would improve working-class morals.
He condemned retailers who, he said, deceived customers into buying aesthetically questionable items.
Home, he said, was “the place of Peace . . . a sacred place, a vestal temple, a temple of the hearth. . . .” He suggested “making all retail dealers salaried officers in the employ of trade guilds” who would dispense Ruskin-approved advice on taste.
Charles Eastlake (1836–1906) in Hints on Household Taste in Furniture, Upholstery and other Details (1868) also worried that an aesthetically innocent public were in danger of being exploited by shopkeepers.
Customers abetted by shopkeepers continued to buy what they liked, a Darwinian process in which the popular, however meretricious, survived.
For the less wealthy and less idealistic, machine-made wallpaper could transform a room cheaply and quickly but there were conventions: flock papers were appropriate for drawing rooms, sitting rooms, dining rooms and libraries; marble patterns with a gloss finish were correct for halls, stairwells and corridors; moire —suggestive of watered silks—or small-patterned flocks were favored in bedrooms.
W.
M.
Thackeray, the author of Vanity Fair (1838), writing in the British humorous magazine Punch in 1848 said, “. . . the public wants a thing, therefore it is supplied with it; or the public is supplied with a thing therefore it wants it.”

## Morris
William Morris (1834–1896) was the driving force of the Arts and Craft movement.
The son of a wealthy businessman, he was a typical young Victorian of independent means who presumed himself suited to artistic endeavor and became a poet, a novelist, a translator of Icelandic sagas and a socialist activist.
While a student at Oxford, he was inspired by the city’s medieval buildings and began to oppose industrialization.
Although he would become an atheist, he was influenced by Ruskin’s Christian Socialist writings and used his inherited wealth to set up rural craft communities.
In 1861 he formed a decorative-arts company with three Pre-Raphaelite painters Dante Gabriel Rosetti (1828–82), Edward Burne-Jones (1833–98), and Ford Madox Brown (1821–93).
They were unlikely businessmen but were joined by the engineer Peter Paul Marshall (1830– 1900), the academic Charles Faulkner (1833–92), and the architect Philip Webb (1831–1915).
They called themselves The Firm.
They were ideologically committed to craft techniques and explained to customers the vulgarity of the machine-made.
The Firm established itself as a radical purveyor of furniture, wood and stone carvings, metal work, stained glass, and murals.
It aspired to have handmade decoration accepted as a fine art and to introduce a guild to control the quality of artisan output.
It recruited apprentices from the Industrial Home for Destitute Boys in Euston, London.
Inevitably, given their backgrounds, the original partners diverged.
In 1859–60 Webb designed the Red House for Morris (13.1), who designed parts of the interior (13.2).
Philip Webb, Red House, Bexleyheath, Kent, England, 1859–60.
While the stretched newels of the stair and the elongated finials that crown them might be seen as Gothicisms, the simplicity of the solid banister, the exposed soffit of the stair, the simple architrave and skirting moldings all demonstrate a movement away from Gothic Revival flamboyance to an aesthetic shaped by Arts and Crafts principles.
The Firm became Morris and Co. and flourished under the patronage of artistically inclined and wealthy customers.
It was not the clientele Morris might have hoped for.
Around 1870, Webb designed a chair with an ingenious adjustable back that Morris and Co. manufactured.
It became known as the Morris chair (13.3) as it is not unknown for the partner with the higher profile—or indeed a husband in partnership with his wife—to be given credit for work produced in a partnership.
Phillip Webb, adjustable chair, manufactured by Morris & Co., England, c.
1870.
A precursor, in an early version, of the modern adjustable chair that became known as the Morris Chair because it was made by the firm founded by William Morris.
In the midst of setting up and funding social experiments, creating and funding the Kelmscott Press, for which he wrote twenty-three of the fifty-three handmade books it published, Morris designed the textiles and wallpapers (13.4) that made his reputation and continue to help sustain the press.
These were distinguished from other products of the period by their restrained simplification of plant forms.
William Morris, Pimpernel wallpaper design, manufactured by Jeffrey & Co., for Morris & Co., England, 1876.
The Pimpernel design, with its rich blues and greens could dominate any interior.

## Ashbee
The Arts and Crafts movement flourished and the Arts and Crafts Exhibition Society was formed in London in 1887.
It held its first show in 1888.
The same year, architect and designer Charles Robert Ashbee (1863–1942) established the Guild and School of Handicraft, a cooperative based on the model of a medieval guild, to train and improve the lot of a few disadvantaged inhabitants of London slums.
The guild employed around fifty men and, in 1902—still in pursuit of the ideal of a rural community of healthy, well-behaved artisans—relocated to the bucolic Cotswolds.
There, Ashbee designed jewelry and silverware that was made by craftsmen and proudly bore the marks of their hammers.
The objects were exquisite but expensive.
It is impossible to say if, had they cost less, their elegance would have triumphed over the market-led outpourings of industry.

## Voysey
The most complete and accomplished exponent of Arts and Crafts principles was the architect Charles Francis Annesley Voysey (1857–1941) who designed every fixture and fitting in the irresistibly pretty houses he created for prosperous middle-class clients.
Typical of these is Hollymount of 1907 in Knotty Green, Buckinghamshire, for which he designed all the furniture and fittings.
He made subtle variations on individual pieces so that his interiors seem to have been assembled over time—but by one discerning eye (13.5).
He worked extensively as a consultant to manufacturers over a wide range of products, from beautiful yet simple cast-iron fireplaces (13.6) to a comprehensive range of wallpapers, carpets, rugs, tiles, and textiles.
Like Morris, he favored “flatness” in motifs derived from nature, explaining that “an attempt at realism provokes [unfavorable] comparison with the subtleties of nature” (13.7).
13.5 Charles Francis Annesley Voysey, Hollymount, Knotty Green, Buckinghamshire, England, 1907.
Voysey designed the elements and furniture in his buildings to be simple but beautifully made in the Arts and Crafts tradition.
Each piece shared materials and detail but was unique, suggesting a long evolution rather than a single installation.
Charles Francis Annesley Voysey, Fireplace Number 647, Falkirk Iron Company, London, 1899.
13.6 Voysey’s exquisitely proportioned objects look modestly modern but seem to incorporate something timeless.
Charles Francis Annesley Voysey, wallpaper design, 1906.
This design with stylized roses, rosehips, and leaves illustrates Voysey’s principle of simplifying imagery to avoid unfavorable comparison with nature.
Robert W.
Edis (1839–1927) was an architect working in the Queen Anne vocabulary, but in his book Decoration and Furniture of Town Houses (1881) he illustrated interiors where Morris wallpaper and Godwin furniture were to be used (13.10).

## 13.10 Robert W. Edis, interior, London, 1881. This plate from Edis’s Decoration and Furnit
ure of Town Houses (1881) shows an interior with furniture by Edward Godwin, a frieze by Henry Stacy Marks and wallpaper by William Morris.
Edis was a proponent of the ideas of the Arts and Crafts and Aesthetic movements.
His book urged readers to follow the design lead shown by these movements and to adapt them for use in their own homes.

## Scott
Mackay Hugh Baillie Scott (1865–1945) was an architect and designer who, like Voysey, carried on the Arts and Crafts tradition deep into the twentieth century.
His design in c.
1914 for a music cabinet has painted decoration reminiscent of work by Morris.
He was not averse to stylistic shifts, and traveled from Neo-Tudor to Neo-Georgian by way of Arts and Crafts (13.8).
M.
H.
Baillie Scott, music cabinet, Marvel Hill, Witley, England, c.
1914.
Scott continued to design in the spirit of the Arts and Crafts movement well into the twentieth century.
This cabinet is covered with painted ornament in the manner that Morris had introduced fifty years earlier.

## Asian
Influences In 1853 the U.S. navy under Commodore Matthew Perry sailed their steam-powered, paddlewheeled frigate into Japanese waters with orders from President Millard Fillmore to oblige the Japanese to open their ports to American trade.
Coercion worked and Japanese goods began to filter through to the West.
For those in Britain who had had enough of Neo-Gothic excess the elegant restraint of Japanese artifacts offered an alluring alternative, even pieces produced for the Western market were made by artisans with traditional tools and skills and appeared to be suffused with a pagan spirituality that offered an alternative to the Christianity that shaped the nineteenth century’s social and cultural mores.
Edward Godwin, sideboard, London, England, c.
1870.
The influence of Japan is clear in the thin, ebonized mahogany frame and silver-plated handles.
Architect and designer Edward William Godwin (1833–86) deserted his polychromatic Neo-Gothic palette for ebonized finishes and delicate, fragile furniture.
(13.9).
