His Art Furniture Company produced furniture, textiles, wallpapers, and tiles, all influenced by Japanese examples, and were sold in Liberty & Co.
He designed a studio house for, and probably in collaboration with, James Abbott McNeill Whistler (1834–1903), an American painter infatuated with Japanese art.
Whistler had been involved in the decoration of the dining room in a London House that became known as the Peacock Room (13.13).
Originally created in 1876–7 by architect and designer Thomas Jeckyll (1927–81), another enthusiast for things Japanese, it had Godwin furniture, leather-covered walls and an intricate system of shelves idiosyncratically arranged to display Japanese blue and white porcelain.
Whistler painted the room, including its doors and window shutters, with decoration based on peacock feathers and called it A Harmony in Blue and Gold; he had called his portrait of his mother Arrangement in Gray and Black No.
1 (1871).
13.13 Thomas Jeckyll and James McNeill Whistler, Peacock Room, London, 1876–7.
Within this dining room, Whistler introduced Japanese themes into an Arts and Crafts environment.
The room, with shelves to display Japanese porcelain, had been designed by Jeckyll.
Whistler’s blue and gold wall painting was inspired by peacock feathers.
Peacock feathers were a popular device among artists and designers of the Aesthetic movement that marked the descent of Arts and Crafts into fey self-regard during the 1890s.
Its figureheads were the flamboyant playwright and arbiter of taste Oscar Wilde and artist Aubrey Beardsley whose drawings, undoubtedly influenced by Japanese prints, were—when not obscene —undoubtedly perverse.
Wilde was said to have complained, “I find it harder and harder every day to live up to my blue china,” at a time when imported blue china—from China—was definitively chic.
As a diligent aesthete, Wilde would have been distressed by the British designed and manufactured quasi-Chinese Willow Pattern range that was exceptionally popular in humble homes.
However degenerate its proponents might appear, the Aesthetic interior was ascetic, denying itself the visual gluttony that had devoured the High Victorian interior.
The author and cartoonist Sir Osbert Lancaster explained that “cheerful magentas and sulfur yellows were banished . . . in favor of sage green, peacock blue, and every variety of ocher.” Decadence was not confined to London.
In France, writer Joris-Karl Huysmans published his novel A Rebours (Against Nature, 1884), in which a reclusive aesthete, contemptuous of bourgeois society, retreated into a world of studied aestheticism—the interior of his home.
Huysmans wrote that it was about a man “seeking refuge in illusions of extravagant fantasy, living alone, far from his century, among memories of more congenial times, of less base surroundings.” The hero was said to be based on Robert de Montesquiou, a French count and aesthete who had curated his own world within his Paris home and who declared that “an apartment is a mood” so suggesting that an interior need not conform to prevailing taste but should defy it to define the personality of its inhabitant and creator.
Whistler painted Montesquiou’s portrait and called it Arrangement in Black and Gold (1891–92).

## ARTS
AND CRAFTS IN THE UNITED STATES

## The
Craftsman Movement Strong links between Britain and the United States made it likely that an Arts and Crafts movement would appear in the United States, a reaction, as in Britain, to the ornate mass production for the popular market.
The leading figure in what came to be called the Craftsman movement was Gustav Stickley (1858–1942).
His family owned furniture factories and he began his career by selling historic reproductions before becoming interested in the writings of Ruskin and Morris.
In 1898 he traveled to England and to Paris and, when he returned to the United States, he began to design and produce solid oak furniture that was simpler in form but large and bulky in the American way.
Ornamental detail was provided by the pegs, and mitered, and dovetailed joints of traditional furniture making (13.11).
The style was also known as Mission, because of a perceived similarity to furniture made for Californian missions or Golden Oak after the yellow-brownish tone given to the wood by “fuming,” a smoking process that darkened the wood and accentuated its grain.
Gustav Stickley, armchair, United States, 1905.
An illustration from a catalog from L. and J.
G.
Stickley’s Onondaga shop where many Craftsman-style designs were produced.
In 1901, Stickley founded The Craftsman magazine to promote Arts and Crafts ideals with illustrations of “Craftsman” houses (13.12).
It also carried articles on women’s rights, childcare, and social justice, along with photography, poetry, fiction, and other material that Stickley thought might appeal to his likely audience.
The master of English Arts and Crafts, Voysey, contributed an article that was illustrated by photographs of his work.
Dining room, United States, 1904.
The magazine Craftsman, from which this illustration is taken, promoted the Craftsman movement.
The chairs, the table, and sideboard shown are from Gustav Stickley’s shops.
The room itself with its wooden wainscot and simple window detail is in strong contrast to popular taste of the time.
Stickley was briefly joined in 1903 by Harvey Ellis (1842–1904) an architect and architectural illustrator, and unsigned illustrations of furniture that appeared in late 1903 in The Craftsman have been credited to him.
The designs show less bulky forms and ornamentation that suggest the influence of Voysey and other British designers.
However, given Ellis’s short time with Stickley it is thought more likely that the change of detail was made by his established employees such as LaMont Adelbert Warner (1876–1970), who was Stickley’s designer and head draftsman and responsible for many of the new designs.
Warner and his wife, Emma V.
Smith (1876–1923), designed and built a Craftsman-style house in Bronxville, New York in 1908.
When it was featured in Good Housekeeping in 1909, the magazine noted that Warner also designed much of the furniture—including the electric-light fittings.
Stickley’s commercial success encouraged other manufacturers to follow Craftsman principles and he found himself in competition with the Onondaga, New York, shops of his younger brothers, Leopold (1869–1957) and John George (1871–1921).
Will H.
Bradley (1868–1962) was a commercial illustrator who developed an enthusiasm for the Craftsman style and similar work from Britain.
He was commissioned by the popular and influential Ladies’ Home Journal to develop ideas for houses, rooms and furnishings (13.14).
His accomplished illustrations were rich in detail depicting lamps with stained-glass panels, metal objects in hammered copper, and art-pottery pieces.
13.14 Will H.
Bradley, interior illustration, 1902.
Renderings of Bradley’s interior designs became familiar to an extensive American public through publication in the popular magazine Ladies’ Home Journal.
His support for designs in the Arts and Crafts and Craftsman style, and his references to the work of Charles Rennie Mackintosh and the Vienna Secession designers (see Chapter 15), helped lead to acceptance of the furniture that came to be known as Mission style.
Elbert Hubbard (1856–1915), who had begun as a traveling salesman for the Larkin Soap Company, set up his own community and a craft-based venture called Roycroft in New York state.
Inspired by Morris’s Kelmscott Press, Hubbard published elegant handmade books and pamphlets, many of which he wrote, on art and literature.
Roycrofters produced Mission furniture and artifacts, and Roycroft became something close to a cult built around Hubbard, but it, and its products, faded in importance after he and his wife died aboard the RMS Lusitania when it was torpedoed by a German U-boat in 1915, an event that brought the United States into World War I (1914–18)—and precipitated the end of the community.
Traces of Craftsman influence survived after the war in the small single-story timber “bungalows” that had evolved in Bengal, India (hence the name) as comfortable homes for colonial administrators.
Like many Indian ideas, the bungalow was imported into England, where the first example was built in 1869.
Typically, they were wooden structures with shingled walls, porches, and verandas under overhanging eaves that were supported on wooden posts.
Stickley saw the bungalow, with well-executed Arts and Crafts detailing, as perfect accommodation for the enlightened, and the artistic and the modest structure was well suited to embellishment by natural materials, in harmony with its location.
It benefited from benign climates and became a popular building type in California and familiar in the backgrounds of early silent films that were shot on location in the suburbs of Los Angeles.

## Japanese
Influences Charles Sumner Greene (1868–1957) and his brother Henry Mather Greene (1870–1954) established an architectural practice in California that drew on Craftsman tradition, Stick style, and the bungalow vernacular.
Their wooden houses had low, pitched roofs and long overhanging eaves but it is the quality of the interiors, in the Robert R.
Blacker House (1907) and the Gamble House (1908) in Pasadena (13.15) that distinguishes them.
Wood is used with careful and intricate joinery details that draw on Japanese precedents and Arts and Crafts respect for quality handwork.
Greene and Greene, Gamble House, Pasadena, California, 1908.
The Greene brothers’ work is based on an understanding of craft ideals, with woodwork detailing influenced by Japanese traditional design.
Finely detailed furniture, lantern-like light fittings, and stained-glass inserts in windows generate original interiors that have a sense of tradition.
In 1893 the brothers had visited the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago and saw examples of Japanese architecture.
They were impressed by Japanese commitment to refinement of detail and Henry cited the example as important in the development of the practice they established a year later in Pasadena—even if the connection was not obvious.
When Charles saw more Japanese work at the St.
Louis World’s Fair of 1904, the influence became clearer.
They exposed structural components, with each element clearly articulated without added decoration.
Ornament is present in their interiors but restrained, panels of stained glass, pendant electriclight fittings and simple elegant, beautifully crafted furniture fill spacious entrance halls which flow, often unobstructed by doors, into major public rooms.
Color comes principally from wood tones, mahogany, teak, rosewood, ebony, and maple, finished by polishing or oiling.
Reds, blues, and greens feature in their stained glass and rugs.
Bernard R.
Maybeck (1862–1957) was born in New York and studied at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris before moving to California in 1892.
His output was eclectic; he believed that each project deserved to be treated in a style appropriate to its function.
He produced bungalows in what became known as the Western Stick style but, when he considered it appropriate, introduced traces of Gothic Revival, and Beaux-Arts Classicism.
This mélange is obvious in his Christian Science Church of 1910, considered his greatest work (13.16).
The ostensibly classical entrance portico also suggests Japanese influences with its clear articulation of structural elements.
The interior dominated by the cruciform roof structure of raw, gently curved, timber beams, which might be found in a warehouse but are decorated by intricately carved wooden panels.
The pulpit stands in front of a pierced screen that looks Gothic.
The whole is frantically overwrought, a willful tour de force.
13.16 Bernard R.
Maybeck, Christian Science Church, Berkeley, California, 1910.
An almost anarchic mix of rough-hewn timber roof beams incorporating carved panels and a pulpit that stands in front of a wooden screen that might be Gothic Revival.

## EMERGENCE
OF WOMEN DESIGNERS In the nineteenth-century world of architecture and, to a lesser extent, interior design, the interior decorator was usually a woman and regarded as an amateur.
Many women slipped into the activity because friends and acquaintances admired their work and then asked for advice thus offering creative opportunities.
Most women decorator/designers had useful social connections and the self-confidence to deal with conducting and expanding businesses.

## United
States

## Wheeler
The emergence of professional woman designers began toward the end of the nineteenth century.
Candace Wheeler (1827–1923) was a textile designer who became an early authority on interior decoration, working first in Colonial Revival, then the Arts and Crafts and Aesthetic movements.
In 1877 she established the Society of Decorative Art in New York to help impoverished women support themselves through the decorative arts.
Another founder member of the society was Louis Comfort Tiffany, and he and Wheeler formed Tiffany & Wheeler and collaborated on the interiors of significant private houses and public buildings.
Yet Wheeler’s most significant job was the design of the interior of the Woman’s Building at the World’s Columbian Exposition held in Chicago in 1893.
The building was designed by Sonya Hayden (1868–1953) the first female architectural graduate at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and was filled with exhibitions of women’s fine arts, crafts, and industrial products.
In the same year, Wheeler wrote Household Art and, in 19o3, Principles of Home Decoration.

## Wharton
Wheeler was not the first American woman to write about interior design.
In 1897 Edith Wharton (1862–1937), before she had produced any of her novels and appalled by what she considered to be the vulgarities of the newly rich, collaborated with American architect and interior decorator Ogden Codman Jr., (1863–1951) to write The Decoration of Houses.
It became a standard in American interior design.

## Britain

## Agnes
and Rhoda Garrett In Britain, two campaigners for women’s right to vote were prepared to take on the men who had, incongruously, monopolized interior design.
Agnes Garrett (1845–1935) and her cousin Rhoda Garrett (1841–82) were at the forefront of the emergence of specialist interior practice in both residential and commercial work (13.17 and 13.18).
They moved in artistic social circles and in 1874 founded A. & R.
Garrett, House Decorators, the first British interior-decorating business to be run by women.
Two years later, they published Suggestions for House Decoration in Painting, Woodwork and Furniture.
They facetiously advised readers to take advice offered by decorators “cum grano salis” (with a grain of salt) and then, among other opinions, advised against making “a thing or a material look like what it is not,” against hiding the “construction of your house or of any part of your furniture,” for the use of a “considerable amount of plain neutral color in your rooms,” and, significantly given the year, against “overloading . . . rooms with ornament.” All are sentiments that might have been voiced by the architectural reformers of their time—and later.
A fragment of the ceiling hand-painted by the Garretts for their home and studio at 2 Gower Street, close to the Senate House Library of London University where the ceiling has been stored, in fragments, since 1975.
Its lightness of touch and color clearly set it apart from the aesthetic prevailing in middle-class domestic interiors.
Agnes and Rhoda Garrett, painted ceiling, Bloomsbury, London, 1875.

## 13.17

## 13.18 Agnes and Rhoda Garrett, cabinet, London, 1875 It is interesting to consider this ca
binet in the light of the Garretts’ exhortation to reveal construction and materials.
The woods are left in their natural state, supports are distinctly expressed.
To a modern eye the finished piece seems generously decorated but the modest moldings are largely used to cover, and strengthen, joints.
In comparison to the full-blooded Victorian pieces that dominated the retail market it is self-effacing.
The movements that emerged, in Britain and the United States, as reactions against the excesses of Gothic Revival shared with it an inclination to look for a new aesthetic in the past—with the revival of hand skills and creative communities.
Both found their models in medieval Europe but they also found something in the unfamiliar artifacts and attitudes of Japan.
Both examples encouraged restraint but restraint could not counter the popular appetite for excess, and, as Gothic Revival faded, that appetite was satisfied in increasingly eclectic ways.
Eclecticism and a New World CHAPTER FOURTEEN Painting of interior designed by Jean-Louis-Charles Garnier, Opéra, Paris, 1861–75.
The splendor of the stair, the marble columns, the gilt detail, and the painted ceiling area are visual overtures for the experience of the opera to come.
Architects and designers of the nineteenth century picked their styles from the past and—apart from the adjustments necessary to accommodate new functions—stayed largely true to the original model.
By the end of the century, new social and economic structures created a climate, and a confidence, in which assiduous respect for the past seemed less deserved.
The development of new materials and techniques at a greater and faster rate than ever before encouraged an increasingly relaxed and eclectic approach to the fusion of the familiar and the unfamiliar.
This encouraged creative borrowing that shaped the extraordinary build-ings of the latter part of the century as in pursuit of an appropriate style—for skyscrapers in particular—architects and designers experimented with collaging elements of different styles within single buildings.
If they were skillful, the hybridized Eclecticism, had coherence—and panache.
The post-Revolutionary French government wanted physical expressions of national unity and commissioned Jean-Nicolas-Louis Durand (1760–1834) to evolve standards for public buildings.
In 1800 he published Recueil et Parallèle des Edifices de Tout Genre Anciens et Modernes (Collection and Comparison of All Kinds of Ancient and Modern Buildings) and established rules for every building type, whether assembled from masonry or cast-iron components.
Plans were simple diagrams, sections and elevations followed the logic of construction.
Provincial towns benefited from well-resolved buildings and the formulae gave Paris Les Halles (1853–70) the iron and glass pavilions of its wholesale food market.
When these were demolished in 1971, their destruction—and the crass shopping mall that replaced them—made a convincing argument for the preservation of utilitarian buildings that, with age, acquire romantic glamour.
Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc (1814–79), the great restorer of French national monuments, excited controversy when he used cast-iron components in traditional structures, most notoriously in restoring the flèche of the cathedral of Notre Dame in Paris in 1859.
In drawings, for a concert hall (14.2) and a theoretical interpretation of Gothic structure (14.3) he suggested how cast-iron structural strength could be married to traditional interior architecture.
It was an indisputably eclectic approach.
Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc, design for a concert hall, Entretiens sur l’Architecture (Discourses on Architecture), 1863–72.
14.2 A speculation about the structural strength of cast iron in the cause of improving sight lines.
Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc, sketch of cast-iron structural members, Discourses on Architecture, 1863–72.
An examination of the decorative potential of a molded cast-iron structure.

## ECOLE
DES BEAUX-ARTS While architects and their clients remained wedded to stylistic revivals, the principles of classical and Gothic architectures had to be adapted to the scale and practical functions of the new building types that emerged in the wake of the Industrial Revolution.
The skills to master this hybridization of traditional form and modern function were learnt at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris.
The Ecole taught rational planning, with a preference for symmetrical composition, and a compendium of primarily classical detailing.
Beaux-Arts teachers were also the designers of the great buildings of late nineteenth-century France that defined the school’s philosophy.
Pierre-François-Henri Labrouste (1801–75) created the unprecedented libraries of S.
Geneviève (1844–50) and the Bibliothèque Nationale (1859–67).
The interiors of both exploited the potential of cast iron, as a structural and a decorative material.
The Geneviève demonstrates Beaux-Arts clarity of planning (14.6).
In a large entrance hall, with rooms for book stacks and special collections on either side, square Neoclassical piers support iron segmental arches that carry a plain, flat ceiling.
The entrance hall passes through the building to a double stair leading to the reading room, lined with bookshelves.
A row of thin iron columns, on the central axis of the building, supports decoratively perforated iron arches that carry two plastered barrel vaults.
Labrouste recognized that iron had potential for more delicate decoration than carved stone.
14.6 Pierre-François-Henri Labrouste, Bibliothèque S.
Geneviève, Paris, 1844–50.
The reading room, the main space of the library, is one of the first iron structures.
The outer walls are stone, but the roof structure is iron, with a row of slim columns down the center of the room supporting iron arches in which the circle forms are structural and ornamental.
The Bibliothèque Nationale is larger and more complex (14.7).
In the main reading room, thin iron columns support iron arches that form nine square bays, each topped by a dome of curved ceramic segments.
An oculus in each dome spreads natural light across the great room.
The outer masonry walls are independent of the iron structure and are lined with three tiers of bookshelves accessed from balconies.
A glass wall gives views from the reading room to the stacks.
Pierre-François-Henri Labrouste, Bibliothèque Nationale, Paris, 1859–67.
A square reading room topped by nine domes, each with an iron frame supporting tile panels.
Light comes from an oculus in each dome.
The thinness of the structural iron columns makes for a well-lit, almost fragile, room.
Labrouste’s libraries are the most radical—and eclectic—buildings produced by a Beaux-Arts graduate.
He was more interested in taking advantage of cast iron’s structural and decorative potentials than in replaying ancient motifs.
Both buildings are heroic, with modest details defined by the capabilities of cast iron.
Both suggest that a new decorative language was waiting to be discovered.
Beaux-Arts’ greatest monument, the Paris Opéra (1861–75), by Jean-Louis-Charles Garnier (1825–98), is a more conventional adaptation of classical principles but overwhelming in its scale and richness of decorative detail (14.1, 14.4, and 14.5).
The Petit Palais exhibition building (1897–1900) by Charles-Louis Girault (1851–1932) and the Gare du Quai d’Orsay railroad station (1898–1900; 14.8) by Victor Laloux (1850–1937) demonstrated how architectural rhetoric could glorify buildings dedicated to modern functions.
Both men lived to see the first manifestations of functional, decoration-free modernism, which, as graduates of the Ecole des Beaux-Arts, they may have regarded as a descent from the sublime to the ridiculous.
14.5 14.4 Jean-Louis-Charles Garnier, Opéra, Paris, 1861–75.
The most admired Beaux-Arts buildings combines a nineteenth-century love of ornament with a monumental presence.
The functional organization of the building seen in the plan, a basic strength of Beaux-Arts thinking, provides generous circulation spaces for the movement of large audiences.
Jean-Louis-Charles Garnier, plan of Opéra.
1 Entrance for those arriving by carriage 2 Entrance for those arriving on foot 3 Stage 4 Emperor’s entrance Victor Laloux, Gare du Quai d’Orsay, Paris, 1898–1900.
Laloux overlaid the railroad station with Beaux-Arts classical detail.
Tracks ran through the station at a lower level and platforms were reached by stairs from the street.
In the skylit main hall, a huge clock underlined the railroad company’s commitment to schedules.
The building survives and has been converted into the Musée d’Orsay.

## UNITED
STATES In the United States, Neoclassical exteriors and interiors were considered appropriate for banks and courthouses, Gothic Revival for some churches, and Colonial for other denominations.
House styles were eclectic: Colonial, Norman, French Renaissance, half-timbered Tudor, Gothic, Spanish Mission, Ranch House, or combinations of some or all.
While necessity and financial restraints shaped most American architecture, immensely rich American industrialists, railroad magnates, and bankers were uninterested in practicalities.
They wanted houses to rival those of the asset-rich, cash-poor European aristocrats to whom they married their daughters, and they needed architects who understood and could adapt European precedents.
Richard Morris Hunt (1827–95) was the first American to study at the Beaux-Arts, from 1846– 55, and with that cachet he attracted clients such as the Vanderbilt family, who were rich from building railroads and steamboats, and stock speculation.
For William K.
Vanderbilt, he adapted an early French Renaissance château in an eclectic interpretation of the style forced by the exigencies of its city-center corner plot.
He used the style again for George Washington Vanderbilt II’s country house in North Carolina.
He used it yet again, around 1895, for The Breakers, Cornelius Vanderbilt II’s Newport, Rhode Island, mansion although there he adapted Italian Renaissance for the dining room (14.9).
He employed a more eclectic conglomeration of arches, dormers, mansard roofs for the eight stories of the New York Tribune Building (1873–5) to which he added a skinny clock tower that rose another four floors.

## 14.9 When Hunt returned to the United States from France, he brought back his enthusiasm f
or the classicism of his Beaux-Arts training.
In The Breakers, he created his own variation on Italian Renaissance design.

## Building
High As cities grew, distinct districts were devoted to commercial activities, for ease of communication and commuting.
Specialist support businesses were drawn to such concentrations of potential customers.
“Business districts” commanded high rents and high land values.
Taller buildings maximized profits and they could go taller with the invention of the passenger elevator.
Until the introduction of cast-iron columns and beams, the height of buildings was limited by the structural potential of masonry walls and columns.
The world’s first iron-framed building was the five-story-high Ditherington Flax Mill (1797) in Shrewsbury, England, and the technique employed there became common for the factories of the Industrial Revolution.
Stone or brick remained the preferred options for external walls, however cast iron was strong and fire-resistant and could be poured into molds to make ornamental detail.
In the United States, James Bogardus (1800–74) developed the iron-framing techniques introduced at Ditherington and established a factory in New York to make cast-iron cladding panels, in various Italianate styles for his own and other architects’ projects.
These story-height units accelerated construction and allowed larger window areas.
Floors remained wooden and vulnerable to fire, and inadequate fire escape stairs made them more dangerous.
Fire safety was improved when brick or terracotta, laid in shallow arcs for compressive strength, replaced masonry.
Fire-proofed structural elements and light tile cladding made twelve-story-high buildings feasible.
In 1856, a British engineer, Henry Bessemer (1813–98), invented the Bessemer process for producing steel economically.
The stronger steel columns and beams superseded their iron equivalents and the “skyscraper” would grow taller by the end of the century.
The world’s first passenger lift was installed in the Equitable Life Company headquarters building in New York in 1870.
By 1890, the electric elevator, invented in Germany in 1880, was sufficiently refined to make very tall buildings feasible.
The prevailing Beaux-Arts aesthetic determined the aesthetics of the open tracery of the elevator cage that allowed passengers to view the spectacle as they were hoisted through central atria that ran the full height of buildings (14.10).
The first examples, such as that in Los Angeles’ Bradbury Building of 1893, were spectacular if rudimentary.
However, as the Beaux-Arts obligation to decorate asserted itself so the open metal traceries of the sides of the “birdcage” elevator cars became elements that designers attacked with relish.
The monumental stair that in low-rise buildings had been centrally located on plan and led to the principal floor, had no effective role to play in the skyscraper.
It was replaced by a battery of elevators, preferably on axis with the front doors.
They were less imposing but indisputably practical and satisfied the Beaux-Arts preference for symmetrical planning.
They also offered opportunities for extravagant decoration on the doors that confronted waiting passengers and the walls of the cabin that enclosed them.
In the twentieth century, as passenger cabins were enclosed for safety and users’ peace of mind, internal decoration became perversely bland.
George Herbert Wyman, Bradbury Building, Los Angeles, 1893.
The emergence of the modern, large office building poses new problems for architects of the eclectic era.
Wyman introduced the skylights over a central atrium to provide light for the perimeter galleries that replaced dark corridors and gave access to offices on each floor.
The elevators moving in open cages and the stairs connecting the various gallery levels present an image more functional than eclectic.

## Office
Interiors Office interiors were utilitarian with rows of small rooms ranged along corridors with external windows for light and ventilation.
Floors, ceilings, partitions, and furniture were usually wooden, in shades of somber brown oak.
Glazed partitions between offices allowed some daylight to reach rooms without external walls.
Patterned glass gave visual privacy and opening panels provided cross ventilation.
Directors’ offices and boardrooms might be distinguished by a rug or leathercovered upholstered chairs, perhaps some pictures.
As corporations grew, so general offices evolved to accommodate hives of clerks, stenographers, and typists (14.11).
Specialist equipment including filing cabinets, rolltop desks, swivel chairs, typewriters, adding machines, and time clocks became common.
The telegraph and then the telephone changed basic communication and the nature of work.
As gas gave way to electricity, improvements in artificial lighting reduced the need to locate offices on the external walls.
14.11 Illiustration of the office in a publishing company, New York, c.
1890.
Cast-iron columns support wooden beams.
Daylight is augmented by gaslight on dark days.
Large businesses required larger office spaces for clerks and bookkeepers, and an industry developed to supply office desks and chairs.

## Apartments
and Hotels The economics of building high changed apartment blocks and hotels in major cities.
In The Dakota $( 1 8 8 0 - 4 ; 1 4 .
1 2 )$ apartments and the Waldorf Hotel (1893; 14.13), both in New York and by Henry Janeway Hardenbergh (1847–1918), secondary rooms were arranged around roofless wells for light and ventilation.
Principal rooms, with street views, had rich timber paneling, monumental fireplaces, parquet floors, generous allocations of stained glass, and other prestigious materials: sliding pocket doors created generous areas for entertaining.
Tenants added more decorative luxury to the impressive basics.
Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, The Dakota, New York, 1880–4.
A room in The Dakota in which the high standard of decorative joinery and plasterwork is augmented by the owner’s voracious Victorian appetite for color, pattern, and intricate detail.
14.13 Henry Janeway Hardenbergh, Waldorf Hotel, New York, 1893.
The hotel, built in what has been described as German Renaissance style, was the first to have private bathrooms, electricity, and telephones in all its rooms.
New York’s wealthiest citizens congregated in its magnificent public spaces.

## Public
Buildings Public buildings replicated, and frequently surpassed, the grandiose flourishes in the commercial and private sectors.
Second Empire style, the public architecture of France during the reign of Napoleon III (1852–70), was admired and emulated in the interiors of Philadelphia’s enormous City Hall (1872–1901; 14.14) by John McArthur Jr., (1823–90).
The interiors have a bold vitality that eschews restraint.
U.S. government buildings by Alfred B.
Mullett (1834–90), such as the massive State, War, and Navy Building (now Eisenhower Executive Office Building) in Washington, D.C., (1871–88) follow a similar model.
14.14 John McArthur, Jr., and Thomas U.
Walter, City Hall, Philadelphia, 1872–1901.
Conversation Hall, as it is known, is a monumental interior in the huge building that was the governmental center for the large city Philadelphia had become.
Admiration for the French Second Empire style had led to excessive grandeur in the public buildings of a democratic society.
This room glories in colored marble, a spectacular gaslight chandelier, and a ceiling rich in color and gilding.
The work of Frank Furness (1839–1912) was underpinned by Second Empire influence but it was also tuned by a robust monumentality that drew freely on Gothic Revival, Stick, Shingle, and Arts and Crafts precedents.
The entrance hall in his Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts (1888–91) used stubby columns with truncated pointed arches loosely based on Gothic sources, heavily textured wall surfaces, florid iron railings, and light fittings (14.15).
His vast reading room and rotunda for the library at the University of Pennsylvania is lined with brick and stone walls that might be surrounding an external courtyard (14.16).
There are complex arch details and a great fireplace with a clock above it with much intricate detail.
A complex iron stairway is embellished with ornamental iron railings.
Frank Furness, entrance hall, Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts, Philadelphia, 1888–91.
French Second Empire style becomes more robust with stubby columns, pointed arches, and heavily textured wall surfaces.
Frank Furness, Fisher Fine Arts Library, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, 1888–91.
The brick and stone dressings of the library’s perimeter have the materials and scale of exterior walls, but the enormous fireplace dominates the room.

## Furniture
and Fittings in Excess Factory production in the Victorian age made extravagantly decorated objects relatively inexpensive.
New materials and techniques were developed and whole new categories of object became possible.
The ancient Egyptians and Greek had discovered that by gluing thin panels of wood, with grains of alternate layers running at right angles, it was possible to produce a panel more resistant to warping than natural wood of the same thickness.
In 1797 an English naval engineer, Sir Samuel Bentham (1757–1831), patented a number of machines capable of cutting very thin layers, or veneers, of wood by hand and described the gluing together of several veneers to form a stronger single sheet.
Fifty years later, the Swedish engineer Immanuel Nobel (1801–72) invented the rotary lathe, which cut much thinner, much larger veneers from a log that was rotated as on a spit.
In 1928 the standard size of 8 × 4 feet (2,440 × 1,220 mm) was established for all sheet materials and endures.
Iron and brass tubing, which had first been used for utilitarian pipes, were promoted to make ornate bedhead and foot boards (14.17).
They were much lighter and often more convoluted in shape than their wooden counterparts and therefore more desirable to the Victorian eye.
14.17 Sears Roebuck, page from catalog, United States, 1901.
This page from a mail-order catalog shows a “massive” bed of iron tube and steel spring construction, the result of the adoption of industrial materials for domestic use.
The Austrian–German cabinetmaker Michael Thonet (1796–1871) developed the technique of using steam in pressure chambers to bend strips of wood, which he then glued to make chairs that, without heavily upholstered bulk, went some way to satisfying the Victorian enthusiasm for visual complexities.
In 1851 he received a bronze medal for his bentwood chairs at the Great Exhibition in London.
In 1853 he received a silver at the Exposition Universelle (Universal Exhibition) in Paris.
Following financial problems, he transferred the business to his sons and it continued as Gebrüder Thonet (Thonet Brothers).
A chair produced in 1859, and known as Komsumstuhl Nr.
14, became ubiquitous in modest cafés and restaurants (14.19).
No.
14 pioneered industrial chair production.
It was assembled from a number of components that could be exported in space-saving packages across the world; components for thirty-six chairs could be exported in a box of 35 cubic feet (1 cubic meter).
The chair won the Thonets a gold medal at the Paris World’s Fair in 1867.
More than 50 million units of the model had been sold by 1930 and it remains in production.
The seats and backs of Thonet chairs were usually of woven cane, which afforded a certain amount of cushioning, or plywood that could be shaped and decorated with cut-out patterns in the cause of decoration (14.18).
Thonet Brothers, page from catalog, Austria, 1904.
This page from the Thonet Brothers’ chair catalog illustrates rocking chairs made with steam-bent wooden timbers and woven rattan or plywood seats and backs.
Thonet Brothers, Chair No.
14, Austria, 1859.
Also known as Komsumstuhl Nr.
14 (Coffee-house Chair No.
14).
It became the world’s first mass-produced item of furniture.
More than 50 million chairs have been sold since its launch and it remains in production.

## Furnishing
the Home In his New York workshops, the German-born cabinetmaker John Henry Belter (1804–63) produced chairs, sofas, and tables that incorporated extravagantly curved and heavily upholstered elements, which were further embellished with elaborate floral carvings (14.22).
Much of his output was made by mechanized processes in which slivers of shaped plywood were glued together to produce intricate carved ornament.
The complexity of these and pieces by other makers imitating his style and techniques, have been labelled Rococo Revival.
John Henry Belter, sofa, rosewood and rosewood laminate, New York, c.
1850.
German-born Belter developed a technique for bending and laminating rosewood, cutting and combining layers of laminate to create elaborate openwork carvings in the Rococo Revival style.
The undulating silhouette and intricate floral ornament made his designs among the most popular of their time.
At the end of the nineteenth century, Gustave Herter (1830–98) and Christian Herter (1839– 83), who were also born in Germany, emigrated and founded their eponymous company in New York with cabinet and upholstery workshops, a design office to provide an interior-decoration service, and a reputation for high-quality work in the most expensive and fashionable houses.
Different lines were given names that suggested interpretations of historic styles: Renaissance Revival, Neo-Grec, Aesthetic movement, and Anglo-Japanese.
The quality of the Herters’ work, both as designers and manufacturers, is typified by a mahogany and marquetry sideboard of c.
1880 in their Renaissance Revival style (14.21).
14.21 Herter Brothers, Renaissance Revival sideboard, mahogany with marquetry ornament, New York, c.
1880.
The Herter Brothers designed and made furniture and interiors for some of the most lavish homes in the United States.
Their revivalist styles included Renaissance, Neo-Grec, Aesthetic movement, and the Anglo-Japanese style.
Well-padded upholstery provided comfort and signaled opulence.
Thickness was emphasized by quilting, tufting, and padding pulled tight by buttons to create regular patterns of indentations.
Metal springs beneath cushioned elements increased softness.
Fabrics were usually colorful with elaborate woven designs but leather and woven horsehair, usually in black, were alternatives.
Leather was favored in rooms considered to need a “masculine” atmosphere: dining rooms, smoking rooms, billiard rooms, and studies.
A side chair of 1846–47 by upholstered seat and back demonstrated how the vogue for Gothic Revival furniture in ecclesiastical architecture influenced furniture in the home (14.20).
The lighter touch of Rococo Revival, typified by the work of Belter and the Herter Brothers, was thought more appropriate for parlors and boudoirs.
Size was prized, and large, mirrored hat racks appeared in halls and vestibules.
Pianos made in rectangular, grand, and upright forms were status symbols embellished with rich and complex ornamentation, their flat surfaces offered additional opportunities for displays of ornaments and framed photographs.
Thomas Brooks, side chair, black walnut, New York, 1846–7.
At a time of enthusiastic churchgoing, the new Gothic Revival style would have been familiar, particularly to members of the numerous and prosperous middle class.
Its influence is apparent in this chair, which was probably intended for a dining room or a library.
Something less ecclesiastical and more Rococo Revival would have served in a drawing room or boudoir.
Textiles that had been produced slowly by hand lent themselves easily to factory production.
Powered looms in efficient mills could produce large, elaborate and colorful patterns on woven or printed cloth.
Floral designs were particularly popular and braiding, fringes, and tassels added to the luxuriance.
Lace curtains provided auxiliary privacy when heavier curtains were opened, and those with integral woven patterns satisfied the Victorian need for decoration and, by filtering daylight, contributed to the Gothic gloom that characterized the Victorian interior.
Carpets were generally produced on power looms and, like furnishing textiles, favored repeat patterns of natural forms, arabesques and scrolls.
Standard lengths could be sewn together and laid from wall to wall.
Linoleum was invented in 1855 in England by Frederick Walton (1834– 1928), using solidified linseed oil, pine resin, and ground cork dust on a canvas backing.
It was easily adapted to incorporate floral patterns and imitations of wooden parquet and tiled floorings.
Printed wallpapers were the most economical way of dispatching plain walls and could match the colors and patterns of fabrics while offering more delicate detail.
Floral and geometric patterns, Chinese and Japanese themes, even scenic motifs were popular.
Some papers were embossed for a slight bas-relief effect and printed paper strips replicating egg and dart and Greekkey motifs would be applied just below ceiling level as a cornice, with deeper triangular short sections used at corners.
The illustrations in The Grammar of Ornament (1856) by English designer and architect Owen Jones were brightly colored and, at first, had encouraged the use of strong hues.
However, within a short time they were considered frivolous and were replaced by duller, darker colors.
Browns, olive greens, and mauves were considered more tasteful and muted in candlelight and gaslight.
After 1854 and Captain Perry’s ventures in Japan and China, references to Asia were rife.
Bamboo—and imitations of bamboo—furniture became popular both in the United States and Europe.
Bamboo objects were imported or made locally from imported material.
Folding screens with painted or fabric surfaces on wooden frames had an ostensibly practical function but were principally prized for their decorative potential.
Wicker furniture made from woven rattan (thin strips of palm-tree bark) or similar flexible materials was popular in less formal rooms such as porches, conservatories, or children’s bedrooms and nurseries

## Shopping
The new cast-iron framed buildings served many functions most obviously factories and warehouses but also the “dry goods” stores that were forerunners of the department stores (14.23) that first emerged in the cities of the East Coast offering comprehensive selections of goods that allowed Victorian shoppers to compare, select, and buy everything necessary for home decoration.
Oil lamps, from the simple to the very ornate, were the most common lighting devices until supplanted by gaslights, which tended to replicate the design of candle brackets.
Chandeliers, often ornamented with brass work and hanging glass prisms, were popular and usually as big as a room could accommodate.
With the introduction of electric light, gas brackets were converted to take the new filament bulbs that Thomas Edison invented in 1879.
The first electric fan appeared in 1889 and in 1893 a fully electric kitchen was displayed at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago.
14.23 Schuyler, Hartley & Graham shop, New York, 1864.
Guns and military goods were in demand during the U.S.
Civil War (1861–5).
The shop interior has counters, cases, and cabinets in the vernacular of the period, while the upper walls and ceiling are richly decorated.
As the United States began to colonize its own empire in the west, and frontier towns and cities became respectable, retailers invented ways to service their household needs.
Mail-order catalogs by Sears Roebuck, Montgomery Ward, and many smaller companies illustrated the products necessary to set up a respectable home far from the department stores of the East Coast.
At a prosaic level, plumbing fixtures and water pumps, cast-iron stoves for heating, and ranges for cooking that, inevitably, sported decorative flourishes were shipped west.
Generally, the more expensive the item, the more it would be decorated.
Bathroom fixtures, including flushing lavatories, bathtubs, and washbasins were offered in a plethora of styles, from the utilitarian to the flamboyant.
Decoration and furnishings in the most isolated homes needed to pass muster with aesthetically inclined visitors.
As transport improved, so coal replaced local wood as fuel and, as towns became cities, gas superseded coal.

## High
Style Sites in the commercial centers of prosperous cities increasingly became fewer, but technology made tall buildings an option.
Early examples of what became known as “skyscrapers” show architects’ reluctance to move away from pre-industrial conventions but tall buildings caused aesthetic problems.
There were five classical orders of architecture and, initially, buildings higher than five stories posed aesthetic conundrums.
Classical columns had been conceived to rest on the ground and support a pitched roof and the orders were not designed to be mixed or stacked.
A reversion to the Georgian plainness that had evolved for tall London townhouses made sense and worked for the Monadnock Building (1889–91) in Chicago by Daniel Burnham (1846–1912) and John Wellborn Root (1850–91).
Its sixteen stories were totally unornamented with load-bearing, red brick walls that were enormously thick at lower levels to take the weight of the upper levels.
The wall of the lowest floor projected slightly to make a “plinth” and a simple projecting “cornice” finished the fourteen identical floors between with a modest flourish.
Internally, the iron elevator structure and cages provided the only decorative elements.
After Root’s death in 1891, Burnham hired Charles B.
Atwood (1849–95) to complete the Reliance Building (1895) and he replaced load-bearing masonry with a steel structure clad in “curtain” walls of large windows and white, glazed terracotta panels.
The Reliance also offered electricity and telephones to all its tenants.
A central top-lit courtyard provided daylight and ventilation.
The Rookery (1886), a Chicago office block, had a central court covered at groundfloor level with a glass and iron-framed roof, designed by Frank Lloyd Wright in 1905.
An alternative solution, typified by the Bradbury Building (1893) in Los Angeles (see here), was to install the glass roof at the top of the building and to use the huge central void for elevator cages, stairs, and access balconies, all of which gave opportunities for cast-iron decoration.
Ernest Flagg (1857–1947) applied Second Empire style to the forty-seven floors of the Singer Building in New York, which was designed and constructed in phases between 1897 and 1908 (14.24).
It was, briefly, the world’s tallest building at 612 feet (187 m).
A mansard-topped tower rose from a larger block in which lower floors were open to the public, with monumentally ornate stairs and balconies under vaulted ceilings.
Ernest Flagg, Singer Building, New York, 1897–1908.
The monumental interiors of the lower floors, of what was briefly the tallest building in the world, were open to the public.
In 1913, the Woolworth Building (14.25) in New York by Cass Gilbert (1859–1934) became the tallest building in the world at 792 feet (241 m).
Its steel frame, elevators, and sixty stories of offices were clothed in white glazed terracotta tiles among the tracery and pinnacles of French Gothic ecclesiastical architecture.
The public interiors included spacious elevator lobbies, stairs, balconies, and arcades, all detailed in a Gothic/Byzantine hybrid style.
Executive office interiors sported tapestries and an eclectic mix of ornamental furniture and wood carvings.
Gargoyles caricatured Gilbert holding a model of the building and Frank Winfield Woolworth, the founder of the F.
W.
Woolworth Company retail chain, clutching money bags labeled “5c” and “10c” in reference to the prices of goods in his cut-price stores.
Cass Gilbert, Woolworth Building, New York, 1913.
On its completion, the Woolworth Building became the world’s tallest building and, like the Singer (14.24), its entrance lobbies were open to the public.
It became standard practice for shop units in lobbies to be rented to independent businesses that relied on the custom of people who worked in the building.

## Ocean
Liners Interior design reached remarkable levels of opulence in the interiors of the great ocean liners (14.26).
On the British RMS Mauretania (1906) passengers in first class could enjoy halls, lounges, and smoking rooms in Italian Renaissance and Francis I French styles designed by the British architect Harold Peto (1854–1933), who specialized in lavishly eclectic interiors for town houses, country mansions, and hotels.
The smoking room of the British RMS Franconia (1923) masqueraded as a Tudor half-timbered hall with a huge brick fireplace.
The Great German pre-World War I liners excelled in excess eclectic decor.
The swimming pool of the German SS Vaterland (1914) later renamed Leviathan was “Pompeian” with Roman Doric columns two stories high around the tiled pool.
The main lounge of the Italian liner Conte di Savoia (1931) recreated the gallery of the seventeenth-century Colonna Palace in Rome, complete with statuary and fresco painting.

## 14.26 The ocean liner SS France, 1910. Some of the most spectacular eclectic interiors wer
e found in first-class accommodation on ocean liners.
The grand stair and dining room with rich—supposedly Baroque—decoration was intended to suggest the comforts of a grand hotel and to minimize the effect of the rigors of an Atlantic crossing.

## Movie
Theaters Eclecticism continued deep into the twentieth century.
Film, the new mass entertainment, and spectacular Hollywood film sets prompted eclectic design within movie theaters, which themselves became a part of the visual experience.
Traditional theaters and opera houses had always been elaborately decorative, but now a mass audience could find lobbies loaded with decoration.
Thomas W.
Lamb (1871–1942) specialized in creating vast auditoria suggesting exotic and fantastic settings—Spanish, Persian, Indo–Chinese, or an amalgam of styles.
Lamb created more than 300 theaters in the 1920s and 1930s.
John Eberson (1875–1954) specialized in “atmospheric theater,” where the ceiling performed as a sky with moving clouds, stars, and a moon floating above complex architectural and sculptural detail.
Grauman’s Egyptian (1922) and Chinese (1927) theaters in Hollywood, by Meyer and Holler, were extravaganzas that became nationally famous.
At the Egyptian theater (14.27), the open-air forecourt was flanked by a “bazaar” of shops and, during screenings, an employee dressed as a Bedouin would intone the title of the feature.
The proscenium surrounding the screen was lavishly decorated and gilded in the manner of the Egyptian king, Tutankhamen, whose tomb had been uncovered in 1922.
The rest of the interior was simple but monumental, still referencing ancient Egyptian tombs and temple architecture but almost modernist in its aesthetic.
Hotels and restaurants also drifted toward historical pastiche.
14.27 Meyer and Holler, Egyptian theater, Hollywood, 1922.
Inspired by the opening of Tutankhamen’s tomb—or the success of Rudolph Valentino’s film The Sheik (1921)—the columns and “hieroglyphics” live up to the theater’s name.

## EUROPE
In Europe, eclecticism was not unknown but did not develop on the scale it achieved in the United States.
Perhaps the presence of real historic buildings and interiors gave imitation less appeal but a few bombastic examples, such as the Palace of Justice in Brussels (1866–83) by Joseph Poelaert (1817–79) or the monument to Victor Emmanuel II in Rome (1885–1911) by Giuseppe Sacconi (1854–1905), were exceedingly grandiose.
Classicism came to be the official style of governmental design in Europe in the 1930s.
The combination of formality and tradition, with a touch of modernism and a sense of efficiency and economy, contributed to its appeal.
An example is the Finnish Parliament House in Helsinki (1927–32; 14.28) by Johan Sigfrid Sirén (1889–1961).
Its façade of fourteen classical columns, at the top of a monumental flight of steps, fronts a symmetrical plan generated by the circular legislative chamber at its center.
In the 1930s, it became the favored style of Adolf Hitler in Germany and Benito Mussolini in Italy.
Demagogues understand the political gains to be made from giving people their preferred architectural style.
14.28 Johan Sigfrid Sirén, Finnish Parliament House, Helsinki, 1927–32.
Sirén stripped the building of all the conventional signifiers of classical architecture, except for the fourteen columns on the entrance façade but even these were stretched so that they lacked the load-bearing solidity of their ancient antecedents.
The flat roof—and the consequent lack of a pediment—brought the building close to modernist massing even if the symmetrical organization of plan and elevations contradicted that.
Eclecticism was primarily an American phenomenon; perhaps it was a way of not only acquiring the pedigree of established European styles but of having them express something of a new confident country on the verge of dominating the old continent in the next century.
Eclecticism had been less strong in Europe where old buildings, in a variety of styles, were abundant.
Europeans in search of a new style were searching for something more radical.
Some of them believed that a response was needed to the technological changes being pioneered in the United States, others continued to look for inspiration in nature.
Art Nouveau and the Viennese Secession CHAPTER FIFTEEN Mackintosh’s work stands at the border between the Arts and Crafts emphasis on simplicity and craftsmanship, and the shift towards more radical new forms in this interior.
There are also elements in the furniture, hanging lights, and carpet pattern that anticipate the second phase of his work where the square replaces the sinuous lines of Art Nouveau.
John Ruskin had advised those in search of a new architectural language to look at nature for inspiration because, he argued, that was God’s work.
A new decorative language did evolve in the last decade of the nineteenth century and the first of the twentieth that drew very obviously on nature and capitalized on the malleability of metals to imitate its forms.
The style emerged and flourished in the decadent cities of Western Europe but regional variants arose that shared the spirit, if not the excesses.
The most significant of these variants emerged in Vienna in 1897 when a group of artists and designers seceded from the Vienna Academy in protest against the institute’s refusal to show their radical work.
They formed the Secessionist group and their collaborations would be important in the early searches for a style appropriate to the fledgling twentieth century.
Word of both Art Nouveau and Secessionist work was spread by ever-faster modes of communication.
In distant Glasgow, Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh and a few of their contemporaries would be inspired by evidence of the work from Brussels, Paris, and Vienna that was published in London’s Studio magazine and reassured that they were not alone in their obsessions.

## ROOTS
AND CHARACTERISTICS OF ART NOUVEAU Art Nouveau designers exploited the potential of new production methods to create the languid flowing curves that were characteristic of the style and appeared across the breadth of Art Nouveau creativity, in the graphic arts, fashion, jewelry, ceramics, glassware, silverware, furniture, and interiors.
They took inspiration from the most delicate natural forms, flowers, vines, shells, birds’ feathers, and insects’ wings.
The movement took its name, rather prosaically, from a Paris store called L’Art Nouveau, which sold artifacts that were characteristic of the style.

## BRITAIN
While France is generally regarded as the birthplace of Art Nouveau, it has been argued that the style began with a few individuals who were associated with Britain’s Arts and Crafts movement but whose designs embodied the characteristics of Art Nouveau.
In 1882, Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo (1851–1942) created a chair-back carved with writhing floral forms.
Sinuous lines also appeared in his metal work, textile designs, and graphic art—in his title page for his book Wren’s City Churches (1883) the suggestion of flames has been compared to the sinuous lines of Art Nouveau (15.2).
William Morris and Charles Voysey used stylized, if rather static, natural forms in their wallpapers and textile designs (see Chapter 13).
Christopher Dresser (1834–1903) designed metalwork, ceramics, textiles, wallpapers, glassware, and silverware that drew on his knowledge of botany (15.3).
Aubrey Beardsley (1872–98) reveled in sensuous curves.
Mackmurdo, a devoted supporter of Arts and Crafts principles, was the author of a book urging the preservation of Sir Christopher Wren’s London churches.
His title page seems unrelated to the content and suggests Art Nouveau, which had yet to surface fully.
Arthur Heygate Mackmurdo, title page, Wren’s City Churches, 1883.
Christopher Dresser, silver teapot, 1879.
Dresser advocated simplicity in design and foreswore applied decoration.
However, the extraordinary shapes of the objects he created seem to be substitutes for applied decoration.
They are reminiscent of objects produced in Germany by the Bauhaus (see Chapter 17) forty years later.

## Mackintosh
Despite these precedents, Art Nouveau’s only significant British appearance was in the northern city of Glasgow where Charles Rennie Mackintosh (1868–1928) and his wife Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh (1864–1933) created their own domestic world in which stylized pink stained-glass roses and heart shapes cut into wooden panels suggest a romantic origin for their work.
It is reasonable to assume that his architectural instincts were lightened by her decorative skills.
They explored their complementary ideas in two homes they created for themselves with distinct Art Nouveau elements in his furniture and her decoration (15.5).
He was invited to design a room for the Eighth Exhibition of the Vienna Secession in 1900 and it allowed him to create a concentrated interpretation of his own brand of Art Nouveau, in particular the delicate free-standing structure around the fireplace, the chair which is similar to those used in his tearooms, and the wall panels which are larger versions of those in the tearooms and may well be by Margaret (15.4).
His influence on Viennese architects, and Josef Hoffmann in particular, is acknowledged.
15.4 Charles Rennie Mackintosh, exhibit in the Eighth Exhibition of the Vienna Secession, Vienna, 1900.
This exhibit offers a concise summation of Mackintosh’s design in his first Art Nouveau period.
He designed a room setting including a fireplace and chair.
The wall decoration is, in all probability, by his wife Margaret.
Charles Rennie Mackintosh and Margaret MacDonald Mackintosh, The Mackintosh House, The Hunterian, Glasgow, 1906–14.
This reconstruction of the main rooms of the Mackintoshes’ home at 6 Florentine Terrace, Glasgow conveys the volumes of the existing rooms exactly.
The furniture by Charles and the decoration by Margaret are original.
Some of Charles’s most interesting interiors were for Kate Cranston, a businesswoman whose mission was to create decorative and decorous tearooms as alcohol-free alternatives to the city’s bars.
She commissioned Mackintosh to expand her chain and he designed four.
The most spectacular was his Salon de Luxe in the Willow Tea Rooms with its gray high-backed chairs and tables, its mirrors, and stained glass in sinuous black wooden frames (15.6).
Charles Rennie Mackintosh, doors to the Salon de Luxe, Willow Tea Rooms, Glasgow, 1904.
The muted pastel colors and the vigorous play of lines in these leaded glass doors are typical of Mackintosh’s blending of Arts and Crafts and Art Nouveau aesthetics.
Again, Margaret’s hand is clearly visible.
Mackintosh would move on from the relaxed curves of Art Nouveau to the squares and more formal composition that appeared in his work after 1900.
In the entrance hall to a private home, Hill House in Dunbartonshire, Scotland, the square appears on all surfaces and the pink and green decorative panels become minor elements in the composition (15.1).
The transition is seen even more clearly in his interiors for Glasgow School of Art (1896–1909).
The first phase, completed in 1899, sports sinuous curves in its stained glass and metalwork, but squares predominate in the same elements in the second phase, completed in 1909.
He was moving from the floral to the geometrically formal.

## FRANCE

## Guimard
French expertise with ironwork, prompted by Eugène-Emmanuel Viollet-le-Duc’s proposals for the use of cast-iron structural elements in new and restored buildings (see here), enriched the French interpretation of Art Nouveau, which was defined by two-dimensionality rather than the three-dimensionality of classical or Gothic architecture.
It was an attempt to break from eclectic historicism.
France’s principal exponent was Paris-based Hector Guimard (1867–1942).
He designed entrances to the Paris Métro subway system that have become monuments to the enthusiasm, even at municipal level, for the style (15.7).
The malleability and strength of cast iron, which could be molded to form frames and extravagant cantilevers for glass panels, allowed him to create the extraordinary decorative structures that still sit obtrusively in the stone-built streets of the city.
Guimard designed the exteriors, interiors, decorative elements, furniture, and fittings for a number of buildings that offer the most complete interpretations of the movement.
The entrance to Castel Béranger (1894–9), a six-story Paris apartment house, is flanked by two stubby, vaguely classical, stone columns around which curl carved stone tendrils (15.8).
Writhing lines continue in the vestibule with heavily molded terracotta tiles, the metal bars that retain them and the stenciled ceiling patterns.
The interiors of apartments vary according to the taste of their owners but old photographs of Guimard in his studio in the building give a clear indication of his vision for the whole.
He built his own four-story house (1909–12) in Paris on an awkward triangular corner site but the twists and turns of Art Nouveau could handle, and even exploit, such awkward geometrics.
In contemporary photographs the interiors show non-rectangular rooms with furniture and decorative elements that epitomize high Art Nouveau (15.9).

## 15.7 Hector Guimard, entrance to Porte Dauphine Station, Paris, c. 1900. Guimard used stan
dard metal elements that could be assembled to form different sized entrance kiosks to the Paris Métro.
All made use of curved details with nature-inspired forms.

## 15.8

## Hector
Guimard, Castel Béranger, Paris, 1894–9.
In the vestibule of this apartment block, Guimard uses bespoke terracotta wall tiles, metal wall details that continue up to and interact with the lines on the painted ceiling, and a metal entrance gate.
The cream background and blue– green painted detail use the pastel palette favored by Art Nouveau designers.

## 15.9 Hector Guimard, group of furniture, France, 1900–5. All three pieces of furniture exh
ibit the contortion of form and line that is the hallmark of Art Nouveau.

## School
of Nancy The Northern city of Nancy rivaled Paris as the center of French Art Nouveau.
In 1903 Eugène Vallin (1856–1922) created Masson House, designing wall paneling, ceiling moldings, lighting fixtures, and furniture.
It, and the dining room in particular, was a concentrated composition of plant-inspired, curvilinear forms (15.10).
Louis Majorelle (1859–1926) was a specialist in the design of furniture using carving, inlay, and ormolu—a decorative technique using an amalgam of finely ground gold and mercury that was outlawed for health reasons c.
1830, but such was its splendor that its use continued discreetly into the 1900s (15.11).

## 15.10 Eugène Vallin, Masson House, Nancy, 1903 (now in the Musée de l’Ecole de Nancy). Val
lin was responsible for the design of everything in this dining room: the built-in cabinet, fireplace surround, overmantel, ceiling detail, hanging light feature, rug, table, and chairs.
They are all shaped by the flowing curves typical of Art Nouveau.
15.11 Louis Majorelle, desk, mahogany with ormulo mounts, c.
1900.
Majorelle was one of the most celebrated of the Art Nouveau designers with a workshop in Nancy in northeastern France.
This desk has the characteristic floating lines and nature-inspired ornamentation of the style.

## Other
French Designers Emile Gallé (1846–1904) designed glass and furniture and opened showrooms across France (15.12).
People were enthusiastic for artifacts in the style but few could afford to build a house in it, so Art Nouveau had its exponents in other areas of design.
As well as furniture, Edouard Colonna (1862–1948) and Eugène Gaillard (1862–1933) designed jewelry.
René Lalique (1860– 1945) was best known for his glass but also designed lamps, jewelry, and textiles.
The style attracted those involved in or interested in fashion but fashions change and, by the beginning of World War I, French Art Nouveau had lost its audience.
Emile Gallé, Libellule cabinet, rosewood and walnut with fruitwood marquetry and bronze hardware, c.
1900.
While most famous for his glassware, Gallé also designed Art Nouveau furniture.
His understanding of botany informed the pieces, which feature distinctive trailing-vine marquetry and edges shaped like stalks or branches.

## BELGIUM

## Horta
In Brussels, Victor Horta (1861–1947) designed his own house and studio (1898), including furniture, light fittings, stained-glass panels, door and window frames, and hardware (15.14).
In the Tassel House (1892), by Horta, the curves of balustrades and column capitals are reprised more freely and sinuously in stenciled wall decorations and the mosaic-tiled floors (15.13).
In the van Eetvelde House (1895), a glass dome is framed by florid curves and supported on iron columns.
These extraordinary confections were his juvenilia and, after them, he abandoned Art Nouveau.

## 15.13 Victor Horta, Tassel House, Brussels, 1892. Stairways offered the Art Nouveau design
er opportunities to develop flowing curves in steps, railings and, as in the Tassel House (now the Mexican Embassy), painted or stenciled colored patterns on walls and ceiling.
The slim column confirms metal as a suitable material for Art Nouveau detail.
The hanging light explores the decorative potential possibilities of the then new electric light.
15.14 Victor Horta, Horta House, Brussels, 1892.
In his own house (now the Horta Museum), Horta included tiled walls and ceilings, built-in cabinets, woodwork with stained-glass inserts, electric lighting fixtures, and furniture, all with flowing curves.
The white tiles and the color palette are typical Art Nouveau.

## Van
de Velde The second significant Belgian Art Nouveau designer was Henry van de Velde (1863–1957).
He designed his own house in Bloemenwerf, Uccle, near Brussels in 1894–5.
He was clearly influenced by British Arts and Crafts and designed his own furniture, fixtures, fittings, and utensils (15.15).
He moved from Brussels to Paris and became designer to Samuel (born Siegfried) Bing (1838– 1919) owner of L’Art Nouveau, the store that gave the style its name.
He established links with the British designers producing proto-Art Nouveau, then moved to Berlin in 1900 where he influenced the evolution of German Art Nouveau or Jugendstil (Young Style), which he demonstrated in his cigar store of 1899 in Berlin (15.16).
In 1902 he moved to Weimar in Germany, to become artis-tic advisor to William Ernest, Grand Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach.
In 1907 he set up the Grand-Ducal School of Arts and Crafts, designed its building, and became its first director.
When war broke out in 1914, he was required to leave Germany and he suggested that Walter Gropius succeed him as director.
Gropius merged the school with the Weimar Art Academy to form the Bauhaus, the cradle of modernism.
Van de Velde also became an advocate of rational design, which distanced him distinctly from Art Nouveau.

## 15.15 This dining chair originally designed for van de Velde’s first marital home, Bloemen
werf, near Brussels.
Although the chair has curved elements, it lacks the exaggerated twists of Art Nouveau, suggested the he was already looking toward simpler forms.
Henry van de Velde, Bloemenwerf chair, Germany, 1898.
Henry van de Velde, Continental Havana Company cigar store, Berlin, 1899.
A Jugendstil interior in which flowing, curved lines confirm a connection to Art Nouveau yet lack the lightness and fluidity of the best French and Belgian examples.

## AUSTRIA:
THE VIENNA SECESSION The group of artists and designers who formed the Viennese Secession were led by the painter Gustav Klimt (1862–1918), whose paintings show a taste for two-dimensional decoration that sits comfortably with Art Nouveau from France and Belgium.
Yet it was the Secessionist architects and designers who created the work that was to shape European architecture and design in the next century.

## Olbrich
Joseph Olbrich (1867–1908) designed the Secession Building (1897) in Vienna as an exhibition hall and headquarters for the movement.
It is symmetrical with cornice moldings, but refutes any suggestion of classical precedents with a great hollow, perforated dome of gilded leaves that pops up between its four squat corner towers (15.17).
Old photographs of the gallery show a low arched ceiling and walls painted with flowing lines and elongated imagery that are distinctly Art Nouveau (15.18).
The tradition of decorative wall painting, often using floral imagery on the rendered exteriors of Middle European buildings transferred easily to Art Nouveau interiors.
The drawing of a room in Olbrich’s Villa Friedmann of 1898 in Vienna (15.19) shows floral painted wall decoration and affinities with Charles Mackintosh’s interiors—and drawing style.
15.17 Joseph Olbrich, Secession Building, Vienna, 1897.
The elements of the building are visually and, apparently, physically independent.
The sphere of gilded leaves appears to be held between the four corner blocks of the entablature that rest lightly on the walls of the structure.
15.18 Joseph Olbrich, interior of Secession Gallery, Secession Building, Vienna, 1897.
The squares for door glazing and other openings in the gallery confirm the Secessionist commitment to pure geometry, while the wall painting uses the flowing lines of French and Belgian Art Nouveau.

## 15.19 Joseph Olbrich, drawing of a room in the Villa Friedmann, Vienna, 1898. Olbrich’s dr
awing of a room for Johanna Friedmann in the Friedmann villa in a Viennese suburb.
The style and content of the drawing, with their natural influences, are typically Secessionist.

## Wagner
Otto Wagner (1841–1918), an established Viennese architect, published Moderne Architektur (Modern Architecture) in 1895 and argued against reuse of historical styles and in favor of design led by function.
In the 1890s he designed major public projects, including a canal system, buildings, and viaducts for the urban rail network, all of which he gave a suitably monumental identity.
Then, in 1898, he designed twin entrance kiosks for the Karlsplatz railroad station that were distinctly delicate, with wall panels of thin marble and glass that hung from a light iron structure (15.20).
In 1899, he borrowed from the vernacular tradition of decoratively painting exteriors and clad the walls of his Majolikahaus (Majolica House) apartment block in weatherresistant brightly colored tin-glazed majolica tiles (15.21).
Thin marble wall panels are hung from a light iron structure.
The central section suggests the cross-section of a railroad car, which may be deliberate.
Otto Wagner, entrance kiosk, Karlsplatz Stadtbahn Station, Vienna, 1898.
15.20 15.21 Otto Wagner, Majolikahaus (Majolica House), Vienna, 1898.
While painting patterns on building façades is an Eastern European tradition, the imagery employed on the majolica tiles of the Majolikahaus, particularly on the top story, has the curvaceous vigor of Art Nouveau.
His most significant project however was the headquarters of the Postal Savings Bank (1904– 6) in Vienna, a convincing step towards the new architecture he had advocated in Modern Architecture.
The exterior of the building is clad in stone panels fixed by bolts with exposed heads as decorative detail.
Interior lobbies, stairs, and corridors are enriched with Secessionist detail in metal and stained glass.
The main banking hall has a high central area with lower spaces on either side, all under a metal-framed glass roof supported by white painted columns again with exposed bolts (15.22).
A structural glass floor filters light to the basement below.
Electric light fixtures and tubular metal hot-air inlets serve a decorative role.
Wooden counters, check-writing desks, and stools are all in Wagner’s increasingly simple design.
The room can be seen as the first modern interior that is practical and aesthetically successful, with elements refined to make practical detail decorative (15.23).
For an architect, like Wagner, with a traditional nineteenthcentury training and experience, the inevitable response was to add detailing grace notes to practical necessities.
15.22 The main banking room is a monumental interior softened by small-scale details.
Painted steel columns support the glass roofs.
Black and white bands in the tiling separate areas in the glass floor, which allows natural light to penetrate the basement floor below.

## Otto
Wagner, Postal Savings Bank, Vienna, 1904–6.
Otto Wagner, Postal Savings Bank, Vienna, 1904–6.
A more detailed view of the discreet detailing in the main hall: the horizontal banding at the base of the hot-air outlet tube, the little spheres that embellish the fixing rings around the outlet grill and the bolts that secure the wall panels, and the thin broken black line that runs around the hall.

## Hoffmann
Josef Hoffmann (1870–1956) had a long career but his most influential work belongs to the Secessionist period.
In 1903 he and Koloman Moser founded the Wiener Werkstätte (Vienna Workshop), a guild of craftworkers producing Secessionist designs.
In their search for a modern style, the Secessionists frequently resorted to geometry—which was at odds with the French and Belgian penchant for flowing tendrils in Art Nouveau.
Hoffman usually made his first sketches on graph paper, which is convincingly demonstrated by his Kubus chair of 1910 (15.25).
Squares dominated his designs for carpets and wallpapers, the perforations he made in metal and wood, and the right-angled corners of his furniture.
By 1903, in the Purkersdorf Sanatorium near Vienna (built 1904–6), Hoffman had embraced the square and eschewed color (15.24).
Its walls were white with a paucity of decoration and the floors were a checkerboard of black and white tiles.
Only a side chair with small circular perforations in its back strays from the right angle.
His obsession with the square is clear in his drawing Corner of a Living Room (1909) made for Ver Sacrum (Scared Spring) magazine (15.26).
His chair for the Cabaret Fledermaus café in Vienna (1906; 15.27), with its little spherical corner pieces and rounded corners, is a curious exception that proves the rule.
15.24 Josef Hoffmann, Purkersdorf Sanatorium, near Vienna, 1904–6.
Hoffmann’s interest in square and simple forms is evident in the entrance hall of the building.
15.25 Josef Hoffmann, Kubus armchair, Austria, 1910.
Hoffmann’s chair is an eroded cube and an extreme expression of the Secessionist commitment to the square.
15.26 Josef Hoffmann, Corner of a Living Room for Ver Sacrum magazine, 1909.
This drawing of an interior from the Secessionist magazine Ver Sacrum shows Hoffmann’s commitment to geometric pattern.
Josef Hoffmann, Fledermaus chair, 1906.
The chair’s structural details, indicate Hoffmann’s wish to dispense with applied decorative elements.
Hoffmann was prolific and designed stores, bars and restaurants, tableware, silver, glassware, leather goods, jewelry, and furniture.
His Morris armchair—inspired by the chair by Philip Webb and produced by William Morris’s company Morris, Marshall, Faulkner & Company—had a structural frame of bentwood and an ingenious adjustable back with square perforations (15.28).
His most famous work is in Brussels, an enormous asymmetrical three-story house (1905–11; 15.29) for the Belgian financier Adolphe Stoclet.
The walls are clad in thin marble sheets edged with narrow bands of gilded metal.
It has a double-height hall and a small theater or music room.
The principal rooms are decorated with marbles of various colors.
The walls of the dining room house the Stoclet Frieze (1905–11), a series of three monumental mosaics designed by Klimt and implemented by Austrian Secessionist artist Leopold Forstner (1878–1936).
An exceptionally large bathroom has marble walls, floors, and fittings along with silver toilet articles by Hoffmann.
Josef Hoffmann, Morris armchair, Vienna, Austria 1900–6.
An interpretation of a chair designed by Philip Webb and produced by William Morris’s firm.
15.29 Josef Hoffmann, Stoclet House, Brussels, 1905–11.
In the dining room, Hoffmann designed the marble walls, built-in cabinets, floor tiles, furniture, and carpet.
