The black and white floor and dark furniture are brightened by the warm marble colors and the mosaic frieze in marble, glass, and semi-precious stones.
These were designed by Gustav Klimt and executed by Leopold Forstner.

## Moser
Koloman Moser (1868–1918) designed stained-glass windows and graphic ornament for the Secession Building and he was also fixated on the square.
The square kneehole in his writing desk of 1903 (15.30) exactly accommodated his Zuckerkandl chair (15.31), which is in essence a hollowed-out cube; both are decorated with squares and a motif that curiously suggests Gothic fenestration.
Despite their impulse to simplify, Secessionist designers still struggled to forego ornament.
The form of both Moser’s pieces is simple but elaborated with a mix of exotic woods and veneers.
The desk and chair exhibit traces of Art Nouveau but their simplicity anticipated something less flamboyant.

## 15.30 Koloman Moser, writing desk, Vienna, 1903. A writing desk designed by Moser and made
by the Werkstätte craftsman Caspar Hrazdil (c.
1890–1945).
Moser’s matching Zuckerkandl chair exactly fitted the kneehole.
Koloman Moser, Zuckerkandl armchair, Vienna, c.
1903.
The chair used thuya wood, mahogany, oak, and deal with inlays of satinwood and brass.

## GERMANY:
JUGENDSTIL

## Riemerschmid
Jugendstil (Young Style) was Germany’s Art Nouveau.
It lacked French and Belgian panache.
Richard Riemerschmid (1868–1957) designed a music room for an exhibition in Dresden in 1899 that included his furniture, lighting, and wall decoration.
Its relative simplicity seems to predict later design directions.
His chair with angled side supports, now seen as influential in the development of modernist chairs, contorts established form but lacks the writhing whimsy of the best Art Nouveau furniture (15.32).
The awkward junctions between diagonal and vertical members, would have been more elegantly achieved in modernist metal.
Riemerschmid collaborated with Bernard Pankok (1872–1943) on the design of a dining room for the 1900 Paris Exposition at which Pankok also designed a smoking room lined with wood carvings, in Art Nouveau style, for windows, ceilings and light fittings.

## 15.32 Richard Riemerschmid, chair, Germany, 1899. Despite the slightly curved corners and
the cross-bracing struts, there is little indication of Art Nouveau (Jugendstil in Germany) in this chair.
Its simplicity suggests it is the result of Riemerschmid’s interest in functionalist design.

## Endell
In 1896 August Endell (1871–1912) designed Atelier Elvira, a two-story photographer’s studio, which has since been destroyed (15.33) There was no hint of historical reference but a bas-relief, which may be derived from waves or sea creatures but which is essentially abstract, dominated the upper façade.
It might be seen as a Jugendstil equivalent to the painted lines that decorated flat walls in interiors by Horta and Guimard.
The window mullions are bent like plant stems, and the shapes are repeated in the entrance hall and stairs.
15.33 August Endell, Atelier Elvira, Munich, 1896 (destroyed 1944).
This small photographer’s studio embodies the essence of Art Nouveau (Jugendstil in Germany) in its avoidance of historicism and the use of curving lines and elements that relate to natural forms.

## SCANDINAVIA
AND THE BALTIC The decoration in paint, plaster relief and tiles used on the façades of buildings around the Baltic and into Middle Europe owed more to local traditions of façade painting than to Art Nouveau.
The strong vernacular traditions of Scandinavia rendered it resistant to influences from the rest of Europe and only Finland, in the throes of its Romantic Nationalism movement, showed evidence of a regional expression of Art Nouveau in which Nordic themes dating to the Viking era were combined with vernacular craft traditions.
The originality and decorative inclinations of Art Nouveau blended with this revivalist work to produce St.
John’s Cathedral in Tampere (1902–7; 15.34) by Lars Sonck (1870–1956).
The stained glass, wall painting, and ornamental plasterwork had more affinities with German Jugendstil than the Art Nouveau of France and Belgium.
In Helsinki Railroad Station (1906), Eliel Saarinen (1873–1950) displayed a style that was transitional between Jugendstil and an early form of modernism.
He would become influential as a promoter of early European modernist theory in the United States.
Lars Sonck, St.
John’s Cathedral, Tampere, Finland, 1902–7.
Art Nouveau was welcomed in Finland.
Sonck was influenced by the brick churches he saw in Germany, but the flowing curves of the architectural elements, the painted ornamental details, the murals, stained glass, and the hanging lights suggest a distinct Finnish interpretation.

## SPAIN

## Gaudí
Antoni Gaudí i Cornet (1852–1926), based in Barcelona, was the leading figure in the Catalan Modernisme movement, the Spanish equivalent of Art Nouveau.
It exhibits the same tendency to twist and distort but it has a primitive quality that may be the result of links to, and respect for, Spanish traditions of strong bright colors and murals of broken ceramic tiles.
Gaudí’s interiors, with their bulging plaster planes and woodwork studded with small irregularly shaped mirrors, are as busy as those of Guimard or Horta but lack the delicacy of line that makes their work quintessential Art Nouveau.
A glance at the plan of his Casa Batlló apartment block demonstrates a persistent need to contort the plans of even the smallest rooms, distortions that are only discernible on a drawing and inconvenient for those using the rooms (15.35 and 15.36).
Gaudí’s work may have lacked the delicacy of the great Belgian and French Art Nouveau interiors but it shared their rejection of the right angle.

## 15.35 Antoni Gaudí, Casa Batlló, plan of second floor, Barcelona, Spain, 1904–6. 1 Dining
room 2 Grand staircase 3 Waiting room with fireplace 4 Salon The building, which stood on a narrow city site, already existed but was reconfigured to Gaudí’s design.
The rooms have unusual plans, produced by curving walls.
Note the swirling ceiling forms indicated with dotted lines in the salon (4) on the street frontage.
15.36 Antoni Gaudí, Casa Batlló, Barcelona, Spain, 1904–6.
The dining room of Casa Batlló has tables and chairs, doors and window frames, paneling, hanging light fixtures, and undulating plaster ceilings in Gaudí’s personal form of Art Nouveau.

## UNITED
STATES Art Nouveau in the United States is almost completely confined to the work of two men, Louis Comfort Tiffany (1848–1933) and Louis H.
Sullivan (1856–1924).

## Tiffany
Tiffany studied painting in the United States and Paris before settling in New York where, at the end of the 1890s, he became interested in the decorative arts.
In 1897, he established Louis C.
Tiffany & Associated Artists, offering design and workshop production of bespoke pieces and his interiors showed awareness of Arts and Crafts work.
In 1885 he reorganized his business as Tiffany Glass Company, concentrating first on stained glass in churches, often with conventionalized pictorial treatment of religious subjects.
In domestic and social interiors, his landscape, floral and semi-abstract themes showed similarities to French Art Nouveau (15.37 and 15.38).
A window titled Four Seasons, with a panel for each season, was exhibited at the Exposition Universelle in Paris in 1900 and established his international reputation.
Bing sold Tiffany’s work in his L’Art Nouveau store in Paris and he began to specialize in the production of vases, bowls, paperweights, and lamps with metal bases, all with colorful floral or abstract motifs.
They rivalled the work of the French glassworkers Gallé and Lalique, both of whom had visited Europe in the 1890s when Art Nouveau was emerging as the most radical movement across all design disciplines.
Whether either were strongly influenced is debatable.
It is as likely that they had absorbed the spirit of their age.
Louis Comfort Tiffany, window, Rochroane, Irvington-on-Hudson, New York, 1905 (now in the Corning Museum of Glass, New York).
Tiffany’s fame rests primarily on his work in stained glass.
He developed techniques for its use in lamps with glass shades and in vases.
Windows such as this in a reception room were executed in a pictorial style that related to painting of the period.
Louis Comfort Tiffany, Tiffany Residence, New York.
Reproduced from Artistic Houses, 1883–4.
In his work as a decorator, Tiffany used ornamental elements based on Victorian taste, Arts and Crafts principles, and his own artistic impulses.

## Sullivan
The delicate traceries of Louis H.
Sullivan’s door furniture for the Guaranty Building, in Buffalo, New York $( 1 8 9 4 - 5 ; 1 5 .
3 9 )$ have been compared to the best of European Art Nouveau.
However, chronologically, it is unlikely that he would have been aware of events in Europe and it is more likely that he had taken John Ruskin’s advice and looked to nature for inspiration.
Until the emergence of his pupil and colleague, Frank Lloyd Wright, Sullivan was the most influential of the Chicago architects who were setting examples in the design of skyscrapers and his capacity to create exquisitely detailed, usually plant-inspired decoration for cladding cast-iron columns and beams clearly offered a possible language for modern buildings.
His decoration, generally executed in unglazed terracotta which allowed fine modeling and batch production, was indisputably modern but was sidelined when the new architectural establishment banished ornament from its vocabulary.

## 15.39 Louis Sullivan, Guaranty Building, Buffalo, New York, 1894–5. The comparison made wi
th Art Nouveau for decorative detail designed by Sullivan for many of his buildings is supported by these doorknobs.
His detail was based on natural forms although his writings on architecture emphasized function in a way that pointed to modernism.
American Art Nouveau directions had, in the end, no more lasting presence than they had in Europe.
Critics and historians in the early twentieth century took to referring to Art Nouveau as a “style that failed,” or to dismissing it as frivolous, tasteless, and even overly decorative.
Rediscovery of Art Nouveau began only after World War II, when exhibitions, publications, and fresh study brought it back into its rightful place as an important step in the development of modernism.
The Emergence of Modernism CHAPTER SIXTEEN Adolf Loos, interior, American Bar, Vienna, 1908.
Although the little basement room of this bar has no applied decoration, it is intense with a mix of marble, onyx, mahogany, brass, frosted glass, and mirrors, all on a green and white tiled floor.
Art Nouveau was an attempt to find an architectural language that did not revive past styles.
It was extremely decorative, briefly fashionable, and faded away within twenty years.
In the United States, and Chicago in particular, commercial forces were driving technological innovation and a confident national identity encouraged the idea of a unique American architectural style.
When Louis Sullivan created ornament, he did not draw on classical precedents but on nature—and American nature, not European nature.
Frank Lloyd Wright would also look for his inspiration to the American landscape in the shape of the prairies of the Midwest.

## SULLIVAN
Louis H.
Sullivan (1856–1924) has been described as the first modern architect but his persistent commitment to decoration separates him from twentieth-century European modernists for whom the elimination of ornament became an article of faith.
He was born in Boston where he worked briefly with Frank Furness before moving to Chicago in 1873, when the city was in the midst of a building boom following the Great Fire of 1871.
There, he worked with William Le Baron Jenney (1832–1907), who had built the city’s first steel-framed building, but Jenney’s practice may have been too prosaic and he decamped to Paris.
After a year at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts he returned to Chicago and, in the office of Joseph S.
Johnston & John Edelman, designed stencils for a decorative frieze in the Chicago Avenue Church (now Moody Church, c.
1875) that established his reputation as a designer of decorative motifs.
In 1879 German-trained Dankmar Adler (1844–1900) hired him and, a year later, took him into partnership.
Adler dealt with technical matters and finding commissions, Sullivan led on design.
His first significant work was the Chicago Auditorium Building (1886–90; 16.2), an opera house hidden in the center of a hotel and office complex.
His principal contribution was the interiors of lobbies, public areas in the hotel, and the auditorium, which demonstrated his ability as both a spatial tactician and designer of ornament.
The ceiling of the auditorium was a series of great arches concealing electric partitions that could be lowered to reduce the size of the 4,200- seat auditorium.
The hotel dining room was at roof level overlooking Lake Michigan, under an arched ceiling with skylights.
Its walls and ceilings were edged with Sullivan’s decorative friezes.
16.2 Louis Sullivan, Auditorium Building, Chicago, 1886–90.
With Dankmar Adler, Sullivan designed the building that combined offices, a hotel, and the opera house that gave the building its name.
Sullivan designed many of the interior spaces, of which the auditorium is the most spectacular.
It was unlike any older theater or concert hall in its decoration: the ceiling arches with their painted detail, the proscenium design, and the organ grills brought light, color, and texture.
He became a virtuoso in cladding the raw steel structures of the new commercial buildings, such as the Bayard-Condict Building in New York (16.3 and 16.4) or the Carson Pirie department store in Chicago (16.5) in strips and panels of terracotta moldings, all inspired by natural forms.
Thus it was significant when in 1892, in his essay “Ornament in Architecture” for The Engineering Magazine,” he suggested a moratorium on the use of ornament until an appropriate decorative language could be evolved.
He said, “It would be greatly for our aesthetic good if we were to refrain entirely from the use of ornament.” It was a rhetorical statement, a plea not for the abandonment of ornament but for reflection on an appropriate form for the new urban contexts.
He offered another homily in 1896 when he said that “form ever follows function and this is the [natural] law,” giving modernists a mantra, although for them function referred to practical efficiency and ignored that one of a building’s traditional functions was to give pleasure and denied the human instinct to decorate that had been prodigiously manifested in Victorian homes.
The building is on 65 Bleecker Street between Broadway and Lafayette Street.
Its steel frame is overlaid with small scale moldings that give the façade a soft texture at a distance.
Louis Sullivan, Bayard-Condict Building, New York, 1897–9.
16.3 16.4 Sullivan was the master of cladding iron structural frames in terracotta moldings of his own design, and the intricate interweavings of plant forms is clear when viewed up close.
Louis Sullivan, Bayard-Condict Building, New York, 1897–9.
16.5 Louis Sullivan, Carson Pirie department store (now the Sullivan Center), Chicago, 1904.
Detail of the intricate molding above the main entrance bears no resemblance to any historical precedent.
It is modern, but satisfies the popular enthusiasm for ornament and becomes visually richer as the viewer comes closer.
In 1914 Sullivan’s Merchants’ National Bank, in Grinnell Iowa, was in essence a plain brick cuboid with a large, modestly decorated side window and cornice but his greatest offence to modernist eyes was his full-blooded embellishment of the monumental entrance door.
There is no precedent for the decorative language he used but the pure geometry of the major elements and the leaves and twigs of secondary elements offered a comprehensible decorative language, free from familiar Neoclassicism and Neo-Gothic heritages (16.6).
Within only a few years, ornament in any form would be declared a crime against modernity.
Louis Sullivan, Merchants’ National Bank, Grinnell, Iowa, 1914.
A modest brick cuboid building with strategically placed decorative detail.
The isolation of decorative elements in an otherwise blank façade is a break from tradition but the over-scaling of the entrance is traditional.
Modern buildings seldom signal their entry point so dramatically.

## WRIGHT
Early in his career, Frank Lloyd Wright (1867–1959) was employed in the offices of Adler and Sullivan, from 1887 to 1893, and he worked closely with Sullivan, who recognized the value of his contributions.
Wright later acknowledged Sullivan as a significant influence: the pronouncement that form should follow function freed Wright from the conventions of Beaux-Arts eclecticism and Sullivan’s nature-inspired ornament encouraged his inclination toward “organic” forms.
They had a fractious relationship however.
Wright wanted creative independence, and broke his contract by working for his own clients outside office hours and later resigned.
Once independent, Wright was prolific, completing more than four hundred projects over an eighty-year career that can be divided into two phases.
The first phase extended until c.
1920.
The second phase began after 1930.
He set up practice in 1893 in the Chicagoan suburb of Oak Park, designing his own house (1889) and an adjacent studio.
He received commissions from successful businessmen who, with good private and public transport, could now live in desirable suburbs.
The houses Wright designed for them were categorized as Prairie houses by critics and academics, who presumed that the long, low buildings were influenced by the flat plains of the Midwest.
They were also influenced by the British Arts and Crafts movement but Wright’s intellectual insularity and response to the landscape in which he built produced dwellings in what has been described as the first uniquely American architectural style.
The Winslow House (1893; 16.7) in River Forest, Illinois has a symmetrical elevation but a strong horizontal emphasis, particularly in a low-pitched hipped roof that extends significantly beyond external walls and the horizontal bands of different external finishes.
Internally, rooms were clustered around a central fireplace and this became Wright’s standard planning strategy.
The entrance hall has an arcaded alcove with seats on either side of a fireplace.
The dining room on the other side of the chimney extends into a semi-circular conservatory.
Ornamental detail, which includes stained-glass inserts in some windows, suggests Sullivan’s influence but shows signs of moving toward Wright’s own more abstract geometric motifs.
Frank Lloyd Wright, Winslow House, River Forest, Illinois, 1893.
In his early work, Wright often used details that hint at architectural tradition and the influence of his association with Louis Sullivan.
Off the entrance hall, this small loggia holds a fireplace flanked by built-in seating.
The Hickox House (1900) in Kankakee, Illinois retains symmetry only in its interconnecting living, dining, and music rooms.
It has the overhanging gabled roof, long horizontal bands of windows, and low walls extending into the garden that characterize Prairie houses.
The street façade is entirely asymmetrical.
Its white plastered wall surfaces divided by strips of wood have a Japanese flavor, which may reflect Wright’s interest in Japanese prints, which he shared with the Aesthetic movement in Britain.
In 1907 Wright designed a house surrounded by gardens, a pool, and service buildings for Avery Coonley in Riverside, Illinois, another Chicago suburb (16.8).
The plan is developed on a modular square grid, a device Wright often used to unify elements.
Squares are the unifying theme for decorative tiling and plaster patterns on exterior walls, and for interior details such as patterned woven rugs and stained-glass window inserts.
A drawing of the interior, which Wright made for the Ladies’ Home Journal in 1901, shows interconnecting living areas, extensive built-in joinery, and bespoke furniture.
Ceilings reflect the profile of the roofs, wooden strips suggest the patterns of structural members, and decorative ceiling panels conceal light sources.
As in most of Wright’s interiors, warmth and color were provided by natural materials.
In 1954, in his book The Natural House, he wrote, “A plain flat surface cut to shape for its own sake, however large or plain the shape, is, the moment it is sophisticatedly so cut, no less ornament than egg and dart.” He was in agreement with those who would see in the natural colors and textures of building materials all the decoration they needed.
He differed in that he was prepared to call it decoration.
16.8 Frank Lloyd Wright, Coonley House, Riverside, Illinois, 1907.
By the time this house was designed, Wright had established his own modern style as is evident in this drawing, reproduced in magazines and books in the Netherlands and Germany.
The ceiling pattern reflects the roof structure but is strongly decorative.
Geometry underpins the design of stained glass and the bespoke rug.
The furniture is designed by Wright.
Wright’s greatest Prairie house is considered to be the Robie House for Frederick C.
Robie in south Chicago (1908–10).
It has long, cantilevered roof overhangs with long, low horizontal windows, and long brick walls that stretch into the garden.
On plan, two rectangles “slide” past one another.
The southwest block holds the principal living areas above a playroom and a billiard room.
The entrance hall is at the top of a central stair and leads to a living room to the west and a dining room to the east (16.9).
The rooms flow together, separated only by a central fireplace and the open stairway behind it.
On the south side, a range of twelve doors with stained-glass panels open to a balcony that runs the length of the building.
At the west end, a triangular, glazed bay window is flanked by a pair of glazed doors with stained-glass inserts.
Decorative wooden bands across ceiling surfaces and lighting fixtures unify the interior.
Wright designed furniture, rugs, and textiles.
His high-backed dining chairs were intended to give a sense of enclosure for diners sitting around the table in the open space of the dining area.
He only supervised the early stages of construction for the Robie House because he closed his studio in 1909 amid a scandal over his affair with Mamah Cheney, the wife of a client for whom he had designed a Prairie house in 1903.
16.9 Frank Lloyd Wright, dining area, Robie House, Chicago, 1908–10.
The high-backed chairs and the lamp structures that rise above tabletop level to give diners a sense of intimacy were designed by Wright, although it is likely that he collaborated with George Mann Niedecken on the design.
The built-in cabinet work, the stained-glass windows, and ceiling detail are typical of Wright’s work at the time.
Wright’s growing reputation brought him a number of non-residential commissions, including a six-story office building for the Larkin Company in Buffalo, New York (1904; 16.10).
The company sold soap by mail order and Wright designed its offices around a central atrium, 76- feet (23-m) high, crowned with inscriptions in praise of honest labor.
The well-lit central space protected workers from the pollution of surrounding railroad yards.
At the base of the five-story atrium there were desks set at right angles to the long axis, and each desk could accommodate six members of staff.
Parapets of cream brick on each of the upper floors were set back by one brick width—9 inches (23 cm)—from the face of the structural brick piers that thus rose uninterrupted for the full height of the atrium until crowned by discreet Wrightian molded detail.
Wright designed every element of the interior, including clusters of lights on the ends of each desk in the atrium, and introduced various technical innovations: glass doors, air conditioning, radiant heating, built-in desks for storage, and toilet bowls cantilevered to aid cleaning.
Wright described it as “a genuine expression of power directly applied to purpose, in the same sense that the ocean liner, the plane or the car is so.” European modernists would also consistently express their admiration for those examples of technological modernity.
The Larkin building demonstrated how to strip away decorative excess while still creating a place that inspired awe and wonder but, at its unveiling, critics regretted the lack of Beaux-Arts embellishments.
Frank Lloyd Wright, Larkin Building, Buffalo, New York, 1904, (now demolished).
Wright organized spaces for office workers on several levels around a top-lit atrium.
Filing cabinets were housed in alcoves.
He designed the furniture, which included chairs attached to desks by swinging arm supports.
Electric-light clusters of his design augment daylight.
In 1905 Wright designed Oak Park Unity Temple, a Unitarian Universalist church.
The site 16.11 bordered a busy road, so he located the church entrance on the opposite side and turned once more to the introspective Larkin formula of blank exterior walls and a glazed ceiling.
It was his first use of reinforced concrete into which he sparingly cast decorative motifs internally (16.12).
Projecting balconies, a ceiling with a grid of square skylights, bands of wood on white walls, pendant light fittings, and geometrically patterned, stained-glass windows created an abstractly complex space suggestive of directions that were to surface in Europe a few years later (16.11).
The minister, Rodney Johonnot, had asked for a building embodying “unity, truth, beauty, simplicity, freedom and reason,” words that might have been borrowed by fledgling European modernists for their cause.
Wright pronounced that Unity Temple represented the first expression of an entirely new architecture.
Frank Lloyd Wright, interior, Oak Park Unity Temple, Chicago, 1905.
The interior of building was considered so unconventional, when compared to the prevailing classical or Gothic reviva designs that it was felt that calling it a “church” would be inappropriate, so it became a “temple.” 16.12 Frank Lloyd Wright, exterior, Oak Park Unity Temple, Chicago, 1905.
The decoration cast into Unity Temple’s reinforced-concrete walls takes no obvious inspiration from classical or Gothic precedents but has some resemblance to the abstract geometric patterns in the stained glass of Wright’s Prairie houses.
In 1909 Wright left his wife and children to go to Europe, ostensibly to oversee the publication of one hundred lithographs of his work by the German publisher Ernst Wasmuth Verlag but also to rendezvous discreetly with Mamah Cheney.
The book was to have a significant influence on the evolution of European modernism.
Wright’s most valued assistant and a renowned architectural illustrator, Marion Mahony (1871–1961), made more than half the drawings but, when Wright left for Europe, Mahony declined to take over the practice and he offered it to Hermann V. von Holst (1874–1955), a prominent Chicagoan architect, stipulating that Mahony should have control over the design of ongoing projects and George Mann Niedecken (1878–1945), who had worked on the interiors of three Prairie houses, should deal with interiors.
Niedecken was a successful designer of furniture, stained glass, lighting, tapestries, and murals in his own right but chairs for the Gilmore House of 1908 were collaborations with Wright and his table lamp for the Edward P.
Irving house, which he designed and which belongs to the Prairie school, treats wooden elements and stained glass in a Wrightian fashion (16.13 and 16.14).
It would be easy to give Wright primary credit but the fact that he specified that Niedecken should take responsibility for interior design when he retreated to Europe suggests that he saw his contribution as crucial.
Frank Lloyd Wright and George Mann Niedecken, chairs for Eugene A.
Gilmore House, Madison, Wisconsin, 1908.
The chairs are the result of a collaborative effort between Wright and the furniture specialist Niedecken.
George Mann Niedecken, table lamp for Edward P. and Florence Bernice Irving House, Decataux, Illinois, 1909.
The lamp of quarter-sawn white oak, colored glass, and copper, measures 24 inches (61 cm) high, 23 inches (60 cm) long and 15 inches (38 cm) wide.
It was manufactured by the Niedecken-Walbridge Company.
In Chicago, Wright had been much closer to the consequences of the technological changes that were agitating European radicals and he was offering examples of the form modern architecture might take.
In 1909 the Wasmuth portfolio of his Prairie house drawings galvanized Europe’s architectural radicals.
It is easy to see how the horizontal emphasis in the houses offered a subversive alternative to the verticality of classical and Gothic traditions.
Wright was pleased to accept his role in influencing European modernists but refused to acknowledge that he had learned anything from them and the buildings he designed later in his career show nothing to suggest he did.

## CHANGE
IN EUROPE In Britain, Queen Victoria died in 1901, after ruling for sixty-three years.
She was succeeded by her sixty-year-old son Edward VII and, like her, he gave his name to an era, but one remembered, not for rectitude, but for moral laxity and conspicuous consumption.
The British Empire continued to generate enormous wealth but the country was losing its place as the dominant world power to the United States, which, 125 years after breaking loose from that empire, was colonizing its own vast, western hinterlands and absorbing the immigrants who were deserting Europe for the opportunities it offered.
Americans, old and new, seemed to have an entrepreneurial gene that allowed them to understand the potential of European innovations and find a way to make them practical and profitable.
In England, Sir Humphry Davy (1778–1829) developed the first practical electric arc light in 1806 but it was Thomas Edison (1847–1931), from Ohio, who created the incandescent filament light bulb in 1879 that eliminated the gloom of the Victorian interior and changed how it would be used and decorated.
At the end of the 1870s, the unstoppable Edison took out patents on the recording machines and gramophones that replaced the piano as the source of domestic entertainment, and the telephone that changed the practices of business and social intercourse.
In France, the Lumière brothers, Auguste (1862–1954) and Louis (1864–1948), along with George Méliès (1861–1938) pioneered cinema but it was Edison who, in 1891, filed patents for the filmmaking equipment that allowed escapees from Eastern European ghettoes to play major roles in the transformation of popular mass entertainment and replace vaudeville with cinema.
In Germany, Karl Benz (1844–1929) developed the first operational automobile but Henry Ford (1863–1947), from Michigan, pioneered the production-line techniques that democratized automobile ownership and established the template for a second industrial revolution.
The Wright brothers, Orville (1871–1948) and Wilber (1867–1912), made their first short motorpowered air flight in 1903.
The airplane, the automobile, and the possibilities they suggested are cited as inspiration for the seismic artistic upheavals.
The Futurists, a group of Italian poets and painters, declared in their manifesto of 1909 an intention to destroy everything old.
The world was awash with “modernity,” even warfare in World War I would be described as “modern.” The arts appropriated the word.
In 1930, the English novelist E.
F.
Benson (1867–1940) reflecting on change at the beginning of the twentieth century, wrote of “such manifestations of scientific marvels as no other short period can point to, motorcars and moving pictures, telephones and electric lighting, X-rays and other ultra-spectrum potencies.” He was not alone.
In the first decades of the century, it seemed to a few radicals that industrialization and new technologies had delivered change that deserved its own architectural style.
New and old building types had been shaped and reshaped by necessity.
In 1899 the French engineer Auguste Choisy (1841–1909) published L’Histoire de l’Architecture (The History of Architecture), in which he argued that significant changes in architectural styles had been the result of engineering innovation, citing classicism’s post-andbeam construction, and Gothic’s flying buttresses.
Nineteenth-century engineers like him had created the iron and glass roofs of railroad termini and raised the skyscrapers.
Practical changes were accepted for the practical benefits they brought, but the architectural, and popular, consensus was that they should be clad in familiar decorative skins.
Nineteenthcentury innovation was challenging the capacity of accepted architectural styles to deal with new building forms and the architects, whose job it was to create façades for cast-iron structures, appeared to be intimidated by the task and looked backward to find ways, however incongruous, to dress the new.
Even the nineteenth-century radicals who had disapproved of Gothic Revival’s excesses sought their solution in another revival, the neo-vernaculars of Arts and Crafts.
Fin-desiècle aesthetes had struck blows, and sardonic poses, against Victorian orthodoxies but the rebels of the new century chose to be serious, to destroy not just revivalisms but the aesthetic instincts to decorate that had prevailed since caves were painted.

## The
Radicals

## Duchamp
In 1917 the French painter, sculptor, and chess player Marcel Duchamp (1877–1968), aka R.
Mutt, displayed a urinal in an art gallery and introduced the idea of the readymade object as sculpture— a precedent and validation for interior designers who would learn to complement new and extant elements when empty utilitarian buildings became prized for their intrinsic qualities.
This became important with the advent of postmodernism in the 1970s when the found object and the recycled material provided a way to evoke ersatz character within bland building shells.

## Loos
Adolf Franz Karl Viktor Maria Loos (1870–1933) had strong opinions on decoration.
He was an Austrian and Czechoslovak architect and designer, a theorist, and a journalist.
He enjoyed being provocative and, among other things, declared his admiration for English tailoring and American plumbing.
His entry for a competition to design offices for the Chicago Tribune newspaper in 1922 confirms his mischievous inclination.
He proposed a tower in the form of a Doric column that rose twenty-four stories from twelve stories of a ziggurat-topped cube (16.15).
It looked absurd but little more than the winning Gothic Revival entry by John Mead Howells (1868–1959) and Raymond Hood (1881–1934)—a tower that fused the verticality of American commercial architecture with Gothic flourishes, under a buttressed crown inspired by that on the thirteenthcentury cathedral in the French city of Rouen.
That crown would have a significant influence on the topping out of the American skyscraper over the next two decades.
Adolf Loos, competition entry for design of the Chicago Tribune Tower, 1925.
Loos’s design for a tower is supposedly a visual pun on the idea of a newspaper column.
Loos visited the United States between 1893 and 1896 and would have been aware of Sullivan’s suggestion that ornamenting buildings should be temporarily suspended.
In his essay “Architecture” of 1910 he suggested that “only a very small part of architecture belongs to the realm of art: the tomb and the monument.” Everything else, from factories to railroad stations to shops and restaurants he pronounced to be mere buildings and conceded that they could pander to the untutored taste for decoration.
In 1910, in a lecture in Vienna, he suggested that civilized people had no need for ornamental superficialities and explained, perhaps facetiously, that tattoos were the self-inflicted, self-loathing ornament of the criminal underclass.
In 1913 the text of the lecture was published, as Ornement et Crime (Ornament and Crime) in the French magazine Les Cahiers d’Aujourd’hui.
To anglophones “ornement et crime” sounds like “ornement est crime” (ornament is crime) as if ornament was being criminalized but, in 1913, few agreed with Loos.
The Emperor Franz Joseph I of Austria (1830–1916) changed his route to and from his palace in Vienna in order to avoid seeing the department store Loos designed for Goldman & Salatsch in 1909, which was alarmingly free of moldings.
16.16 Adolf Loos, street-level interior, Knize men’s fashion store, Vienna, 1910.
Oak cabinets house shirts and accessories.
To the rear of the store, a helical stair leads up to workshops and an oakpaneled retreat for customers In 1910 Loos designed a small store for a men’s outfitter and tailor, Knize, which was a brusque intrusion on a Viennese street of luxury shops and banks.
Elements of the façade—the plinth, frieze, and flanking columns—were black Swedish granite, with modest inset glass display sections (16.17).
The narrow ground floor displayed shirts and accessories in simply detailed glass-fronted oak cabinets.
A more generous sales area shared the upper floor with a tailoring salon, workrooms, fitting rooms, and an oak-paneled retreat for favored clients (16.16).
Adolf Loos, Knize men’s fashion store, Vienna, 1910.
The black granite façade of the Knize store is bulky and polished but without decorative detail.
When constructed it stood out on a street of banks and luxury stores with conventional wooden framed windows.
Like Hoffmann and Wright, Loos proposed that the inherent beauty of favored building materials was superior to applied ornament.
In 1908 he tested the theory in the dark basement of the American Bar in Kärntner Street in Vienna—it has also become known as Kärntner Bar (16.1).
Materials included marble, onyx, mahogany, and brass above a green and white checkerboard floor.
Light was filtered through frosted-glass tabletops and the kaleidoscopic mélange was bounced back and forth to infinity between mirrored walls, one above the bar and one on the opposite wall.
Had Loos applied ornament it is doubtful if it would be noticed in the visual cacophony.
He treated his residential interiors similarly, using veneers of wood grains and marble veins.
His other contribution to the domestic interior was his raumplan, in which areas were subdivided by changes of level, and walls—when unavoidable—were cut away and pierced to give glimpses from one area to another.
The strategy was most effectively demonstrated in the Villa Müller (1930) and was, perhaps, another idea he had picked up in the United States where he encountered the areas of Wright’s Prairie houses separated only by fireplaces and stairwells (16.18).
16.18 Adolf Loos, Villa Müller, Prague, 1930.
An example of Loos’s raumplan, in which areas are decided by changes in level and walls are opened up to give views between rooms.
Having dispensed with applied decoration, he relied on the grain of marble to decorate his surfaces.
Stripped of decoration, Loos’s houses were raw, with flat wall surfaces pierced by windows that were free of any decorative moldings.
The exception was an unsolicited and unbuilt project of 1928 for the celebrated African American entertainer Josephine Baker, for whom he proposed façades of narrow horizontal black and white marble stripes, which are presumed to have symbolized her integration into white society.

## WAR
AND REVOLUTION World War I (1914–8) and the Russian Revolution (1917–23) seemed to energize architectural revolutionaries.
They poured out manifestoes and demanded the rejection of social and cultural norms on the presumption that traditional architectural languages had legitimized and celebrated the social and political structures, precipitating World War I.
Adopting the cause of detoxifying architectural culture, they proposed to eliminate its familiar forms and motifs.
In doing so, they ignored the enshrined principles and decorative devices that made buildings aesthetically enjoyable and sometimes uplifting.
An evolutionary rather than a revolutionary process might have produced a popular modernity but avant-gardists were disinclined to compromise and keen to outrage those beyond their circle.
The removal, at the end of the war, of incumbent political and cultural dinosaurs left the way clear for political and cultural totalitarians.
It was a time of belligerent, hyperbolic sloganeering.
In their manifesto of 1909 Italian Futurists had rhapsodized about the “red sword of the sun slashing for the first time through the shadows of a thousand years.” In 1918 the Dutch radicals of the De Stijl movement called on “all those who believe in the reform of art and culture to annihilate these obstacles of development that prevent further development.” Le Corbusier began his 1923 polemic Vers Une Architecture (Toward an Architecture) with “A great epoch has begun.
There exists a new spirit.” (The title of the English-language translation was “Toward a New Architecture.” The original title suggested something portentous and systemic, the translation suggested a change of style.) Most of the venom was directed against decoration, the essential component of interior design, which was abruptly deemed synonymous with degeneracy and reaction.

## Le
Corbusier World War I granted Futurists their wish for powerful machines and mass destruction.
Charles-Edouard Jeanneret, known as Le Corbusier (1887–1965), was a Swiss architect working in France and retreated to his neutral homeland at the outbreak of war in 1914.
There, excited by airplanes, automobiles, ocean liners, and grain silos, he formulated the theories that became modernist dogma.
In 1915, in collaboration with the engineer Max Dubois, he revealed his design for Domino House, which was essentially a structural diagram showing reinforced-concrete floor slabs supported on reinforced-concrete columns that eliminated the need for load-bearing walls.
With that structural system there was no reason why floor areas could not be compartmentalized and any elevational treatment, including historical pastiches, could not be applied to the exterior.
However, the Domino House diagram suggested empty spaces and transparent elevations (16.19).
Le Corbusier in collaboration with Max Dubois, Domino House, 1915.
A polemical drawing illustrating how reinforced-concrete columns, which eliminated the need for load-bearing externa walls, could support reinforced-concrete floors eliminating the need for structural internal walls.
In 1917 Le Corbusier collaborated with the painter Amédée Ozenfant (1886–1966) to write Après le Cubisme (After Cubism), in which they accused Cubism of having become decorative.
They advocated a form of Cubist abstract painting they called Purism, in which color was considered secondary to form—although it could be used to enhance it.
An important Purist concept was the “objet-type” (object-type), the archetypal object.
They cited examples such as the Bordeaux wine bottle and the violin as objects that had evolved to perform tasks efficiently and, consequently, seemed incapable of being improved.
Le Corbusier would claim that such perfectly evolved objects were all that was needed to make a perfect interior.

## DE
STIJL

## Van
Doesburg In the Netherlands, Theo van Doesburg (1883–1931) founded De Stijl (The Style) magazine in 1917 and exhorted its readers to destroy everything that stood in the way of progress.
Like-minded artistic iconoclasts came together to form the De Stijl movement, among them the painter Piet Mondrian (1871–1944) and the sculptor Jean (Hans) Arp (1887–1966), who were both advocates of pure abstraction.
They eliminated the figurative forms in their work and developed a theory called Neoplasticism, in a number of manifestoes.
It asserted the superiority of geometric form and color (black and the primaries) over all naturalistic and subjective values in art.
Their insistence on the importance of straight lines, right angles, and a limited color range relieved them of the obligation to consider more subtle solutions.
The greatest De Stijl interior was van Doesburg’s Café l’Aubette in Strasbourg, France (1926– 8; 16.20), an amalgam of bar, dancehall, and movie theater that sat behind an eighteenth-century Baroque façade but unwaveringly conformed to De Stijl’s principles.
Van Doesburg “exploded” a De Stijl painting by translating it into three dimensions.
Booths lined two sides of a dance floor.
A white film screen hung in front of a wall of red and gray rectangles angled at 45 degrees.
These were “folded” at the junction of wall and ceiling to generate horizontal triangles, squares, and rectangles across the ceiling.
Walls and ceiling were visually deconstructed.
There is little evidence of modernism’s sober hallmarks.

## 16.20 Theo van Doesburg, movie theater/dancehall, Café l’Aubette, Strasbourg, France, 1926
–8.
In this entertainment center, with bars, ballrooms and movie theater, van Doesburg used De Stijl abstract geometric forms to generate an unsettlingly modern interior.
In the movie theater/dance hall seen here, films were projected onto the central screen while patrons occupied booths or danced on the central dance floor.
Van Doesburg worked with Jean Arp and his wife, the Swiss artist and designer Sophie Taeuber-Arp (1889–1943), on designing the abstract elements, which the public disliked when it was opened.

## Rietveld
The best-known De Stijl work was produced by Gerrit Rietveld (1888–1964), the son of a joiner who became his father’s apprentice at the age of eleven.
He studied at night school and worked as a draftsman for a Utrecht jeweler, then in 1917 set up his own furniture workshop and designed his red–blue chair (16.21).
Its flat, unupholstered planes so blatantly ignored the essentials of comfort that it was, and continues to be, revered by modernists.
Rietveld kept the design simple because he hoped the chair would be mass produced.
In 1918 he set up his own factory and, having become familiar with De Stijl principles, painted the back red and the seat blue, with black structural members sporting yellow ends.
Continuous production has satisfied the demand, principally among architects and designers, to own this icon.
It is said to be reasonably comfortable.

## 16.21 Gerrit Rietveld, red–blue chair, 1917. Two sheets of plywood, held in position by th
e black frame, serve as seat and back in this chair.
Connections between the members are made by hidden metal pins so that the elements are visually independent and painted in three primary colors plus black.
Rietveld’s major work was a small suburban house in Utrecht (16.22) for pharmacist Truus Schröder-Schräder (1889–1985).
Until the death of her husband in 1923, she had lived in a large apartment but, intrigued by De Stijl principles, had collaborated with Rietveld to create her own stark room in the otherwise conventionally furnished interior.
After she was widowed, she commissioned Rietveld to design a house for her and her three children.
She knew what she wanted, collaborated with Rietveld, and has been credited as its joint designer.
Theirs was a harmonious partnership, they became lovers and he lived in the house until his death.
16.22 Gerrit Rietveld with Truus Schröder-Schräder, Schröder House, Utrecht, The Netherlands, 1924.
This colorful, fragmented object sits provocatively on the end of a conventional brick terrace.
Perhaps only a furniture designer and a pharmacist could have created such a deviation from architectural tradition.
The house sits, a colorful abstraction, on the end of a conventional nineteenth-century brick row but embodies the De Stijl manifesto and clearly spurns the past.
It is scrupulously orthogonal on plan and section but projecting elements never quite align, suggesting a building in a state of flux.
The mass is eroded further by balconies and projecting eaves.
The façades are broken up into what appear to be free-floating rectangles painted in shades of light grays; color is provided by vertical and horizontal red and yellow strips that are window frames and balcony supports.
The lower floor is conventionally subdivided into bedrooms.
The upper living area can be subdivided by sliding panels (16.23).
The base colors for walls and ceiling are white and gray; they are broken by black lines of framing and rectangles of primary colors that define areas when the panels slide back.
The house is without precedent or obvious imitators.
It was an early warning of rumblings in architecture and design.
16.23 Gerrit Rietveld with Truus Schröder-Schräder, Schröder House, Utrecht, The Netherlands, 1924.
Sliding panels can screen off individual rooms, or open up to make one space, as shown.
The color scheme of white, black, red, and blue is undiluted De Stijl.
Rietveld went on to produce more conventional modern architecture that is good but solidly in the mainstream.
In 1934 he produced another extraordinary chair, made again from flat wooden panels, assembled in the shape of the letter “Z” with an added back panel.
It appears fragile but rivals the red–blue chair’s status as an example of modernism.
It has generally held that Wright’s Prairie houses, as revealed in the Wasmuth volumes, influenced the development of modernist design theory and it is easy to see how the low profiles and oversailing roofs, prompted by the flat plains of the American Midwest, struck a chord with the Dutch who had claimed their own flat lands from the sea, but De Stijl had little in common with the definitive brand of modernist architecture that would evolve in France and Germany in the 1920s.
The Dutch variant would have appeared a little frivolous and its principles too open to individual interpretation.
French and German modernism had rules and restrictions that left little room for input from interior designers.
Modernism CHAPTER SEVENTEEN With this early structure, Mies van der Rohe established the austere decorative palette to which he would adhere for the remaining forty years of his career and which would become stylistic models for his followers and the preferred international style of corporate architecture.
Modernism might be characterized as a movement to reject architectural conventions, to impose new rules.
In the 1920s, there were competing strands of modernity and, in any history of interior design, the different intentions of rival factions are important because they created divergent architectural cultures to which interior design was obliged to respond.
In the beginning, the most aggressive of these factions was identified by a number of labels, which implied a new, unemotional response to the act of designing.
In German it was Neue Sachlichkeit (New Objectivity), in French L’Esprit Nouveau (The New Spirit), in English it was Functionalism.
It was fortunate in the end to be modernism, which gave it custody of the word labeled “modern” and the progressive virtues deemed to accompany it.

## PIONEERS
OF MODERNISM One perception of the emergence of architectural modernism is that it was defined and driven by four men: Frank Lloyd Wright in the United States, the Swiss Le Corbusier in France, and Walter Gropius and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe in Germany.
Throughout his career, Wright’s projects, with the exception of the Prairie houses, were too diverse and too personal to constitute a definable style but he did have an early impact on the European trio.
All three were working in the Berlin office of Peter Behrens (1868–1940) when a copy of the Wasmuth portfolio arrived and their excitement at its content is recorded.
It was Le Corbusier who set out rules for a new architecture in his Vers une Architecture (Toward an Architecture) in 1927.
He proposed it would eliminate the social and political shortcomings that all previous architectural styles had embodied and perpetuated.
He argued against established architectural conventions and, most vehemently, against ornament on—or in—buildings.
Over the course of his career his own architecture strayed from his first precise strictures.
Mies coined aphorisms, most memorably “less is more” and “God is in the details.” He issued no manifestoes, but his buildings set out his arguments for an architecture of steel and glass.
He refined that simple formula throughout his career, particularly in the United States when he immigrated from Nazi Germany in 1938.
Gropius established the Bauhaus school in Weimar, Germany, which rejected the evolutionary progression of European design culture across all disciplines in favor of a revolutionary rejection of all precedents.
The Bauhaus became the model for art and architecture schools in Europe and North America but imitation diluted and distorted its message.

## Le
Corbusier and His Five Rules Between 1920 and 1925, Le Corbusier, French painter Amédée Ozenfant (1886–1966), and Belgian writer Paul Dermée (1886–1951) produced the magazine L’Esprit Nouveau (The New Spirit).
In it, Le Corbusier set out his five rules for a modern house, which should have: Pilotis Columns to raise main living areas one story above ground.
Free plan Internal floors that are free of structural internal walls.
Free façade Exterior walls that are non-structural.
Horizontal ribbon windows Continuous horizontal strips of windows to light rooms evenly.
Roof garden Flat roofs with garden terraces.
In theory, the free plan offered opportunities for interior designers.
However, proscription of decoration and prescription of plain flat surfaces limited their opportunities.
Le Corbusier’s five rules became standard theory in schools of architecture and were absorbed by new waves of architects and designers but the new architecture never found favor with the laity on whom it was foisted.
Elimination of applied decoration and enthusiasm for raw concrete had a Calvinistic rigor.
Yet it was revolutionary, and in the spirit of a time when the Soviet Union was establishing itself and National Socialism was picking up momentum in Germany.
Modern architecture, as defined by Le Corbusier, announced itself to be philanthropic but its instincts were totalitarian.
It was not for the frivolous.
Le Corbusier declared: “Decorative art, as opposed to the machine phenomenon, is that final twitch of the old manual mode and is a dying thing . . . [the new architecture] will contain only standard things created by industry in factories and mass produced, truly the objects of today.” In 1924 Le Corbusier designed a small house for his parents at Vevey on Lake Geneva in 1924.
It was an opportunity to demonstrate his newly formulated principles and he achieved three of his five points: the free plan, the ribbon window, and the roof terrace.
Concerns his parents might have about inhabiting a “machine for living in” were ameliorated by traditional wooden furniture.

## Early
Work In Paris, in 1925, Le Corbusier, supported by his cousin, Pierre Jeanneret (1896–1967), designed the Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau for the Exposition Internationale des Arts Décoratifs et Industriels Modernes (International Exhibition of Decorative Arts and Modern Industries).
Sponsored by the French government, it was a showcase for the exhibition of interior design, objects, and rooms in the new post-World War I style.
Le Corbusier, however, designed the pavilion to demonstrate his architectural response to the “machine age” that was to last from approximately 1918 to 1939 and during which the new machines, cars, airplanes, radios, and cinemas reshaped public and private lives, and held a romantic fascination for modern artists in all disciplines.
Ironically, a lot of the pavilion’s success depended on an existing tree on the plot, which the cousins were required to retain.
They built around it and it emerged through a hole in the floor of the terrace, which was contained within the pavilion’s cuboid volume, and protruded through a circle cut in its roof (17.3).
Le Corbusier, Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau, Paris, 1925.
The glazed area to the right fronts the double-height living area.
A tree grows through the terrace floor and roof.
On the left is the rounded structure containing an exhibition of supporting material.
At the beginning of his career, Le Corbusier had ambitions to be a painter and, in the prototype dwelling that was the pavilion, the artist manqué, attempted to incorporate the glamor of an artist’s studio into a family home: the living area was a double-height space with a fully glazed external wall, the kitchen and dining area were beneath but open to the bedroom, which looked over a balcony to the living area below.
The furniture included Thonet chairs (see here) and simple bourgeois armchairs.
Metal-framed furniture, with painted and glass panels, replaced traditional free-standing wooden pieces.
Purist paintings hung on plain white walls, rugs were hand-crafted Berber weavings from North Africa, laboratory glassware served as vases, and stones and shells, mass-produced by nature, were the only ornamental accessories (17.2).
Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau, Paris, 1925.
The double-height living area with the kitchen and dining area, behind a built-in storage unit and below the bedroom.
The pavilion was decidedly out of step with both the intentions of the exhibition organizers and popular taste.
The public preferred the materials and techniques displayed in the highly crafted decorative pieces in what was an identifiable emergent style that the exhibition was intended to showcase.
For Le Corbusier, rooms needed only simple factory-made chairs and tables, created by scientific analysis of how the human body, free from outmoded social conventions, would disport itself.
They would be made with the precision that only metalworking processes could achieve.
Objectivity fell victim to Le Corbusier’s aesthetic instincts.
His chaise longue of 1929 is elegant but its form determines that a user must bend their knee lying on one’s back is possible, lying on one’s side is impossible (17.4).
The flat surface of the Victorian chaise offered more options.
Le Corbusier’s Grand Confort armchair (1928–30), which he created with Charlotte Perriand (see here), is visually sumptuous but the aesthetic that required backrest and arms to be level did not allow the languid sprawling of the club armchair that had inspired it.
In pursuit of anthropometric perfection, Le Corbusier later created his Modular Man for whom data was determined by a male figure, based on the heroes of the English crime novels Le Corbusier enjoyed who were invariably 6 feet (183 cm) tall.
In 1950, the average Frenchman was 5 feet 7 inches (170 cm).
17.4 Le Corbusier and Charlotte Perriand, chaise longue, 1929.
This modernist version has an upper structure that slides on the base to permit the seating surface to be placed at an angle to suit the user.
Further evidence of Le Corbusier’s interiors may be deduced from his Villa Savoye in Poissy, near Paris (1929–31), which is generally accepted as the best and most influential of his early houses and a clear application of his five rules.
The ground floor, containing an entrance hall, a garage, and service rooms is set back behind pilotis and painted dark green to minimize its presence (17.6).
A ramp and a spiral stair lead up to a living and dining area that stretches the length of the building with a floor-to-ceiling window looking on to an open terrace (17.7).
The link between the interior and the exterior is crucial.
An unglazed ribbon window on the terrace offers views of the surrounding country.
The flat roof garden is punctuated by curved concrete walls (17.5).
In keeping with his Purism, Le Corbusier used blocks of flat color in the interiors.
Walls were bright blue and orange, the floor was square yellow tiles laid on the diagonal.
There was no door between the master bedroom and bathroom, which has a blue–gray mosaic tiled sunken tub and a built-in chaise longue.
17.5 and 17.6 Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, Villa Savoye, Poissy, France, 1929–31.
The villa is the definitive expression of Le Corbusier’s Domino House strategy: reinforced-concrete floors supported on reinforced columns are here used to create ribbon windows, glazed and unglazed; a principal floor is supported on pilotis—or columns—above a recessed ground floor and a roof garden.
The glazed slot of window to the salon is replicated by an unglazed slot in the roof garden to allow views of the surrounding landscape.
Le Corbusier and Pierre Jeanneret, interior ground level, Villa Savoye, Poissy, France, 1929–31.
A spiral stair and a ramp at the ground-level entrance area.
Neither are the most efficient or functional way of moving between floors, and are perhaps evidence of Le Corbusier’s need to break away from the orthogonal emphasis in modernist work.

## INSIGHTS

## Le
Corbusier and Color It is often assumed that Le Corbusier’s interiors were white in the name of modernist reductivism.
In reality, he used color extensively and daringly, presumably drawing on his painterly instincts.
Even his exteriors were not always plain white boxes, a misinterpretation derived from their publication in black and white photographs.
He was commissioned to design workers’ houses in 1926 in Pessac, Bordeaux.
In keeping with his Purism, they were painted yellow, blue, pale green, or dark maroon to underline the elements of their composition.
He used similar colors in his interiors, where often one wall would be painted to contrast with other lighter, often white, walls.
In fact, modernists were not against color and accepted rules for its “correct” use.
Le Corbusier and Amédée Ozenfant prescribed a Purist palette of yellow ocher, red, brown, white, black, ultramarine, and mixes of those basics.
Le Corbusier, always happy to set down rules, produced two editions of Polychromie Architecturale (Architectural Polychromy) in 1931 and 1959 for the Swiss wallpaper manufacturer Salubra.
The first edition comprised forty-three shades in fourteen series of solid colors and gradated tones, all of which were gentle and derived from nature.
The second added twenty more intense colors.
He considered that different hues and combinations of hues could affect perceptions of rooms and the moods of those in them.
Alfred Roth, a Swiss architect who joined Le Corbusier’s studio in 1929 (see here), talked about how painting the walls of a room could unify it or define areas within it.

## Perriand
As his reputation quickly grew, many young and radical architects worked in Le Corbusier’s studio.
Yet—apart from his cousin Pierre Jeanneret—Charlotte Perriand (1903–99) was arguably Le Corbusier’s most important collaborator perhaps because she had skills and an imagination that complemented his.
Perriand was born in Paris and studied furniture design from 1920 to 1925 at the Ecole de l’Union Centrale des Arts Décoratifs (The School of the Central Union of Decorative Arts) with Henri Rapin (1873–1939) and Maurice Dufrêne, (1876–1955), both of whom were interior designers and early exponents of Style Moderne (see here).
In 1927, for the Salon d’Automne (Fall Salon) exhibition in Paris, she created the Bar sous le Toit (Bar under the Roof) using generous amounts of aluminum and nickel-plated steel, leather cushions, and glass shelves.
She was interested in machine production and low-cost housing and, inspired by Le Corbusier’s writings, applied to work with him in 1927.
He turned her down, explaining that his studio did not embroider cushions.
Yet when he visited Bar sous le Toit he was impressed and, soon after, offered her a job designing furniture.
She was also responsible for interiors and exhibitions to promote Le Corbusier’s ideas.
In 1928, when Le Corbusier proposed three chairs—the B301 sling-back armchair for conversation, the LC2 Grand Confort armchair for relaxation, and the B306 chaise longue for sleeping—Perriand developed all three with tubular steel frames.
They became the quintessence of modernist seating and, at the time, were exclusively attributed to Le Corbusier.
Perriand said that she and Le Corbusier worked harmoniously, and in 1934 she designed furniture and fixtures for his new apartment in Paris.
She left the Le Corbusier/Jeanneret studio to work with the painter Fernand Léger (1881– 1955) on a pavilion for the Exposition Internationale (Universal Exhibition) in Paris in 1937 and a ski resort in the Savoie region of France where her grandparents lived and to which she often retreated.
She became involved with leftist groups and decided to work for a less elitist audience, switching from expensive chromed steel and machine production to wood and hand production.
Her designs were often inspired by Savoyard vernacular models.
In 1939 she returned to Paris to design prefabricated buildings with Jean Prouvé (1901–84).
When Germany occupied France in 1940, Perriand moved to Japan as a government advisor on industrial design.
When Japan attacked the United States in 1941, she tried to get back to France but was marooned in the French colony of Vietnam.
There, she experimented with woodwork and weaving, absorbing Asian ideas about design.
She returned to France and established her independent career while continuing to collaborate with Prouvé.
In 1950 she designed a prototypical kitchen for Le Corbusier’s Unité d’Habitation, a social-housing block in Marseilles.
She worked independently on a succession of interior projects, notably tourism offices for the French government, and offices for Air France in London, Paris, and Tokyo (17.8).
In 1962 she designed a series of large ski lodges at Les Arcs in Savoie, all incorporating her ideas about prefabrication and standardization.
Arguing that visitors would spend most of their time outdoors she designed small, cell-like rooms with big communal spaces that offered dramatic Charlotte Perriand, Air France travel bureau, London, 1958.
When Perriand returned to France after World War II, she had gone some way to becoming a national institution and was a natural choice for a prestige project with the national airline.

## Gropius
and the Bauhaus Modernist iconoclasm acquired its own academy with the foundation of the Bauhaus (Building House) in Weimar, Germany, in 1919 under the leadership of Walter Gropius (1883–1969).
It rejected boundaries between art and design and treated design as a single discipline, supposedly common to all materials and techniques.
Its regard for machine production distanced it from the Arts and Crafts movement but shared its commitment to Gesamtkunstwerk, the total work of art —the idea that a building, its interior and all the elements in it should have aesthetic coherence— to be successful as a single object.
Gropius’ directorial responsibilities embraced both architecture and the decorative arts, and he was obliged to think beyond architectural polemics.
In his book Neue Arbeiten der Bauhauswerkstätten (1925), published in English as The New Architecture and the Bauhaus, he suggested that the first stage of modern architecture should be a “purifying process” with the ultimate goal of creating a “composite but inseparable work of art— the great building—in which the old dividing line between monumental and decorative elements will have disappeared forever.” The disciplinary net of the Bauhaus net was cast wide and included photography and film.
Learning began with a year devoted to two- and three-dimensional abstract design, studies of materials, textures and colors, all intended to be the basis for specialist study.
Gropius recruited an impressive staff that included Paul Klee (1879–1940) who was Swiss, Wassily Kandinsky (1866– 1944) a Russian, Josef Albers (1888–1976) a German, László Moholy-Nagy (1895–1946) and Marcel Breuer (1902–81) who were both Hungarian.
Female staff members were few.
It was Gropius opinion that men thought in three dimensions while women could manage only two and, even then, they were not encouraged to pursue the lofty practice of painting but were steered toward activities associated with domesticity, such as printmaking and weaving.
Anni Albers (1899– 1994), married to Josef, worked in textiles and printmaking, crossing the lines between art and craft.
Gertrud Arndt (1903–2000)was married to Alfred Arndt (1896–1976), who briefly taught interior design, geometric drawing, and perspective, but made her own reputation as a photographer.
Metalsmith Marianne Brandt (1893–1983) became head of the metal workshop in 1927 although she specialized in domestic objects.
In 2007 one of her teapots achieved the highest ever auction price for a Bauhaus object.
The small and sculptural teapot is unconventional and intended to distil a concentrated extract, which, when combined with hot water in the cup, can produce tea of any desired strength.
Gropius’ office was a study in rectilinear geometry and typical of a Bauhausian interior (17.9).
Furniture, textiles, and light fixtures were designed by Bauhaus teachers and students.
An armchair, by Gropius, is shaped more by geometry than anthropometrics.
The color scheme was white and gray, with primary accents suggesting the influence of De Stijl.
Blocks of color were applied to walls and ceiling in unexpected places.
A textile, the height and width of a door, rose from floor level.
Walter Gropius, Bauhaus, Weimar, Germany, 1923.
Gropius designed his own office.
The rug, tapestry, light fixture, and some furniture are by Bauhaus faculty or students.
Gropius designed the armchair and desk.
Economic and political problems in 1925 led to the closure of the school in Weimar and its relocation to the industrial city of Dessau, to be housed in buildings designed by Gropius and conforming to modernist principles.
A workshop block with a glass curtain wall allowed students to produce prototypes.
A bridge over a public street contained a library and offices, with a link to the classroom block and studio bedrooms for advanced students, each with a tiny balcony to enliven the otherwise flat façade.
The school attracted political and artistic opposition from the growing Nazi Party.
In 1928 Gropius resigned and was succeeded by Swiss architect Hannes Meyer (1889–1954), whose communist sympathies proved to be unacceptable and in 1930 he was sacked.
The school was closed in 1933 but Ludwig Mies van der Rohe relocated the institution to Berlin, transformed it into a private school, and banned followers of Meyer from teaching or studying there.
He had invested his own money in the bowdlerized institution and in 1934 was the only member of staff to sign a letter supporting the Nazis.
Mies left Germany in 1938 when it became clear that Adolf Hitler preferred the faithful replication of architectural classicism of German architect Albert Speer (1905–81) to Mies’s own abstracted re-interpretation.
Mies settled in the United States as head of the architecture at Chicago’s Armour Institute of Technology, which later became the Illinois Institute of Technology.
Gropius was already professor of architecture at Harvard University, and thus European modernism took control of American architectural education.
Socialist idealists among Bauhaus staff went east to the Soviet Union where they found that Joseph Stalin was no more appreciative of their ideas than Hitler.

## Mies
van der Rohe Ludwig Mies van der Rohe (1886–1969) was born in Aachen, Germany.
He moved to Berlin to work with Bruno Paul (1874–1968), a German architect, furniture and interior designer who principally designed ocean liners.
Paul was a founder member of the Deutscher Werkbund (German Work Federation) association of artists, architects, designers, and industrialists, which was created in 1907 to promote German design abroad.
Mies next joined Behrens’s office in Berlin in 1908 before leaving in 1912 to set up his own practice.
His early work, particularly an unbuilt proposal for a museum in the Netherlands, suggests the influence of German Neoclassicism with something of Wright’s Prairie houses in its long low, asymmetrical massing.
Its flat roofs may be early explorations of that modernist essential.
After World War I, he experimented with options for cladding multistory buildings with glass curtain walls or horizontal bands of concrete and glass.
These became templates for his office buildings of the 1950s and 1960s in the United States and Europe.
While Le Corbusier offered prototypes for social housing, Mies speculated about the future of office building.
The pavilion is an archetype of Miesian open-plan design.
The roof is supported by steel columns in place of conventional load-bearing walls.
Non-load-bearing walls of glass and marble establish discrete areas without formal enclosures.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, German Pavilion, International Exhibition, Barcelona, 1929.
Classical restraint would be clear in two buildings that made Mies’ reputation.
The first, the German Pavilion (also known as the Barcelona Pavilion) at the International Exhibition in Barcelona in 1929, made Germany’s case for being the pacesetter of modernism (17.1 and 17.10).
Cantilevers of thin roof slab, supported on free-standing chromed steel columns, partly cover walls of marble and glass that sit on a travertine limestone platform in which two pools reflect the green and red marble walls and a scarlet curtain (17.11).
The structure has no definitive enclosure but implies functional areas, in which chairs and stools, designed by Mies and Lilly Reich, suggest how it might serve as a dwelling.
17.11 Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, German Pavilion, International Exhibition, Barcelona, 1929.
The open space, which had no identified rooms but screen walls of glass and marble to define spaces, has been a key influence on modern ideas of interior planning.
Floor-to-ceiling glass walls subdivide the floor and slim cruciform columns support the roof.
Materials include green and red marbles, travertine, and green glass The Tugendhat House, completed in 1930 in Brno in what is now the Czech Republic, takes the German Pavilion formula of isolated walls and columns loosely defining functional areas (17.12).
The main living area on the middle floor is a single open space divided by two walls: one straight and clad in onyx separates the sitting area from a library and study; the other, a section of curved wall clad in dark ebony, slightly more than a half circle, turns in sufficiently to help define the dining area.
Polished steel cruciform columns provide unobtrusive structural elements, two of which help consolidate definition of the dining area.
Floor-to-ceiling windows may be lowered mechanically into the ground floor to transform the room into a semi-outdoor space.
Mies and Reich collaborated to produce chairs, tables, and a daybed (17.13).
The use of rich natural materials as decorative agents and the strategic placement of the few interior divisions has had lasting influence on the modern interior.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, plan of principal floor, Tugendhat House, Brno, Czech Republic, 1928–30.
As in the German Pavilion at the Barcelona Fair of 1929, the areas here are defined by freestanding walls.
The straight, marble-clad wall divides the sitting area overlooking the garden from a library/study and the part circle of Macassar ebony defines the dining area.
Two rows of cruciform polished steel columns reinforce the separations.
17.12 17.13 Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, Tugendhat House.
A view along the glazed façade of the principal floor, raised above garden level.
The dining area with its bespoke Brno chairs, and its circular polished ebony enclosure, is on the left and the cruciform, chrome-clad columns match those in the German Pavilion.
Mies made his reputation in the United States in rural Illinois with the Farnsworth House (1945–51) in Plano, Illinois (17.15).
Dr.
Edith Farnsworth wanted a weekend retreat on a wooded site of 9 acres (3.6 ha) by the Fox River and Mies chose to locate it on the flood plain.
There is an argument for riparian sites but raising the floor 5 feet (1.5 m) above ground level was perhaps more to justify a concept in which the floor and roof slabs, separated by walls of floor-to-ceiling glass on all four sides, appear to float.
Both slabs, of identical dimensions, are supported on eight steel columns.
A third of the floor area is outdoor deck.
The columns and edges of roof and floor are painted white.
The interior is subdivided only by a central utilities block, with the living room at the deck end, the bedroom at the other.
There are two identical bathrooms at either end of the utilities block, the result perhaps of Mies’s love of symmetry.
Furniture (all designed by Mies and Reich) was deployed sparingly.
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, Farnsworth House, Plano, Illinois, 1945–51.
17.15 The wall on the left, which defines the bed area, sits over a fireplace.
The storage unit at right angles provides some privacy.
The furniture is by Mies and is a variation of the Barcelona chair and the Barcelona ottoman for the German Pavilion.

## Mies
and Johnson There was delay, from 1946 to 1951, between Mies being commissioned to build the Farnsworth House and its completion, caused by Edith Farnsworth having to wait to inherit money from an aunt.
Mies had completed the design by 1947, in time for an exhibition of his work at the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
Philip Johnson (1906–2005), the museum’s director of architecture and a devotee of Mies, cloned the essence of the Farnsworth for his own home in rura Connecticut—and stole a march by completing it in 1949 (17.14).
17.14 Philip Johnson, Glass House, New Canaan, Connecticut, 1949.
Johnson’s home was an interpretation of the Farnsworth House by Ludwig Mies van der Rohe; the homage was clear in his use of Mies/Reich furniture.
The easel (right) displayed a version of Nicolas Poussin’s The Funeral of Phocion (1648) and attempts to deal with the problem of hanging paintings in glass-walled open-plan interiors.
Johnson went on to work with Mies, supervising construction of Mies’s tower, the Seagram Building in New York.
Completed in 1958 it is considered to be the quintessence of the modern office block.
Johnson also designed the interiors of the Four Seasons restaurant in the building, which consists of two rooms, each 60 × 90 feet (18 × 27.5 m) and 20 feet (6 m) high and free of structural columns.
Both had glass walls in bronze frames.
Curtains of metal chains, designed by Marie Nichols, wafted in the breeze from concealed ventilating ducts.
Travertine marble walls and floors matched those in the Seagram’s lobby and were augmented by walnut, rawhide and carpet paneling.
In the Pool Room, tables were arranged around a 20-feet (1.8-m) square white marble pool, with fig trees in enormous planters at each corner (17.16).
Off-white aluminum panels, with recessed lighting sources suggested a coffered ceiling.
In the Grill Room, the bar and lounge were separated by a walnut desk, and are overlooked by mezzanine dining rooms.
Black ceiling tiles had irregularly spaced outlets for light fittings.
17.16 Philip Johnson and Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, Pool Room, Four Seasons restaurant, New York, 1958.
A marble-edged pool, perhaps prompted by Dorothy Draper’s pool ten years earlier in New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art (see here).
The trees underline the monumental proportions of the room in which it would have been futile to attempt to create intimacy.
Johnson’s own architecture, in partnership with John Burgee (b.
