Terragni’s obsession with the square and its predominance over function made for a building that is a visual conundrum.
It has a geometric clarity, which is as easily deciphered as an allegorical wall painting but an expression of simple logic cannot be as popular, or as rewarding for lay observers, as figurative imagery.
Giuseppe Terragni, Casa del Popolo, Como, Italy, 1938.
Originally called the Casa del Fascio, this public building was intended to accommodate political meetings.
Its rational commitment to the square as a planning and elevational device comfortably satisfied the totalitarian appetite for order and monumentality.

## SCANDINAVIA
Scandinavians had developed a Nordic model of social democracy, a mix of welfare state and freemarket capitalism and, in the nineteenth century, an unostentatious Neoclassicism in which influences from abroad were tempered with respect for their own traditions. industrialization was also slow to arrive, which helped to preserve traditional crafts. scandinavians were not inclined to create tubular steel furniture, they preferred to bend timbers and mold plywood.
The Swedish Society of Crafts and Design, founded in 1845, focused on craft rather than factory production but, as industry grew in the early twentieth century and people migrated from country to town, the society began to concern itself with the quality of mass-produced products.
The quest to make objects with high aesthetic values available to a popular market began in earnest during the 1920s and 1930s and, after World War II, schools were established to teach and preserve craft techniques.
The country evolved its own humane modernity.

## Alvar
and Aino Aalto Alvar Aalto (1898–1976), a Finn, was aware of the emergence of modernism in France and Germany and became the most significant of Scandinavia’s early modern architects and designers.
He saw his buildings as complete works of art and designed furniture, textiles, and glassware in close collaboration with his wife, the architect Aino Marsio (1894–1949).
He began as a Nordic Classicist, and the simplicity of that style gave him a stepping stone to modernism.
His first important modernist project was a building for the Turun Sanomat newspaper (1927–9) in Turku, Finland’s oldest city.
The most interesting area held the printing presses in which round-edged columns with flared tops melded into the ceiling slab.
In the most functional area of the building, the columns are incongruously organic while the rest of the building conformed to modernist expectations with ribbon windows and white walls (19.9).
Alvar Aalto, headquarters of the Turun Sanomat newspaper, Turku, Finland, 1927–9.
The tapering concrete columns give this industrial interior—the press room of a newspaper—a curious monumentality that the more conventional office areas of the building lack.
Aalto’s international reputation was established by the Paimio Sanatorium (1933) in Paimio, southwest Finland.
It is a long, south-facing, six-story block of patients’ accommodation, a shorter wing of open-air terraces, and a central entrance block of rooms for communal dining and services.
The reception desk, elevators, light fittings, and clocks were all bespoke.
Furniture included the Paimio armchair with its plywood curves which, along with the four-legged, stackable stool for the Viipurin Library in Vyborg (now in Russia), completed in 1935, has become synonymous with his work.
The armchairs are no more comfortable than the cushioned tubular steel models from mainland Europe but wood made them reassuringly familiar (19.10).
19.10 Alvar Aalto, armchair in molded plywood, 1934.
The techniques of molding plywood made possible the generous curves that make this chair more visually seductive than the chrome and leather pieces by radicals elsewhere in Europe.
At the end of the 1930s Aalto, in close collaboration with Aino, designed the building that marked their transition from modernist rationality to a language of natural materials and organic forms.
Villa Mairea (1938–9) in Noormarkku was designed for Harry Gullichsen, an industrialist, and his wife Maire (1907–90).
She was a director of Artek, the company that produced the Aaltos furniture and artifacts.
The Gullichsens instructed that the house be “experimental.” It was a holiday home deep in a forest with spaces for entertaining, a gallery, and a studio.
The building was organized to have activities flow together, to offer flexibility of use and a different, more immediate, connection between interior and exterior than that offered by modernism’s ribbon windows (19.11).
Alvar and Aino Aalto, Villa Mairea, Noormarkku, 1938–9.
An excellent example of how Scandinavian respect for their traditional materials and craft techniques influenced their modernity.
The pairing and wrapping columns with rattan strip, the rejection of a rectangular grid, are all the result of an impulse to defer to nature rather than to objective logic.
The interior transcribes nature.
The structural grid is irregular with seemingly randomly placed, circular steel columns that are doubled up and bound together with rattan strips.
One column unaccountably changes to concrete, to break from modernist homogeneity.
The integration of exterior and interior is reinforced by thin vertical wooden poles set irregularly along the length of the open-treaded stair that allow glimpses of the forest beyond.
The connecting of interior to landscape is comparable to that achieved by Frank Lloyd Wright, not in Fallingwater in Pennsylvania (1936), which is imposed on the landscape, but with his versions of his home and studio, Taliesin, in Wisconsin (1897–1959; see here).
Alvar and Aino entered the competition to design the Finnish exhibit at the New York World’s Fair of 1939 separately and he won.
Within the pavilion’s rectangular walls, he introduced a flowing, free-form wall of wooden strips that leaned over the main exhibition space and screened a secondary exhibition on an upper level (19.12).
Wright declared it a work of genius.
Alvar Aalto, Finnish Pavilion, New York World’s Fair, 1939.
Aalto’s pavilion was a great success at the fair.
The undulating wall of angled wooden strips and the balcony (barely visible on the right) created a dynamic space to display the products of Finnish industry.
Aino was integral to the Aaltos’ work and, as in most partnerships, it is difficult to apportion precise responsibilities but, as a woman architect and designer, she was invariably cast in a subservient role, and not necessarily named when credit should have been shared.
She joined his office in 1924 and they married in 1925.
What evidence there is suggests that she concentrated on designing the interiors of their buildings.
She was involved in the Villa Mairea interiors and furniture for the Paimio Sanatorium.
It is likely she contributed to the plywood armchair.
The Aaltos’ first buildings were small Nordic Classic houses.
The first project accredited to Aino is Villa Flor, in 1926, their holiday home in Alajärvi, western Finland, a traditional wooden country house.
She was not entirely convinced by modernist ideologies and deployed traditional furniture fabrics and artifacts to achieve comfortable inhabitability.
In 1935 she and Alvar set up the Artek company, with Maire Gullichsen and art historian Nils-Gustav Hahlin (1904–41), to sell the furniture and lighting fixtures they designed.
Aino became head of design and later managing director.
She created hundreds of objects, Alvar only a few.
She oversaw commissions for more than eighty interiors and designed light fittings, textiles, and glassware, for which she won a prize at the Triennale di Milano (Milan Triennial) of 1936.
The same year, she and Alvar collaborated to create the Savoy vase with its base of differently sized, intersecting circles, the outside edges of which are extruded at a slight angle to give a continuous undulating edge.
It is very Art Deco.
Alvar is usually credited as its sole designer.
Aino died in 1949 but she had created the aesthetic that defined Artek and established Finland as a design force.
In 1952 Alvar married an assistant in his studio, architect Elissa Mäkiniemi (1922–94).
When he died, she and other staff completed the projects he had begun.

## SWITZERLAND
Swiss society was comfortable with rational modernism.
The country’s mountainous terrain demanded heroic feats of concrete bridge building.
It has even been suggested that the Swiss Le Corbusier’s early training as a watchmaker gave him an appetite for machine precision and underpinned his enthusiasm for objectivity and his propensity for making rules.
In 1931 Karl Moser (1880–1936), like Auguste Perret, revealed concrete’s potential as an architectural material.
He employed a coffered roof supported on eight slender columns for St.
Anthony’s Church in Basel.
The church is 71 feet (21.5 m) high and 200 feet (61 m) long with a 200-feet (61-m) high angular bell tower, all built of exposed concrete.
Like Perret, Moser’s concrete structure allowed him to devote the side walls entirely to small panels of stained glass that wash color across the raw concrete surfaces.
Some locals found the building so outrageous they called it the “soul silo” (19.13).
Karl Moser, St.
Anthony’s Church, Basel, Switzerland, 1931.
Like French architect Auguste Perret, Moser explored the possibilities of a concrete expression of a traditional ecclesiastic language.
The coffering of the ceiling is evocative but structurally unnecessary.
Alfred Roth (1903–98) was a student of Moser at the Federal Institute of Technology in Zurich and after graduating went to work for Le Corbusier from 1927–8.
Between 1935 and 1936 he and his cousin Emil (1893–1980), working with Marcel Breuer, designed small apartment buildings in Doldertal near Zurich for the architectural historian and champion of modernism, Sigfried Giedion.
Alfred went on to live and work in one of the apartments.
The buildings’ interiors were lit by ribbon windows and the walls were white with patches of light color to define areas within the open plan, something Roth had encountered when working in Paris with Le Corbusier.
Furniture included pieces by Breuer and Aalto.
Max Bill (1908–94) studied at the Bauhaus and returned to Switzerland where, as a member of the Schweizerischer Werkbund (Swiss Craft Association), he became a spokesman for modernism.
He was a leading graphic and industrial designer whose work was characterized by clarity and elegant proportions, exemplified by the clocks he designed for German watch and clock manufacturer Junghans.
He founded the Ulm School of Design in Ulm, Germany, in 1953.
He and his colleague, the Indonesian-born designer Hans Gugelot (1920–65), designed the Ulmer Hocker (1954), a stool that supposedly served as a shelf, a lectern, and a side table.
Although not obviously suited to any of those functions, it impressed by its fragile, elegant detail.
19.14

## FURNITURE
DESIGN Architects committed to the modernist code had problems furnishing their interiors, even the work of radical pre-modernists, like Josef Hoffmann, or Charles Rennie Mackintosh, carried ornamental baggage, so modernists were obliged to do it for themselves and, in the application of their principles, they were ruthless.
Hungarian-born Marcel Breuer (1902–81) became head of cabinetmaking in the Bauhaus.
In 1925 he was inspired by the use of steel tubing in lightweight bicycles to evolve a skeletal version of a traditional armchair.
The chrome frame retained the rough shape of the original but solid slabs of upholstery were replaced by strips of a strong and shiny waxed cotton fabric known as Eisengarn (iron yarn).
The German designer Margaretha Reichardt (1907–84) experimented with the material in the Bauhaus weaving workshop, developing both cloth and strapping.
The Thonet company took over manufacture of the chair and catalogued it as Model B3.
However, it was renamed the Wassily chair after World War II by a subsequent manufacturer who thought the connection with the Russian painter Wassily Kandinsky would have commercial benefits, since fine artists have greater name recognition than designers and a swashbuckling glamor (19.15).
The chair is rhetorically functional but the areas of cloth devoted to seat, backrests, and arms are so reduced that they offer little stability—it is not a chair for lounging.
Breuer also created the more amenable Cesca chair in 1928 with its bent chrome frame with woven straw seat and back, on thin wooden frames that stabilize the frame (19.14).
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich produced something similar to the Cesca, the MR10, in which the solid good sense of Cesca is sacrificed for a more dramatic and elegant profile.
Marcel Breuer, Cesca chair, 1928.
Breuer named his chair in honor of his adopted daughter Francesca.
The tubular-steel-framed chair had woven cane seats and back made with and without arms.
There were also cushioned versions.
The chair remains in production.
19.15 Marcel Breuer, Wassily chair, 1925.
This design uses a frame of chrome-plated steel tubing to support seat, arms, and back of stretched canvas or leather.
It is an exercise in reductive design at the cost of comfort.
While traditional solid wooden frames were rejected in favor of steel and aluminum, plywood, perhaps because it was the result of a manufacturing process, was acceptable to modernists.
In 1935, in retreat from Nazi Germany, Breuer moved briefly to London and was employed by the Isokon furniture firm, owned by Jack Pritchard (1899–1992), an early champion of British modernism.
Pritchard admired Alvar Aalto’s plywood furniture, and suggested the material to Breuer who developed his earlier thoughts on an aluminum-framed chaise longue to design his long chair in 1936 (19.16).

## 19.16

## Marcel
Breuer, plywood long chair, 1936.
After the closure of the Bauhaus in Germany in 1933, Walter Gropius suggested Breuer relocate to London.
He spent two years in the city, during which he designed the long chair for the London-based firm Isokon.
The chair is molded plywood using techniques developed by Alvar Aalto for Artek.
Europe, the second smallest continent, is extraordinarily diverse.
National frontiers reinforced by language, political, economic, social and climatic idiosyncrasies explain how even an architectural and design style as clearly defined as modernism could generate distinct national and regional variations.
Many Europeans, in search of opportunity and prosperity, took the risk of emigrating to North America; most brought ambitions and skills and a few, in the 1920s and 1930s, brought new, modernistic ways to the design of buildings and interiors.
Modernist Design in the United States CHAPTER TWENTY Frank Lloyd Wright, Solomon R.
Guggenheim Museum, New York, 1956–9.
The spiral ramp, down which visitors process, marks out the central rotunda space with dramatic views down to the ground or up to the domed skylight.
All the structure is a creamy off-white with plants providing green accents.
While Le Corbusier, Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, and Walter Gropius were propagating the principles of modernism in Europe, architects and designers in the United States, led by Frank Lloyd Wright, were developing their own version of a modern architecture and interior design.
By the end of the nineteenth century, Americans were in advance of architectural developments in Europe.
The growth of their major cities, and Chicago in particular, with its embryonic skyscrapers, was setting stylistic challenges and their cities were new, development and infrastructure were not inhibited by medieval street patterns and memories of architectural pasts.
In the first decades of the twentieth century, European radicals agitated to destroy the past and write new rules for the future; Americans were content to let the future shape itself.

## ARCHITECTS
AND DESIGNERS

## Wright
After Wright returned from Europe in 1911, he started to build himself a home on land belonging to his mother in Spring Green, Wisconsin, which he called Taliesin (1911–59; 20.2).
The three houses and studios that form Taliesin take their cues from the surrounding countryside.
He broke up exteriors to reflect and add to the natural irregularities of the sites.
Sloping ceilings, often with exposed roughly cut rafters, suggest quite primitive dwellings, closer to pioneering homesteads than the suburbia of the Prairie houses (see here).
He subscribed to the view that the hearth was the heart of the home—as he had in the Prairie houses—and piled up roughly cut local stone to make monumental fireplaces.
Frank Lloyd Wright, Taliesin, Spring Green, Wisconsin, photographed in 1925, 1911–59.
The complex of buildings that forms the Taliesin estate expanded over time, with buildings to house its various functions as a home, a studio, a school of architecture, and a working farm.
Taliesin, like all the homes that Wright designed for himself, continued to evolve over the nearly five decades that he lived there.
It includes many dramatic interior spaces, including this living room, with its pitched ceiling planes and massive stonework for walls and fireplace.
Most great architects are identified by a single style that they evolve and to which they remain faithful, but after the Prairie houses, which exist as a distinct body of work, Wright’s buildings shared few stylistic characteristics, as is illustrated by two projects of the 1930s.
In 1935, he was commissioned to design a weekend house near Bear Run in the Laurel Highlands of southwest Pennsylvania.
He designed Fallingwater, a house of cantilevered concrete slabs that perches above a waterfall and seems to slot into the rugged rock striations of its site (20.3).
It is the antithesis of the buildings for the Johnson Wax Company headquarters in Racine, Wisconsin, designed and built between 1936 and 1939, with its smooth round-cornered research tower and the top-lit forest of tapering columns with their lily-pad capitals in the administration building’s large and lofty general office (20.4 and 20.5).
Both buildings share an architectural imagination driven to unique solutions by the particularities of each brief.
20.3 Frank Lloyd Wright, living room, Fallingwater, Bear Run, Pennsylvania, 1935–9.
The great open living space of Fallingwater uses large areas of glass to look out into the countryside beyond and uses stone for the floor and fireplace.
The glazed ceiling sections mask hidden electric light sources.
Wright designed the built-in benches and movable stools.
20.4 Frank Lloyd Wright, private office, Johnson Wax Company headquarters, Racine, Wisconsin, 1936–9.
The furniture designed by Wright relates to the lily-pad shapes in the “great room” of the administration building.
Curved desk drawers swung open on pivots and desktops end in semicircles.
Frank Lloyd Wright, Johnson Wax Building, Racine, Wisconsin, 1936–9.
The “great room” of the administration building is dominated by concrete structural columns, each of which is crowned by capitals that are often compared to lily pads.
Skylights in the interstices provide daylight.
Wright was a modern architect but not a modernist as understood in Europe, nor was he an adherent of the International Style (see here) in the United States.
He preferred to think of himself as unique.
His Solomon R.
Guggenheim Museum in New York (1956–9; 20.1) attracted criticism because of its unsuitability for displaying paintings, and in its defense, Wright adapted Louis Sullivan’s dictum and pronounced that “form and function should be one—in a spiritual union.” He was already in his fifties when modernists were publishing manifestoes regarding form and ornament and, by then, had already embraced horizontality and expressed his own reservations about ornament.
During his long career he produced nothing that might be aligned with what Europeans or indeed other Americans, increasingly influenced by European immigrants, were doing.
Gropius arrived in 1937 and Mies in 1938.
Both carried on resolutely in their European ways and most American architects accepted their formulae, apart from renegades like Wright and his acolyte Bruce Goff (1904–82), whose instincts were American and who responded to its landscapes with organic forms and local materials.

## INSIGHTS
The Solomon R.
Guggenheim Museum Frank Lloyd Wright began to design the Solomon R.
Guggenheim Museum in New York in 1943.
Its sweeping, spiral curves ignore the constrictions of the four-square grid of Manhattan.
However, the exterior, and therefore internal, walls lean away from viewers, leaving a gap between flat pictures and the curved wall behind them.
The Guggenheim could be said to be a machine for processing visitors who are transported by elevator to the highest point and left to follow the ramp that leads them systematically past exhibits of artworks, a forced march that discourages spontaneous diversions into secondary rooms.
The Guggenheim has spawned a rash of galleries—including its namesake in Bilbao, Spain (1997)—which sacrifice the interior in the cause of the exterior.
A building, particularly one associated with high culture, is permitted to be grand but not attention-seeking and should not set itself above or inconvenience its contents.
Yet this conflict of interests between a building’s self-regard and the experience of its visitors does make an argument for the role of the interior designer: architects are too invested in their exteriors, too locked into the scale and materiality of construction, to deal objectively with the spaces they enclose (see Gae Aulenti, here).
A fresh eye can refine scale and materiality.

## Gill
Californian architect Irving Gill (1870–1936) is regarded as a pioneer of modern American architecture.
He was born in Tully, New York and briefly worked with Wright in the office of Adler & Sullivan in Chicago.
He was aware of Sullivan’s thoughts on ornament, although, like Adolf Loos in Vienna (see here), he interpreted the exhortation to banish ornament literally and relied on natural finishes to decorate his interiors.
His best-known works are the Dodge House in Los Angeles (1915–6; 20.6) and the Scripps House at La Jolla (1917; 20.7).
Both houses have flat roofs without eaves and flat, white-reinforced concrete walls with irregularly shaped windows.
Other than occasional obvious allusions to Mission style (see here) in their arched doors and perimeter arcades, they are as starkly simple as anything produced by Loos.
Gill carried a similar simplicity into his interiors, with white walls and openings all free of moldings.
In place of traditional baseboard he introduced quadrant covings that allowed horizontal and vertical elements to meld together.
Internal walls were paneled wood and floors were concrete or Sorel cement, which could be colored to imitate marble.
20.6 Irving Gill, Dodge House, Los Angeles, 1915–6 (demolished 1970).
Gill was the first American architect to simplify his interiors by rejecting architrave and cornice moldings, but perhaps his most radical innovation was to replace the traditional timber baseboard with a quadrant molding that created a smooth transition between floor and wall.
Irving Gill, Scripps House, La Jolla, California, 1917.
Gill was an early enthusiast for building houses in concrete, perhaps because it allowed him to eliminate dust-collecting junctions.
In this view of the Scripps House, the potential for creating long flat planes is clear—but the owners appeared to have trouble arranging the incongruous furniture in that unfamiliar context.
In 1908 Gill designed and built eight small houses for rent, which he used as testing grounds for new materials and construction methods.
Each house had a small entrance court or porch to provide privacy.
The interiors had smooth continuous surfaces, flush paneled doors, and generous storage, with raised closet floors to ease cleaning.
Architecture critic Joseph Giovannini (b.
1945), author of Irving J.
Gill: Architect 1870–1936 (2006), suggests that “the desire for an easily maintained sanitary home drove Gill’s aesthetic toward purity.” Gill shared with European modernists an ambition to improve the lot of working people.
Yet his work featured frequently in Craftsman magazine and most of his tenants were from the small section of the middle class who were excited by homes designed to utilize the domestic advances of the new century.

## Schindler
Rudolph Schindler (1887–1953) was born in Vienna and trained there before emigrating to the United States in 1914.
He worked with Wright but, having concluded that Wright was not crediting or paying him enough, moved to California in 1920 and opened his own practice.
In 1922 he built the Schindler Chace House in West Hollywood.
It was an architectural and social experiment, a living and working place for four creative individuals: Schindler and his wife Pauline, a composer, and Clyde and Marian Chace, an engineer and a dancer.
Clyde had worked with Gill and brought experience of concrete construction to the project.
Two L-shaped apartments, each with two studios, were connected by a communal kitchen and utility rooms.
There were no designated bedrooms but two sleeping baskets on the roof with redwood fourposted canopies and canvas sidings.
In 1926 Schindler completed the Lovell Beach House in Newport Beach, California, for the Lovell family (20.8).
It is considered a milestone in the development of North American modernism.
Raised high above the beach on raw concrete columns, the two-story house has a white-walled living and dining area with full-height windows on the east and south sides facing the ocean.
The kitchen and breakfast area lie on the north side and share a terrace overlooking the garden.
20.8 Rudolph Schindler, Lovell Beach House, Newport Beach, California, 1926.
A view from the access balcony to the bedrooms.
It is modernist but built with timber technology rather than concrete.
It may be that the exposed roof joists led to its exclusion from the International Style exhibition in 1932 (see here).

## Neutra
Richard Neutra (1892–1970) knew Schindler in Vienna, and followed him to the United States in 1923, and also to Wright’s office.
In 1926 he and his wife moved into the Schindler House when the Chaces moved out.
While Neutra was there, Schindler’s former clients, the Lovells, commissioned him to design the a new house in the Hollywood Hills (1927–9), which became known as the Lovell House, or Lovell Health House because Philip Lovell was a physician and naturopath who advocated sun and exercise.
Neutra’s house is similar to that of Schindler, with ribbon windows, white walls, cantilevers, pilotis, and a flat roof.
The interior walls are white and unornamented, and the floor is carpeted gray (20.9).
20.9 Richard Neutra, Lovell House, Los Angeles, 1927–9.
The panoramic windows and bare white walls provide a California-informed interpretation of European modernism.
Inevitably, the Lovells’ switch of architect from Schindler to Neutra caused tension between them.
Schindler was the more volatile of the two while Neutra responded meticulously to his clients’ wishes and was, consequently, the more successful.
He provided an architecture shaped by the Californian climate and European modernism.
In 1935 he designed a house (demolished 1971) in the California desert for another Viennese, the film director Josef von Sternberg.
It introduced curves to animate the public areas and perhaps to integrate the small building more discreetly into the empty expanse of its 13-acre (5-ha) site.
The walls were steel-framed, clad in painted aluminum sheet, generally white, and free of decoration.
Large windows and screens were assembled from industrial components.
A double-height living area was surrounded by a balcony that served as an art gallery.
The only rooms on the upper floor were von Sternberg’s bedroom, with its view of a rooftop-reflecting pool, and a generously mirrored bathroom.

## Lescaze
In his native Geneva, William Lescaze (1896–1969) had been a pupil of Swiss architect Karl Moser (see here).
He emigrated to the United States in 1920 and opened a practice in New York in 1923.
His first important commission, in 1929, was for the Oak Lane Country Day School, in Bluebell, Pennsylvania, in which he downsized stairs to suit children and specified cork floors to protect their knees.
The same year, he entered a five-year partnership with American architect George Howe (1886–1955), whom he had persuaded of the virtues of modernism.
Howe was a successful designer of houses and banks but Lescaze took the lead in designing the building for the Philadelphia Saving Fund Society (1932).
It was the first tall modernist building in Philadelphia.
Its great size, sternly geometric mass, and black stone-clad base disconcerted the Philadelphian public (20.10).
20.10 William Lescaze and George Howe, Philadelphia Saving Fund Society Building, Philadelphia, 1932.
Large windows flood the tall banking hall, augmented by concealed artificial light from lowered ceiling panels.
The columns are faced with polished black marble.
Lescaze’s own house on East 48th Street in Manhattan, New York (1933–4), was a refurbishment of a four-story brownstone.
His office was on the ground floor and his home above.
He gave the house a horizontal emphasis in contrast to the verticality of neighboring buildings.
The traditional brownstone façade was replaced by story-high glass blocks, within a concrete frame, which were intended to improve sound insulation and give privacy.
The interior had a neutral palette of yellow, blue, gray, and white.
The floors were covered in gray rubber tiles and indirect lighting was used throughout.
He also designed bespoke furniture for the house, including upholstered chairs with metal tube frames and a rosewood table (20.11).
William Lescaze, Lescaze House, New York, 1933–4.
For his own home, Lescaze refurbished a brownstone at 211 East 48th Street.
He introduced a glass block façade that filters light and made his blue, gray, and white color scheme subtler.

## INTERNATIONAL
STYLE The vibrant American economy had created a need for, and ways to construct, new building types, and the tall commercial tower in particular.
American cities were not stifled by revered ancient centers that demanded to be preserved but, despite the United States having its own version of an architectural future, news of radical change in European architecture aroused interest and, in 1930, Alfred H.
Barr, Jr., the director of the Museum of Modern Art in New York felt it was time to acknowledge developments in Europe.
The subsequent show, Modern Architecture: International Exhibition, was mounted in 1932.
Curated by the historian Henry-Russell Hitchcock and the museum’s director of architecture and design Philip Johnson, it was a far from comprehensive overview and ignored De Stijl, among other modernistic strands.
The buildings shown largely conformed to the modernist dicta, with horizontal massing and plain planes, unlike skyscrapers.
A catalog, titled The International Style: Architecture Since 1922, gave a label “International Style” to the American architecture that had less to do with the public and private housing that dominated the exhibition and more to do with steel and glass corporate towers in the manner of Mies.
Exhibitors were grateful for publicity but some objected to having their work categorized to suit the curatorial theme.
Because Wright had undergone a two-decade-long career hiatus since 1909, Hitchcock and Johnson had originally omitted him from the exhibition.
His late inclusion rested on a quickly prepared single exhibit of an unbuilt proposal for a large house in Denver.
Wright objected to being in the company of Raymond Hood (see here), whom he described as a “self-advertising amateur.” He also denounced Neutra as a high-powered salesman.
Hood’s Gothic Revival entry had won the Chicago Tribune Tower competition but he had largely rejected ornament in his designs for the Daily News building (1928–30) and the Rockefeller Center in New York (see here) and so qualified for inclusion.
Neutra’s Lovell House conformed to European modernist ideals.
Schindler was a notable exclusion despite his work on the earlier Lovell House.
Thirty-seven architects from fifteen countries exhibited at the show but only seven were from the United States.
Seventy-five projects were shown; sixteen were from western Europe, with the remainder from the U.S.S.R. whose Constructivism was clearly aligned with modernism, and Japan, which was preparing to integrate into the modern world.
Scandinavian designers were omitted.
Their work had romantic, organic leanings and Hitchcock and Johnson had defined the International Style as having abstract, cubistic, and mechanistic qualities that responded to the twentieth century’s “machine age.” Exhibits shared flat roofs, smooth white walls, large areas of glass, asymmetrical plans and, inevitably, an absence of historic or ornamental detail.
They were “functional” in the modernist sense and that principle determined the nature of the eleven interiors included in the exhibition.
Afterward, the International Style became visible in magazines and books but it did not find general favour.
In 1934 Kenneth Clark, the director of London’s National Gallery, described modernism as “The architectural revolution that is familiar to everyone—at least it ought to be because no aesthetic movement has been more relentlessly publicized.” He offered an explanation for its unpopularity: “We have abandoned the conventions of architecture before abandoning the conventions of life.”

## CONTINUITY
AND MODERNITY While architecture schools were increasingly in thrall to functional modernism, decoration schools continued to teach students to work in historical styles even though clients were not necessarily concerned with historical consistency or accuracy.
Male decorators were more likely to sail close to modernism but tended to treat modernity with a light hand.

## Robsjohn-Gibbings
Terence Harold Robsjohn-Gibbings (1905–76) was born in the English west coast port of Liverpool, which may have encouraged his visits to the United States in 1929 and 1930, when he settled in New York.
In 1936 he opened a decorating shop on Madison Avenue in 1936 and became one of the most successful American decorators of the 1940s.
His furniture clearly showed the influence of ancient Greek forms (20.12).
No original Greek furniture survives but his work was inspired by the furniture depicted on the painted Greek ceramics he drew and studied in the British Museum.
He incorporated original antique artifacts into his interiors but the influence of Art Deco is obvious in his interpretations of original sources.
For one of his most important commissions, Casa Encantada in Los Angeles, finished in 1938, he designed more than two hundred pieces of furniture but his rooms in this and other projects were sparsely furnished and, because of his enthusiasm for the original sources, his new pieces coexisted comfortably with the antique classical artifacts he added.
In 1960 he met the Greek cabinetmakers Susan and Eleftherios Saridis and with them created the Klismos line of furniture (“klismos” is ancient Greek for armchair).
In 1966 he moved permanently to Greece where he continued his work as an interior designer.

## 20.12 T. H. Robsjohn-Gibbings, Klismos chair, 1937. A recreation of a traditional Greek ch
air, as portrayed in classical painted ceramics, with perhaps more delicately curved legs, a more upright back and the removal of painted decoration, suggesting that historical precedents needed to be retuned to suit their time rather than rejected.

## Wormley
Edward J.
Wormley (1907–95) was born in Oswego, a small town in rural Illinois.
After a correspondence course in interior decoration he studied at the Art Institute of Chicago then worked as an interior designer at the Marshall Fields & Company department store.
In 1931 he traveled to Europe where he met Le Corbusier and Emile-Jacques Ruhlmann (see here).
His work aligns with the latter’s.
When he returned to the United States, he met the chairman of the Dunbar Furniture Company from Indiana, which had built horse-drawn carriages until the popularity of the automobile forced them to change products.
Their high level of craft skills adapted easily to producing Wormley’s designs and he created an average of one hundred new pieces each year for more than thirty years.
His furniture was simple and designed for comfort (20.13).
He favored wood, generous upholstery, and craft elements such as tambour drawers, woven-wood cabinet fronts, and caned seatbacks.
He said, “Furniture is needed for practical reasons, and because it must be there, it may as well be as pleasant as possible to look at, and in a less definable psychological way, comforting to the spirit.” 20.13 Edward J.
Wormley, Listen-to-me chaise longue, 1948.
A relaxed interpretation of a traditional chaise longue, modern but not aggressively so, having a light structure and soft upholstery with lines of stitching across the width to ease and express the curve.
He set up his own design practice in 1945 and created the highly successful Precedent collection for the Drexel Furniture Company while remaining as Dunbar’s director of design.
In 1957 he designed the Janus collection for Dunbar which combined new and antique elements— Japanese woodblocks and vintage ceramic tiles were set into the tops of wooden coffee tables.
(Janus was the two-headed Roman god who could look to the past and the present.) He said, “Modernism means freedom—freedom to mix, to choose, to change, to embrace the new but to hold fast to what is good.”

## RESIDENTIAL
AND INDUSTRIAL DESIGN The Great Depression that followed the 1929 Wall Street Crash blighted the American economy throughout the 1930s.
However, it did not inhibit the nation’s consumerist instincts.
American designers from a variety of creative backgrounds coalesced into what became the new profession of industrial design.
They worked principally for the manufacturers of household appliances and while they approved of functional objects, design was ultimately, for them, about styling.
The new profession really owed its birth to clients starting to understand that styling sold products, whether it was a railroad engine that represented the speed and glamour of the company that ran it or a pretier coffee pot. it seemed logical to ask these creative polymaths to improve the interiors in which businesses met their customers.

## Streamline
The new designers’ imaginations were fired by the Supermarine S.6B, a seaplane created by Reginald Joseph Mitchell (1895–1937) in Southampton, England, which in 1931 broke the world air-speed record, with a then astonishing 400 mph (644 km/h).
Its smooth, curved body, with reinforcing corrugations to allow the use of thinner metal, was shaped on aerodynamic principles but perceived to be extremely beautiful.
What began as an objective solution became a styling inspiration for furniture, light fittings, and the most mundane household gadgets.
The romance of speed that had inspired the Italian Futurists to crave mass destruction was now shaping the domestic interior.
The resulting design style was the American equivalent of French Moderne.
It became known as Streamline and shared Moderne’s taste for elegant styling over raw function.
It was long, low and horizontal.
It began a with technical innovation, and became a commercial success.
Public taste appeared to accept modern design when it ventured beyond the utilitarian and became glamorous.

## A New
Breed of Designer Design, especially industrial or product design, likes to promote itself as a problem-solving activity but these first practitioners came from different backgrounds, the theater, film, and particularly what was then called “commercial art”—the making of illustrations for magazine advertisement pages.
All had personal style—commercial artist turned fine artist Andy Warhol (1928 –87) specialized in drawing shoes.

## Loewy
Raymond Loewy (1893–1986) was born in France but began working life as a window designer for New York department stores and an illustrator for Vogue and Harper’s Bazaar.
He designed the Coldspot refrigerator and many of the other machines that became emblematic of the United States and would help establish it as the trailblazer in popular culture—shark-nosed locomotives, and long, low Studebaker automobiles.
For an exhibition in 1934 he created a Streamline office, a room of curves and stylish light fittings (20.14).
As his firm grew, Loewy designed interiors that were accessible to large sectors of the population including passenger cars for the Pennsylvania Railroad, offices, and retail stores.
20.14 Raymond Loewy, mock-up of Streamline office, New York, 1934.
Loewy created this office for a design exhibition.
He is shown surrounded by examples of his work: furniture, lighting, a clock, an automobile model, and a drawing board.
The curved forms testify to his commitment to streamlining as a decorative device.

## Teague
Walter Dorwin Teague (1883–1960) born in Decatur, Indiana, moved to New York and from 1903 studied painting at the Art Students League before becoming a commercial artist.
In 1926, he set up his own product and packaging design studio.
In 1929, Eastman Kodak asked him to redesign its range of cameras.
He insisted on working with the company’s engineers to evolve ideas, a process which he said led to more attractive products and better sales.
His cameras for Eastman Kodak—including the Bantam Special of 1936 with its black enameled aluminum body, curves, and bright metal corrugations—were distinctly Streamline.
The aesthetic worked equally well for other clients, such as the manufacturer of the Sparton radio (20.15), and would go on to shape the interiors of the airliners that would replace 1930s railroad rolling stock as the modern way to travel stylishly (20.16).
20.15 Walter Dorwin Teague, Sparton 457X Euro Sled radio, 1936.
Teague designed this radio for the Sparks-Worthington Company in Jackson, Michigan.
Electrical goods were considered particularly suitable for Streamline treatment and blazed the trail for the rethinking of more traditional household goods 20.16 Walter Dorwin Teague, downstairs lounge, Stratocruiser, 1947.
Teague preserved the tradition of modernistic elegance that had typified railroad travel in the 1930s into the next decade with the gentle streamlining of the interior of the Boeing 377 Stratocruiser.

## Bel
Geddes Norman Bel Geddes (1893–1958) was born in Adrian, Michigan and began his career as a theater designer at New York’s Metropolitan Opera.
After visiting the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts in Paris in 1925, he switched to industrial design.
His proposals included an airliner as big as an ocean liner and a revolving restaurant on top of a skyscraper.
In 1938 he demonstrated he could deliver more modest interior projects with the curved walls and mirrored expanses of the Elbow Room at the Berkshire Hotel.
In 1939 his Futurama exhibit at the New York World’s Fair presented a model of the world twenty years into the future (20.18), and the upholstered curves and sweeping lines that defined it were persistent elements in his later furniture and products (20.17).

## 20.17 Norman Bel Geddes, lounge chair, c. 1950. One of a range of beechwood-framed chairs
that were upholstered in a wide variety of colors.
The stitching of the fabric emphasized its Streamline profile.
20.18 Norman Bel Geddes, Futurama, New York World’s Fair, 1939.
Futurama was an exhibit and ride at the New York World’s Fair.
It was Geddes’s Streamline solution to explaining the future.

## Dreyfuss
Henry Dreyfuss (1904–72) was born in Brooklyn and, like Bel Geddes, began his career as a theater designer.
He worked for Bel Geddes before setting up his own studio in 1929, creating vacuum cleaners for Hoover, telephone handsets for Bell, and tractors for John Deere.
He designed streamline casings and interiors for the 20th Century Limited express locomotive that ran between New York and Chicago, as well as interiors for ships of the American Export Lines (20.19).
He was a stylist but took as his starting point the ergonomic and anthropometric data that he evolved and eventually published as The Measure of Man in 1960.
20.19 Henry Dreyfuss, passenger lounge, 20th Century Limited, 1938.
The 20th Century Limited train connected New York and Chicago in 16 hours.
With space to spare for a lounge, Dreyfuss, who also designed the locomotive and the cars, could indulge passengers.

## Rohde
Gilbert Rohde (1894–1944) was from New York but a trip as a student to France and Germany in 1927 encouraged him to design for mass production, to bring modern artifacts to the greatest number of domestic and commercial consumers.
While an illustrator for New York department stores he designed Moderne interiors and furniture for private clients.
In 1929 he opened his own studio and, in 1930, designed a bentwood chair in an attempt to match the modernistic pieces being produced in France.
A desk, in 1934, marked his switch from wood to tubular metal and a confident use of the curved corner.
He revitalized the then struggling Herman Miller Furniture Company by introducing cautiously modernistic pieces.
He pioneered modular domestic furniture with a range of storage pieces for which customers could specify finishes, hardware, and internal organization (20.20).
In 1942 he brought the modular principle to office furniture: his Executive Office Group system had 137 components including pedestals, table tops, drawers, cupboards, and subdivision options.
His most technically innovative work was a chair with a tubular metal frame, over which he laid a clear Plexiglass membrane (20.21).
Rohde’s ensemble for the furniture company would remain fashionable for the next twenty years.
The furniture was mansonia wood and the dining table could be extended.
Gilbert Rohde, living room for Herman Miller Furniture Company, 1936.
Gilbert Rohde, Plexiglass and steel-tube chair, Museum of Modern Art collection, New York, c.
1938.
A disconcertingly minimal plastic and metal chair that contrasts with Richard Riemerschmid’s less elegant attempt to rethink the structure of a chair in wood (see 15.32).

## Russel
and Mary Wright Wright Accessories Inc., was a company formed by Russel (1904–76) and Mary Wright (née Small Epstein, 1904–52).
Russel worked on the assumption that the dining table was the center of the home and began by producing modernistic tableware and then the furniture that complemented it.
Mary encouraged him to establish himself as an industrial designer and their first products were made in spun aluminum.
She had trained as a sculptor, was vice president of the company, factory supervisor and responsible for publicity and marketing.
She also founded American Design Inc., to promote American industrial design.
The Wright company’s most successful and influential product was American Modern, the first modernistic line to be offered to Americans.
It was introduced in 1939 and by 1959 had sold two million pieces and its success brought the company’s furniture, utensils, cutlery, and table linen to a wide public (20.22).
They also produced lines of melamine plastic tableware for use in restaurants and, in 1953, Residential, a melamine range—in the same colors as American Modern—for domestic use In 1951 the Wrights co-wrote A Guide to Easier Living (1951)—a primer in how to live a modern American lifestyle.
20.22 Russel Wright, American Modern tableware, 1939.
Wright’s smooth forms, presented in pretty pastel colors, introduced the American public to modernity.
The enormous success of the range helped convince American industry that modern design could sell to the general public.

## Liebes
The textile designer Dorothy Liebes (1897–1972) was born in California and established her reputation as an innovative designer and successful businesswoman from her studios in San Francisco, before moving to New York, the center of American design, in 1948.
She created modern fabrics for public and commercial interiors and was known for daring bright colors, extraordinary textures, and mixes of materials, which included metals, leather, and bamboo.
Her use of vibrant color set her work apart from the modernists who preferred monochromes.
She exploited the new plastics that became available after World War II and her pieces were popular with architects, including Frank Lloyd Wright, whom she met in 1935, when he influenced her design thinking.
Like every good designer, she wanted an audience and evolved ways to achieve a popular handwoven appearance using power looms.

## Greta
and Walter von Nessen Greta von Nessen (1898–1975) was Swedish and a graduate of the Stockholm School for Industrial Arts.
She emigrated to the United States with her German husband Walter (1889–1943), in 1925, and they set up Nessen Studio in New York in 1927.
In the interwar years it was Walter’s work that established the studio’s reputation, particularly the swing-arm mechanism that he used in a succession of table and floor lamps (20.23).
During World War II, Greta worked in the United States Office of Information.
Walter ded in 1943 and Greta reopened the studio and workshop after the war ended in 1945.
She specialized in lighting design and her Anywhere lamp consolidated the studio’s reputation.
With its aluminum base and enameled steel shade, its form, particularly the continuous curve of the base, had a beautifully simple visual logic (20.24).
20.23 Walter von Nessen, table lamp with swing arm, 1927.
Von Nessen perfected the swinging-arm mechanism shortly after his arrival in the United States in 1925 and used it for floor, table and wall lamps.
Greta von Nessen, Anywhere table lamp, 1951.
All the electric components used to produce the Anywhere were at least twenty years old.
It was a triumph of styling,

## The
Streamlined Home Streamline came into American homes through the kitchen.
From 1934 the tall Coldspot refrigerator sold through the Sears, Roebuck catalog, and therefore, thanks to the retailer’s national network, was available in the remotest corners of the country.
The fridge and its imitators, all with rounded corners, were domestic monuments to the style.
Smooth white surfaces transformed kitchens into laboratories (20.25).
For Americans, the new kitchen was an introduction to a way of living that would pervade all areas of their homes; bathrooms were overhauled with built-in tubs and showers, basins were set into storage cabinets.
Kraetsch & Kraetsch, Butler House, Des Moines, Iowa, 1936.
The modern kitchen, as it had developed by the 1930s, made use of a continuous counter with overhead cabinets modeled on the practice of scientific-laboratory design.
Ease of cleaning and efficiency of work patterns are implied, while the visual impact relates to the streamlining typical of industrial designers’ work of the time.
Kitchen appliances —such as the range visible in this illustration—were designed to fit into this concept of the modern kitchen.
Streamline seemed particularly appropriate for electrical goods and a new power source deserved new fittings.
Indirect light sources were concealed in cornices or sconces, washed walls, the ceilings, and the fluorescent tube became standard in kitchens and the norm in public, commercial and institutional interiors.
For Europeans, who were still largely deprived of modern conveniences, those household goods represented a promised land of consumer durables.
However excited householders were by household gadgets, they were more conservative in living rooms and bedrooms.
The radios and phonographs that replaced the piano as the source of entertainment were required to match the gravitas of the instrument they usurped and were encased in carved wooden cabinets with doors to conceal dials and mechanical parts.
Caution prevailed in the choice of carpets and fabrics, and geometric or abstract patterns were seldom found in homes.

## Eating
Out The archetypal vernacular American public meeting place was the diner, the ubiquitous shortorder restaurant that took its inspiration from railroad dining cars, and it locked Streamline into popular culture.
Diners appeared in the 1920s with Moderne detailing that evolved into Streamline in the 1930s.
Repurposed railroad cars were narrow but later, purpose-built alternatives persisted with railroad references.
Typically, a counter, with rotating backless stools, ran the length of the plan with a narrow preparation-and-serving area behind and booths against the other long wall.
Colors were brash and materials metallic and plastic.
Floors were usually black and white checkerboard tiles, upholstery was usually red and plastic, and ceilings were often coved, to suggest a dining car on a railroad locomotive (20.26).
For Europeans, diners symbolized an egalitarian culture; their interiors would become familiar in Hollywood films.
But in the Great Depression of the 1930s, Hollywood also offered a less egalitarian environment that was just as seductive, in the bright white Art Deco apartments, restaurants, and nightclubs that were the haunts of the socialite protagonists of mysteries and musicals.
20.26 Supreme Diner, Boston, Massachusetts, 1946.
The diner, a short-order restaurant that set out to recreate the dining car of a railroad locomotive, became a popular feature of the American roadside.
As real railroad dining cars adopted Streamline and Moderne traits, so the diner followed adopting rounded corners, chrome trims, and strong, bright lighting.
When attempts to dress up skyscrapers in Greek and Gothic fragments were abandoned and the later, even taller, towers were allowed to evolve their own identities, an accessible modernistic, American, style emerged.
By the end of the 1930s, despite reverberations from the International Style exhibition of 1932, skyscrapers that are now classified as Art Deco demonstrated how popular modern exteriors and interiors, could find an appreciative audience.
World War II began in 1939 and Europe and much of Asia were forced to fight on their home fronts but, for the United States, it was an overseas war that resuscitated its economy and allowed it to build what seemed, to the rest of the world, a template for the future.
THE POST-WAR WORLD 1945–80 CHAPTER TWENTY-ONE Charles and Ray Eames, Eames House and Studio, Pacific Palisades, California, 1949.
The Eames House was assembled from standard materials intended for the construction of industrial sheds.
The High tech style was born.
It integrated the interior with the garden and bathed the interior with natural light.
The Eameses catholic collection of artifacts personalized the space, suggesting that the empty shell of a building benefits from the humanizing influence of its users.
After World War II, the priority among Europeans was to rebuild acceptable lifestyles and they had the example of the United States as their target.
They did not necessarily wish to mimic it but to equal it—and those European countries that were not part of the Communist bloc would achieve broad parity with it and each other.
Britain, linked to the United States as wartime allies and via a common language was most prone to absorb and recycle its popular culture.
But twenty years after the war, suddenly, unaccountably, with its pop music and its street fashion, Britain would redefine popular culture in Europe and the United States.

## UNITED
STATES In The Life and Times of the Thunderbolt Kid (2006) Bill Bryson, an American travel writer living in Britain, wrote, “I can’t imagine there was ever a more gratifying time or place to be alive than America in the 1950s.
No country had ever known such prosperity.” The United States had rallied economically during World War II.
In the Great Depression of the 1930s, unemployment had peaked at 24.9 percent.
In 1943, after the country entered the war, it was 1.9 percent.
World War II was, like World War I, a social and aesthetic watershed but this time aesthetics were not shaped by radicals in Paris but by American suburbanites who inhabited a world of new oil-based plastics.
Prefabrication techniques, evolved to speed up wartime production, were not adapted for social housing as in Britain, but to build houses for sale.
An East Coast developer, Levitt & Sons, bought and built on enormous tracts of land within commuting distance of cities and major towns.
Returning service members could buy homes without paying a deposit thanks to government aid; their monthly repayments were no more than the rent for a city-center walk-up apartment with no outdoor space.
William Levitt (1907–94) described the company as a manufacturer rather than a builder with teams completing a house every 16 minutes on average.
Each house came with a built-in television, a hi-fi set, and two trees in the yard, included in the price.

## Residential
Design Suburban houses were never going to win critical approval and a quasi-folk song, “Little Boxes” (1964), complained that “they all look just the same.” But they did not stay “just the same” for long.
Proud owners quickly began to customize.
The rich called in designers and decorators but suburbanites did it themselves.
The houses’ open-plan living room, dining room, and kitchen were really one room punctuated by pieces of built-in furniture.
Colors were bright and patterns bold.
They made prewar Art Deco seem restrained.
Natural and artificial materials were mixed, splayed legs supported tables with plastic laminated tops and chairs with gaudy upholstery.
No one wanted machines to live in, they wanted houses that were enjoyable to live in.
They were not interested in philosophical debates about aesthetics—they knew what they liked and there was a consensus that explained how citizens preferred their interiors and, by extension, the public interiors they shared.
Architectural style had been under consideration.
In 1939 the New York World’s Fair (see here), with World of Tomorrow as its theme, had featured a Town of Tomorrow.
New consumer and industrial products such as television, air-conditioning, and color film were introduced to the public at the fair.
Architects contributing to the exhibits were told that their work should be modern but not modernistic—it should incorporate the advantages of technological advance and did not need to be deployed in a particular style, the exterior and/or interior could be deployed in any style, new or old.

## An
Ideal Home In 1940 Daniel S.
Defenbacher (1906–86), an architect by training and an arts administrator at the Walker Arts Center in Minneapolis, initiated the Idea House project to introduce Minnesotans to the positives and pleasures of modern living.
The house designed by local architects, husbandand-wife team Malcolm (1913–2003) and Miriam Lein, and constructed in the grounds of the center.
Local suppliers and retailers provided materials and furniture.
It was open plan with sliding screens offering options for privacy.
It had an electric stove, refrigerator, dishwasher, and washing machine.
Surfaces were easy to clean.
To guide the 20,000 Minnesotans who visited the house, Defenbacher suggested, “As a consumer every man uses art . . . his composition is his environment.” He insisted that Idea House was not a universal answer but a prompt to give visitors an idea of what they might achieve and that they should make their own decisions.
He was identifying interior design as a folk art (21.2).
Malcolm and Miriam Lein, Idea House I, Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, 1941.
A worthy first attempt to introduce Minnesotans to the advantages of modern design using locally available materials and furniture.
In 1947 the project was repeated but with a better budget.
Idea House II, designed by William Friedman and Hilde Reiss (1909–2002) with Malcolm Lein, was again built in the grounds of the center.
It was decorated with a more extensive collection of fabrics, wallpapers, and paint colors.
National manufacturers were interested in the project.
On-site interior designers offered curious visitors explanations and strategic advice but insisted that final decisions about layout and decoration should be left to householders.
The principal room was flexible, designated for relaxing, eating, working, and entertainment, while storage units divided activity areas.
A chimney breast of unplastered concrete blocks provided a focal and pivotal point in the manner of a Prairie house (see here).
Furniture was supplied by Knoll and included chairs by Charles and Ray Eames, lighting by German-born designer Walter von Nessen, and storage walls by George Nelson (21.3).
Defenbacher may have hoped that visitors would appreciate the quality of the superior furniture and fittings in Idea House II, but he continued to insist that, ultimately, decisions about domestic interiors should be made by those who would live in them.
21.3 William Friedman, Hilde Reiss and Malcolm Lein, Idea House II, Walker Art Center, Minneapolis, 1947.
The better-funded second Idea House, with improved furniture and finishes offered a more radical impression of what the new post-war home might be.
Daniel S.
Defenbacher, for all his insistence that householders should make their own decisions about their interiors, was gently pushing modernistic options.
Defenbacher’s insinuation that popular taste deserved to have its say bothered some.
In 1949 Philip Johnson and the Museum of Modern Art in New York appropriated Defenbacher’s idea and had Marcel Breuer design a two-bedroom house for the museum’s sculpture garden.
A number of Breuer’s designs were cloned on the East Coast.
Defenbacher had refused to give people plans of the Idea House since they were bespoke, but the Museum of Modern Art stipulated that Breuer’s design should be replicated precisely and the interior offered limited options for personal expression (21.4).
Marcel Breuer, The House in the Museum Garden, Museum of Modern Art, New York, 1949.
An American step away from the strict minimalism of European modernism of the 1930s.
The furnishings, the fireplace, and the floor patterns are closer to the tastes of the American suburb.
The design community, unsettled by rampaging suburbia, felt obliged to bring the public to heel.
The Museum of Modern Art led the crusade, organizing “Good Design” exhibitions from 1950 to 1955 and, in Los Angeles, Art and Architecture magazine commissioned and built, as exemplars of acceptable modernism, designs for model suburban homes.
In 1949 it invited Charles (1907–78) and Ray Eames (1912–88) to design the eighth house in the series and the Eameses decided to live in their design.
It was constructed, with a speed that rivaled Levitt’s, from steel and aluminum products intended for building industrial sheds and its empty shell suggested an eccentrically glazed warehouse, but the Eameses filled it with plants, rugs, scatter cushions, and knick-knacks.
They demonstrated that modernity benefited from—and was perhaps complemented by—the decorative objects that modernists previously condemned as ornament, and so the Eames House followed the Maison de Verre in Paris (see here) on to the list of interiors that modernists revered.
Both buildings depend on the incongruous juxtaposition of the soft and the intimate against the hard and tectonic (21.1).
Another house in the Art and Architecture series, by Pierre Koenig (see here), built in 1958, was a hybridization of the Eameses’ concept and the Farnsworth House: a black steel single-story structure with white corrugated panels for walls and ceilings, a single space punctuated by a utilities block.
Photographs show it sparsely furnished, a show house with no evidence of a bonafide owner’s idiosyncratic taste.
A house constructed in 1965–6 in Ventura County by Buff, Hensman & Associates had finishes and furniture that belonged to the same band of taste as the Koenig House.
Both were fine and of their time but, unlike the Eames House broke no new ground.
The Eameses, who had married in 1941, were multidisciplinary designers shaped by the Scandinavian ideas of the Finn, Eliel Saarinen (see here), who taught them at the Cranbrook Academy of Art in Bloomfield Hills, Michigan, where they developed an understanding of the structural and shape-making potential of bent plywood.
Their lounger, with its fat leather cushions held in place by the upturned edges of walnut-veneered plywood, and its matching ottoman have become architects’ comfy chair of choice.
The extensive range of chairs created by the Eameses has become popular, striking a chord with twenty-first century designers and householders who have grown to appreciate them.
Their DSR side chair with its plastic seat on wood or metal legs has become ubiquitous.
The plastic seat, with or without arms, is simple to manufacture and, unlike the chairs of Europe’s modernist pioneers, it is affordable.
Eliel’s son, Eero Saarinen (1910–61), was also educated at Cranford and knew the Eameses.
In 1939 he collaborated with Charles to design a chair to be used as auditorium seating for Kleinhans Music Hall in Buffalo, New York.
Formed from a single piece of plywood for seat and back, it appears to have been influenced by Alvar Aalto’s Paimio armchair (see here).
Eero became a partner in Eliel’s architectural practice and in 1942 they completed the First Christian Church (also known as the Tabernacle Church) in Columbus, Indiana (21.5).
Its white walls and simple timber furniture, with a minimal crucifix slightly offset on the floating wall demonstrate that modernism may have a dimension that transcends practicalities.
Eero addressed the problem of creating modernist interiors with something more than the logic of function by becoming an Expressionist, that is creating architecture that expresses a conceptual idea that is not generated by rational analysis of a building’s function.
In his TWA Flight Center airport terminal at Idlewild Airport (now John F.
Kennedy International Airport) in New York (1956–62), the undersides of its soaring roof planes became soaring ceiling planes and are said to be symbolic of flight (21.6).
His 630-feet (190-m) tall stainless steel Gateway Arch in St.
Louis (1963) is an emphatically expressionist gesture.
Eliel and Eero Saarinen, First Christian (Tabernacle) Church, Columbus, Indiana, 1942.
Considered the first American church of modern design.
It is an expression of faith that modernism could create a spiritual and meditative environment without imagery and symbols, apart from the cross.
Eero Saarinen, TWA Terminal, John F.
Kennedy International Airport, New York, 1956–62.
Saarinen exploited the structural capacity of reinforced concrete to create free-form curves, which are said to be a metaphor for flight.
They characterize the building’s exterior and interior in a baroque modernism.

## Furnishings
The development of modern interior design in the 1930s and 1940s was held back by the lack of suitable furniture for commercial and residential contexts.
The Artek company had found some outlets for pieces by Alvar and Aino Aalto and Thonet but, in 1937 Hans Knoll (1914–55) arrived in New York from Germany and set up his eponymous furniture company.
He was not a designer but understood the furniture needed for the modernist interior.
He joined forces with Danish designer Jens Risom (1916–2016), who arrived in the United States in 1939 bringing with him Scandinavian ideas and methods.
Risom designed wooden-framed tables and chairs with wooden backs and seats of ribbed webbing.
When the United States entered World War II in 1941, Knoll’s designs were suitable for military facilities and could be made in small workshops.
The 650 chair of 1941, with its tapered legs and wide-webbing seat and back, is still in production (21.7).
Jens Risom, Knoll 650 low lounge chair, 1941.
A perfect example of how the legacy of Scandinavian craft could be redeployed in the cause of modern furniture making.
In 1943 Florence Knoll (née Schust; 1917–2019) joined Knoll to deal with interior-design projects.
Her career was a triumph of luck and determination.
An orphan, she had attended Kingswood School for Girls in Michigan, which is part of the Cranbrook Educational Community, where her interest in architecture and interiors was encouraged.
From 1936–7 she worked on furniture with Eero Saarinen and Charles Eames and met Alvar Aalto, who recommended the Architectural Association in London as a place to study.
She went there, from 1938 until the outbreak of war in 1939, then became an unpaid apprentice for Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer, and studied under Ludwig Mies van der Rohe in Chicago.
She later used those connections to persuade Mies and Breuer to have their designs produced by Knoll.
Eero Saarinen also contributed pieces, including his womb chair of 1948 and his Tulip chairs and tables of 1955–6 (21.8).
She designed pieces herself to fill gaps in the range (21.9).
In 1946 she married Hans Knoll and began to build the company’s interior-design service.
It became a favored consultancy for modernist architects.
She added a textile division in 1949, led by the Hungarian-born Eszter Haraszty (1920–94), who added stronger colors to the sober, Mies-influenced interiors.
21.8 Eero Saarinen, Tulip range for Herman Miller Furniture Company, mid 1950s.
The Tulip range of tables and chairs was designed in the mid 1950s.
The pedestal support was Saarinen’s solution to what he saw as the visual confusion of chair and table legs in dining rooms.
21.9 Florence Knoll, furniture, 1940s and 1950s.
As design director of Knoll Associates, Knoll was key in maintaining the company’s commitment to manufacturing modernistic products and producing pieces herself to cover gaps in its range.
The Herman Miller Furniture Company was Knoll’s rival.
When Gilbert Rohde (see here) died, in 1944, his place as lead designer was taken by George Nelson (1908–86), who designed a complete range of furniture that was launched in 1946.
His team produced modular cabinets, seating and beds (21.11), and he added a strange walnut and glass coffee table (1947; 21.12) by Isamu Noguchi (1904–88).
The Eameses also contributed.
They had continued their experiments with plywood and, in 1947, produced a series of chairs, including the all-plywood DCW and the LCM with fiberglass seats and backs supported on splayed chrome metal legs (21.10).
21.10 Charles and Ray Eames, the DCW chair (left) and LCM (right), c.
1947.
DCW was the best known of the Eameses’ plywood chairs, with a double-curved seat and back made using molding techniques the Eameses evolved during World War II to make splints for the U.S.
Navy.
It was produced in dining and lounging heights with wood or metal legs.
21.11 George Nelson, chest of drawers, walnut veneer, metal hardware, 1950s.
Nelson’s furniture, produced when he was design director of Herman Miller, exhibits the clean lines and absence of ornament that typified the mid-century modern aesthetic.
21.12 Isamu Noguchi, walnut and glass coffee table, 1947.
This table was a curious organic addition to the Knoll range.
Its free-form base, formed with two identical wooden sections, supported a biomorphic clear-glass top.
It sat incongruously among the straight lines and right angles of the rest of the collection.
In 1952 Nelson recruited Alexander Girard (1907–93) as head of the textile division.
Girard had trained as an architect in London and Rome.
His first collection of textiles with squares, circles, triangles, and stripes worked well with the aesthetic of Nelson’s team and contributed significantly to its influence on post-war interiors.
His collection of folk art inspired his more colorful and densely patterned fabrics and he collaborated with a Mexican textile mill to develop what he called “mexidots” and “mexistripes,” which became popular for upholstery and wall panels (21.13).
In 1971 he developed forty fabric panels to enliven offices which, under the influence of pragmatic space planners, were becoming bereft of visual stimuli.

## 21.13 Alexander Girard, striped textile, 1954. Girard was influenced by the bright colors
he found in his collection of folk art from Arizona, Mexico, South America, and India.
In 1965 Girard worked for Braniff International Airways on “The End of the Plain Plane” project, designing a range of items, from check-in desks to sugar sachets, and the blue, beige, ocher, orange, turquoise, and lemon palette from which a distinctive livery was created for each airplane in the Braniff fleet.
In 1960 he designed everything from floor and wall tiles to tableware and menus for a Latin American restaurant in Manhattan, all on themes prompted by his knowledge of South American folk art.
For The Compound restaurant in Santa Fe (1967), he created eighty different sun motifs as wall decoration.
In 1964 he assembled a mural 180 feet (55 m) long and 8 feet (2.5 m) high from found objects, for the John Deere tractor company headquarters designed by Eero Saarinen in Moline, Illinois.
Hungarian-born interior designer Paul Laszlo (1900–93) was another Jew forced to abandon a successful practice in Europe and leave for the United States in 1936.
Laszlo was based in Beverly Hills, California, creating glamorous homes before moving on to retail and designing individual stores, department stores, and shopping malls.
He designed a wide range of building types including offices, banks, and casinos but he kept his practice small to control its output.
He wanted time to refine detail and built a network of makers and suppliers who met his standards.
He favored wealthy clients who shared his creative ambitions, believing that interaction with a supportive client drove ideas.
His work was restrained and relied for its quirky elegance on fine craft processes.
He expressed approval for the modernism of his fellow Jewish exile in California, the Austrian architect Richard Neutra (see here) but favored decorative devices.
The austere elegance of his furniture suggests fin-de-siècle Vienna and his generous upholstery recognizes the need for comfort.
Laszlo attracted bizarre projects.
In 1955 he designed an underground bomb shelter for the owner of the Hertz car-rental company.
In 1956 he designed a speculative bombproof underground town, Atomville, for an article in the magazine Popular Mechanics, where houses had rooftop (or ground level) helipads for the helicopters expected to replace automobiles.

## INSIGHTS

## Modernism
and Social Environments In the late 1940s, as high-rise social housing demonstrated the grim reality of Le Corbusier’s theories, Architectural Review expressed doubts about modernism’s ability to create successful social environments.
To test this, in 1949, it launched a competition to design the interior of a public house (bar), something progressive without being inhuman and popular without being silly.1 The judges’ report spoke about the importance of atmosphere, colors, intimacy of scale, and decoration.
In 1958 the magazine suggested that architecture and interior design existed in different time frames: The architect’s mind geared to generalized functions that change slowly, or never, is unlikely to be athletic enough to provide an appropriately ephemeral interior solution.2 It advocated that interior designers should have training similar to that of architects but did not suggest that they also needed quite different skills.
1.
Architectural Review, vol.
106, issue 633, 1949, p.
265; 2.
Ibid., vol.
123, issue 735, 1958, p.
227

## EUROPE
After the war, Europe’s priority was rebuilding, literally and metaphorically.
Some countries escaped lightly, such as France which had been defeated quickly, Finland which had limited strategic significance, and Sweden which had asserted its neutrality.
Others had not: Italy had been a war zone as the Allies fought their way to Germany, and Germany had been a battlefield as American, British, and Russian forces converged on Berlin.
Consequently, images of American interiors and American lives were viewed enviously in post-war Europe.
The United States had its military hard power but its soft power was perhaps even more effective.
Its lifestyle was celebrated in films.
Its popular music became pervasive and young Europeans envied and aped the lifestyles of their American contemporaries.

## Britain
Throughout the war, Britain had been on the front line.
From September 7, 1940 German aircraft bombed London for fifty-seven successive days before moving on to more far-flung British cities.
Raw materials were scarce, food and clothing were rationed—the country’s war loans from the United States would not be paid off until 2006.
In 1945 Britain elected a socialist government on a mandate to create an egalitarian utopia.
New schools and hospitals offered citizens their first encounters with the modernist interior, which was hard-edged but brightly optimistic.
By the end of the war, a quarter of a million houses had been destroyed and two million badly damaged by enemy bombing; two and a quarter million people were homeless.
In 1944 manufacturing had already began on small, prefabricated asbestos cement bungalows with a living room, two bedrooms, a bathroom, and a kitchen.
For those who had shared overcrowded, insanitary pre-war houses the “prefabs” were wonderful self-contained family domains with hot running water.
Apartments in high-rises, which were ostensibly cheaper and faster to build than traditional row houses, seemed like permanent solutions to housing shortages.
Britons might dream of Americans’ suburbs, of new houses on their own plots, of bright interiors packed with plastic laminates and electric gadgets but the social housing provided for victims of wartime bombing and pre-war slums was created by modernist architects for the approval of other modernist architects.

## Festival
of Britain In 1943, when wartime victory seemed likely, Britain began planning an event to mark the centenary of the Great Exhibition of 1851 (see here).
The government considered that an optimistic view of its future would boost national morale.
Sir Hugh Casson (1910–99), who understood that exhibitions should entertain and exhilarate, was appointed director of architecture.
He employed the promising young architects and designers who would go on to produce the better interiors of the 1950s.
A few architectural idealists complained that proposals did not conform to modernist thinking.
Ralph Tubbs (1912–96), Dome of Discovery, Festival of Britain, London, 1951.
The dome, with its diameter of 365 feet (111 m), stood 93 feet (28 m) tall, making it the largest dome in the world.
It housed many festival attractions including galleries on various levels that housed exhibitions on the theme of discovery.
Robert Matthew (1906–75) and Leslie Martin (1908–2000), Royal Festival Hall, London, 1951.
The concert hall was the one building at the Festival of Britain that was intended to be permanent.
The ceiling section, with concealed light sources, and the curved fronts of the boxes on the sides were planned to improve acoustics.
The main Festival of Britain site was inevitably in London, on the South Bank of the Thames.
Its centerpiece, the Royal Festival Hall (1951), was to be the first of a future clutch of arts buildings planned for the site (21.15).
It was a major public building but its interiors had light-hearted detailing not usually found in cultural colossi.
Other structures, such as the Dome of Discovery, were on an heroic scale but temporary, which reduced public anxiety about their modernity (21.14).
