An exhibition ship and converted buses brought snippets of new design to more distant destinations.
Principal cities mounted exhibitions.
In Northern Ireland, Belfast featured a mockup of a modern domestic interior (21.16).
Ten million visitors glimpsed the future and mostly 21.16 James Scott, Festival of Britain, Belfast, 1951.
A mock-up of a living room and enclosed garden that gave people outside fashionable London an impression of a new way of living.
Max Clendinning was a member of Scott’s team and became the leading British interior designer of the 1960s.

## The
Home Front The festival prompted a popular style in Britain that became known as Contemporary (21.19).
It was quirky and colorful and had something American and Scandinavian about it.
It photographed well and images of bright laminates, fabrics, and wallpapers with abstract patterns appeared regularly in homemaking magazines.
The feature wall—usually that containing the fireplace and decorated more vibrantly than the other walls in a room—was introduced and suggested that the convention of four matching walls in a room was obsolete.
Light-hued woods and the splayed legs of tables and chairs replaced dark brown stolidity—cacti replaced aspidistras.
The interior designers who, in 1980s Britain, would change the creative ambitions of their fellow professionals and the expectations of those who would use their buildings, grew up in such environments.
Contemporary style, Britain, 1953.
Plastics, bright colors, whimsical shapes, and shiny finishes became popular and common in the years after the Festival of Britain.
Britain had its star designers in the married couple Robin Day (1915–2010) and Lucienne Day (1917–2010).
He designed furniture with molded plywoods and plastics seats perched on chromed or matt black legs (21.17).
Her textiles were brightly colored with imagery derived from plants (21.18) and scientific symbols—it was a time in which science was delivering benefits in the form of plastics and an existential threat in the form of atomic bombs.
Throughout their long careers they shared a long work table in a series of beautiful homes.
They featured frequently in newspapers and magazines, they were glamorous, and made design glamorous.
Robin Day, chair 675, 1952.
A dining chair with molded plywood back, chromed steel legs and leather seat that is still in production.
Lucienne Day, Calyx textile, 1951.
Calyx, produced for the Festival of Britain, is Day’s best-known design and, like much of her work, drew on plant forms.
It and many more of her fabrics remain in production.
Contemporary style made inroads into the public arena.
Italian immigrants introduced coffee shops into London’s racy Soho area as alternatives to traditional bars and tearooms, and the model spread to provincial towns and cities (21.20).
After their enforced insular wartime existence people wanted to feel cosmopolitan.
Most coffee shops were put together expediently by their proprietors who concentrated on creating atmosphere.
Architects designed a few.
In 1955 Marghanita Laski, a British novelist and radio panellist, was asked to comment on the coffee-shop phenomenon in The Architectural Review magazine.
She praised them as “somewhere to go outside home that isn’t hell to look at” and listed their distinguishing features as “wooden vertical slats . . . fleshy green plants, taper-legged, wicker-seated backless stools . . . thick glass coffee cups on the bare organic tabletops.” She did not mention the exotic hissing and spluttering of the espresso machines.
John (1925–92) and Sylvia Reid (1924–2022), coffee shop, Marylebone, London, 1955.
An interior that incorporates many characteristics of a coffee shop: an undulating ceiling, a patterned floor, vertical hardwood wall cladding, a plastic laminate counter front, Arne Jacobsen chairs (see here), Scandinavian light fittings, and a coffee machine.
Underpinning Contemporary’s aesthetic there was, just discernible, the influence of Scandinavian design.
Sweden had remained neutral through-out the war, leaning toward Germany when it seemed likely to win and toward the Allies when the pendulum swung toward them.
Precarious neutrality allowed its factories to carry on producing modernistic pieces shaped by the values absorbed from traditional craftwork.
Denmark spent most of the war under German Occupation but escaped aerial bombing and, after the war, quickly made its contribution to the Scandinavian canon.
Finland was threatened by Germany and the U.S.S.R., but was fortunate not to be on the immediate agenda of either and opened state-sponsored showrooms in London in 1953 and 1958—photographs show plywood furniture, colored-glass light shades, and bright textiles.
Contemporary was undoubtedly modernistic.
Its shapes and colors were prompted by new plastics and production techniques (21.21).
It conformed to the modernist principle of “truth to materials” but its output was too flippant for those who considered modernity no laughing matter.
As rationing ended, the appetite for domestic novelty faded and did not outlast the 1950s, but the appetite for better homes and public places survived.
21.21 Dennis Lennon (1918–91), Jaeger women’s fashion store, Glasgow, 1955.
The Festival of Britain introduced the British public to a new Contemporary aesthetic and this store incorporates contemporary fittings, the mirror-stand, the chair, the light shades, and the carpet.
Following his success with the Festival of Britain, Casson was asked to establish an architectural course at London’s Royal College of Art in 1952.
The Royal Institute of British Architects, which controlled architectural education and professional registration, refused permission so the college settled for a postgraduate interior-design course with a long-term strategy of converting it to architecture.
This conversion would take another thirty years but, over that time, the course evolved an architectural bias that gave its alumni a creative breadth that would eventually filter down to undergraduate courses.

## Italy
Italian designers trained in architecture schools but saw themselves as creative polymaths.
In the 1950s they were excited by the possibilities of plastic and the opportunities it offered to break with tradition.
Anna Castelli Ferrieri (1918–2006), the first woman to graduate in architecture from Milan Polytechnic, was a pioneer of designing with plastics from the 1950s to the 1980s.
Her husband, the chemical engineer Giulio Castelli (1920–2006), formed the Kartell furniture company and led the field in plastic-manufacturing technology.
When his two partners left the business, Ferrieri reluctantly agreed to become Kartell’s inhouse designer and commissioner of consultant designers, on whose behalf she liaised with the production team.
Her own designs, with strong geometric forms and bright colors, established the company’s reputation.
In 1964, in collaboration with Ignazio Garbella, she designed a round, glass-reinforced polyester pedestal table, in 1968 a plastic chair made from a single mold and the Multi-Box range of square stackable, injection-molded ABS plastic storage units.
In 1968 she refined Multi-Box to make the Componibili circular stacking modular storage units, which meant that doors can slide and hinges are eliminated (21.24).
She became Kartell’s art director from 1976 to 1987, during which time she designed a lounge chair, model 4841, made from recycled polyethylene materials, with ball feet at the front and wheels at the back for mobility (21.22).
A strange little chair made from recycled polythene materials, an early green design.
Called Universale because it could be used formally or informally, inside or outside.
Its bright plastic colors and rounded edges were what the progressive market in the 1960s wanted.
Joe Colombo, Universale stacking chair, 1967.
21.23 21.24 Anna Castelli Ferrieri, Componibili storage system, 1968.
Castelli Ferrieri created injection-molded PVC stackable units that can be used in every room of a house.
Their circular plan allows doors to slide and dispenses with hinges and catches.
Cesare “Joe” Colombo (1930–71) studied architecture at Milan Polytechnic, then became an Abstract Expressionist painter.
He switched to design when he inherited his family’s electricalgoods company in 1959 and was prompted to investigate new materials and production techniques.
He had the 1960s impulse to rethink the familiar and worked for innovative Italian manufacturers such as Alessi, Flexform, and Kartell.
For Kartell he designed variations on his Universale (1967) poly propylene and rubber stacking chair, which could be used inside or out, in private or public locations (21.23).
His Boby portable-office storage system was manufactured by Bieffeplast from 1968 and had pivoting trays, shelves and pockets, and could slide under a tabletop.
His Tube chair (1969–70) consisted of four upholstered cylinders that could be assembled in various combinations or nested for storage.
In 1972, for an exhibition at the Museum of Modern Art in New York, called Italy: The New Domestic Landscape, he offered a 301- square-feet (28-sq-m) “machine for living in,” or more accurately a machine containing kitchen, bathroom, clothes storage and bed, which would sit autonomously within a larger living space (21.25).
21.25 Joe Colombo, design for Italy: The New Domestic Landscape, Milan, 1972.
From the 1960s, designers became interested in objects that could be transformed and adapted.
In this exhibition tableau, Colombo offered a cabriolet bed with a folding canopy, a curtain to subdivide a large room, a rotating dining table-shelf and tube chairs.
All were inventive but adaptability compromised efficiency.

## Denmark
In the mid twentieth century, Scandinavian design had a high international profile and, of the four Scandinavian countries, Denmark had the highest.
Its interiors and furnishings were broadly modernist with white walls, light-hued wooden floors, highly crafted wooden furniture, and elegant, witty light fittings.
They demonstrated how hard, modernist lines might be made amenable and their work struck a chord with designers trying to find their own post-war world.
Arne Jacobsen (1902–71) was Denmark’s recognized design doyen.
While still a student, he won a silver medal at the International Exhibition of Modern Decorative and Industrial Arts in Paris in 1925, where he was excited by Le Corbusier’s Pavillon de l’Esprit Nouveau.
He then traveled to Germany to see the work of Mies and Gropius.
In 1929 he collaborated with a fellow Danish architect, Flemming Lassen (1902–84), to win a House of the Future competition in Denmark and their design was built at the Architects Building and Housing Forum in Copenhagen.
It had a spiral plan, glass and concrete walls, and a flat roof that would act as a helipad.
It was considered disturbingly radical.
After 1934 he worked closely with the Fritz Hansen manufacturing company for his furniture designs and with the Louis Poulsen company for his lighting.
When Denmark was annexed by Germany in 1940, Jacobsen, a Jew, was obliged to retreat to neutral Sweden but, when he returned after the war in 1945, his practice grew quickly thanks to a national program of rebuilding.
His commitment to Gesamtkunstwerk—the total work of art—led him to design the furniture and fittings in his most important projects.
For his SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen (1956–60), he designed all the furniture, which included his Egg and Swan chairs.
The former has a high back that wraps around a sitter’s head, the latter a low back with separate armrests and back, which when viewed side on, suggest a swan, both have shape-hugging upholstery and rotate on low steel cruciform bases (21.26).
Jacobsen also created light fittings, and miscellaneous objects.
For St.
Catherine’s College, a new college in Oxford, England, he designed all the buildings, the furniture, light fittings, cutlery, and the garden, where he even specified the breed of fish for the pond.
He was influenced by the experiments of Charles and Ray Eames with plywood and in 1952 created Ant, which is a light, stackable chair with seat and back molded from a single length of plywood that rests on chromed legs (21.29).
Like the Swan chair, it bears some resemblance to the creature that gave it its name.
Arne Jacobsen, SAS Royal Hotel, Copenhagen, 1956–60.
21.26 An interior that illustrates the soft modernism typical of Danish design.
Jacobsen designed all the furniture, including his curving armchair, known as the Egg chair (left).
Arne Jacobsen, Ant chair, Denmark, 1952.
Jacobsen’s habit was to name his chairs after the creatures that inspired them or which they most resembled in their finished form and the Ant is a clear example of that.
Hans Wegner (1914–2007) was a designer of chairs.
From the age of fourteen to seventeen he was apprenticed to a cabinetmaker and, after compulsory army service, attended the School of Arts and Crafts in Copenhagen to refine his skills.
He designed almost exclusively in wood, augmented by traditional materials including cane and paper cord.
His work is characterized by steam-bent, tapering timber frames with exquisitely executed interlocking joints.
He often took traditional chair forms as his starting point and his chair from 1938 for the library in the central Danish city of Nyborg which, with its bent wooden frame and the vertical closely spaced dowels in its backrest, obviously evolves from an English Windsor chair.
His most successful design, the Wishbone chair of 1949, was the culmination of a process begun in 1944 when he saw a painting of Danish merchants sitting in Chinese Ming chairs.
With its simple wooden frame, the generous sweep of the bent top rail of its backrest, and its woven seat it has become a popular dining chair.
His Round chair, also of 1949, with its simple gently curved and angled wooden frame, was hailed by the American design magazine Interiors as “the most beautiful chair in the world” (21.28).
Hans Wegner, Round chair, Denmark, 1949.
With its wooden frame and woven seat the Round chair bears great similarity to Wegner’s Wishbone chair, also of 1949, which has become more popular in homes and restaurants.
The Wishbone had a five-year creative gestation and the Round is obviously a simpler—more modernist—variant on the same theme.
Verner Panton (1926–98) was Danish and an exponent of colors and plastics.
From 1950–2 he worked for Jacobsen but, disagreeing with that exponent of Scandinavian modernism, set up his own practice and worked on the principle that more was never enough.
When used together, his furniture, fabrics and wallcoverings combined to create a visual cacophony of pattern and bright color (21.27).
His chairs are elegant: the S-shaped model known as the Panton chair, and used in 1960 in the Varna Palace restaurant, was the first wholly plastic chair to be made in a single piece.
The majority of his chairs, such as the inverted molded plastic Heart Cone of 1958, appear to have sculptural intent (21.30).
Varna Palace restaurant, Arhus, Denmark, 1971.
Design by Verner Panton. © Verner Panton Design AG A typical Panton interior, an intense world of color and plastic with the S-profiled Panton chair of 1960.
21.30 Heart Cone chair, 1958.
Design by Verner Panton.
An interpretation of the wing-backed chair, with an upholstered superstructure on a sheet steel core, swiveled on a cruciform base.
It was something unexpected from Denmark’s crafted wood furniture industry.

## THE
1960S: BRITAIN AND A SHIFT IN SOFT POWER

## Retail
The fashion designer Mary Quant (1930–2023), popularizer of the miniskirt, opened her first store, Bazaar, in 1955 on the King’s Road in Chelsea, west London, and helped begin the transformation of a conventional main street to the hub of global fashion.
In 1964, the Beatles established Britain’s pop hegemony in the United States and beyond.
British soft power supplanted that of the United States.
Swinging London in the Swinging Sixties became the epicenter of a changing world and the epicenter of Swinging London was Carnaby Street, a street of cheap clothes shops aimed at the young and fashion-obsessed.
Carnaby Street was the invention of John Stephen (1934–2004), who recognized untapped opportunities to sell fashionable clothes to young men and opened His Clothes in Carnaby Street, painting the store’s façade bright yellow and blasting pop music into the street.
Over the next ten years, he opened fifteen shops on the street, all trading under different names, to suggest independent businesses catering for niche tastes.
His strategy of ageappropriate staff selling cheap fashion became, and continues to be, the formula for fashion retailing.
With Stephens’s model in mind, independent boutique owners like the coffee-shop owners of the 1950s were happy to design their own stores, it was part of the romance of ownership.
Interiors were dark and spotlights shone on bulging racks of clothes.
Counters disappeared and customers wandered at will.
Increased prosperity allowed Britons to travel in Europe.
They returned impressed with its apparent sophistication, renaming fashion stores “boutiques” and dance halls “discotheques.” Boutiques spread from inner London to the provinces.
Management responsibilities diluted the glamor of ownership and bankruptcies were frequent but a few, cleverly conceived in the right locations, prospered.
In 1966 Granny Takes A Trip opened at the less fashionable end of King’s Road, far from Quant’s Bazaar.
Its façade was devoted to a sequence of graphic images that had nothing to do with the clothes it sold.
A permanent feature of the façade was the exhortation “One should either be a work of art or wear a work of art.” Boutique owners liked to think they were doing more than selling clothes.
The interior was practical with marbled wallpaper, a beaded curtain at the entrance, and a lace curtain that offered rudimentary privacy to the changing room.
The façade made its reputation and it was featured in “London: The Swinging City” edition of Time magazine.
Biba, the most celebrated of the boutiques, owned and designed by Barbara Hulanicki (b.
1938), opened in 1964 on the very edge of fashionable London and grew in a succession of small stores, each in a better location and each under-lit, with dark walls and dark potted palms.
The influences of Art Nouveau and Art Deco were modest but clear—both styles were fashionable but the latter was in the ascendency.
(Four years later Bevis Hillier would write Art Deco and give the style its name.) Biba’s final upgrade was to the shell of a former department store in which each floor was devoted to a product genre: women’s clothing was augmented by floors for men, children, food, and household goods.
It was an embryonic lifestyle store and continued its black-painted, underlit Art Deco theme but introduced bright Pop Art displays of ironic/iconic merchandise—cans of baked beans were the most incongruous.
The shop’s appeal had been to young women who wanted clothes, not beans.
Theatricality took precedence over selling.
The romance of the small, overcrowded interior, where customers competed to buy from tantalizingly limited stock, declined and it closed in 1976.
Hulanicki then began a second career as an interior decorator.
When they recognized the economic significance of the youth market, established retailers moved into fashion retailing.
Maurice Broughton Associates, an established design company, created Dress Circle, a boutique and coffee shop on the top floor of Harrods, one of the most prestigious London department stores.
A dedicated elevator by-passed the traditional departments below.
Dress Circle was finished to a much more sophisticated level than the boutiques of the King’s Road and Carnaby Street and photographs of the coffee shop show the bulbous plastic curves and seamless coved junctions of floors, walls, and ceilings that were the fashionable details of the time (21.32).
Maurice Broughton Associates, Dress Circle, Harrods, London, 1968.
A haven for the young and fashionable in the dowagers’ department store, it was the epitome of late 1960s design, plastics, rounded corners, and soft upholstered shapes.
Garnett Cloughley Blakemore was an architectural practice adept at creating fantasy, and not ashamed to allude to palm trees, coconuts and bamboo in the hotels and bars it designed.
It also designed a number of King’s Road boutiques, including Stop The Shop, in which a slowly revolving circular platform took up the width of its frontage.
The practice had pioneered the rotational mechanism for a restaurant on top of the Post Office Tower, which was, at 620 feet (189 m), then the tallest building in London.
South Molton Street in Mayfair, London was a fashion node distant from Carnaby Street and the King’s Road, more expensive and closer to haute couture.
In 1968 Rex Wilkinson (b.
1947), Roger Calvert (b.
1948) and Piers Gough (b.
1946) completed a boutique for the knitwear designer Mary Farrin, which provided a model for less glamorous shops on less fashionable streets into the 1970s.
Transparent and opaque glass panels were set in quadrant-cornered, glass-reinforcedplastic frames, colored to suggest brass.
The interior was tiny, 20 × 11 feet (6 × 3.5 m) but stretched by a mirrored back wall.
The geometry of the fenestration was repeated in color blocks on walls and ceiling (21.31).
Rex Wilkinson, Roger Calvert and Piers Gough, Mary Farrin boutique, London, 1968.
The circles, curved lines, and graphics are all precisely of their time and were copied extensively.
In 1968, Wilkinson, Calvert and Gough’s second South Molton Street boutique, Knitwit, seemed to anticipate postmodernism with its sky-blue walls, colored floor tiles, ziggurat display shelves, and palm-tree lights.
Changing rooms were squeezed into the larger ziggurat and described as “among the most sumptuous in London with their walls of quilted brown velvet and diamond shaped mirrors” (21.33).
However, after four months the owners painted the ceiling dark brown, covered the walls with oatmeal-flecked grass paper, and the floor with a dark brown carpet.
Even by boutique standards the project had a brief lifespan.
Rex Wilkinson, Roger Calvert and Piers Gough, Knitwit boutique, London, 1968.
The exotic imagery of palm trees and ziggurats employed in the boutique are an early example of postmodernism.
In the 1970s as fashion retailing continued to grow it became more serious as it passed from the control of idealists to business managers.
Boutiques reverted to being stores.
Stephen Marks (b.
1946), a tactically astute retailer, opened the first store in his French Connection chain in 1972.
He understood the importance of the interior: “To me it’s all quite simple—you can’t get people to go in if they don’t like the look of the store from the outside.” The importance in Britain of innovative interior design to attract newly affluent young customers across all commercial sectors led to the exponential growth, particularly in the 1970s, of interior design as a profession that was increasingly distinct from architecture.
A number of large practices emerged of which the most successful was established by Rodney Fitch (1938– 2014), who famously declared “the purpose of life is shopping.” He remembered that, in drab post-war Britain the glamour of upmarket store windows persuaded him to become a designer and he enrolled at London’s Central School of Art and Design to study theater, television, interior and furniture design.
He empathized with William Morris’s explanation that the purpose of design was to give hope.
He proposed that retail was “the only true democracy in the world”— people voted with their money and therefore cared about where they were spending it.
His declared ambition was “to deliver to ordinary people better places to shop,” better places to cast their votes on the world they wanted to inhabit.
In 1963 he was recruited to Terence Conran’s Design Group and by 1968 was its managing director.
When Conran sold Habitat and his design consultancy, Fitch bought the consultancy.
In 1972 he established Fitch & Company Design Consultants and created a template for multidisciplinary retail-design practice.
He saw design as a visceral or emotive activity.
He encouraged his staff to “read the signs of the street, not remain in [their] insular creative cocoon.” Most of the designers who established London’s leading design practices worked for him early in their careers.
He trusted visceral reaction before rational analysis.
Fitch’s clients were retail chains, department stores, and grocery supermarkets.
He was particularly proud of his work for the Topshop fashion chain that had branches in towns and cities across Britain—because it was popular with young women, a demographic that shared his enthusiasm for shopping.

## The
Modern Home Zeev Aram (1931–2021), was a Romanian Jewish wartime refugee whose family had migrated to Palestine at the outbreak of World War II.
He grew up there but settled in London in 1957.
In 1964, across the street from Quant’s Bazaar, he opened a small furniture store and design consultancy, selling “modern classics” by Le Corbusier and Mies and introducing design enthusiasts to a then unknown Eileen Gray (see here).
In the same year, 1964, Sir Terence Conran (1931–2020) opened his first Habitat furniture store and introduced a wider public to modern design, made more palatable by being sold alongside the vernacular household objects of Mediterranean peasantry.
The store’s décor of white-painted brick walls, reddish-brown, quarry-tiled floor, and batteries of spotlights was a statement of stylistic intent, and a means to seduce and induct customers into the Habitat lifestyle.
The Habitat mail-order catalog carried Conran’s message across the nation (21.34).
Elegant photographs introduced readers to visions of high-ceilinged, white-walled Victorian rooms with extant moldings and fireplaces filled with Habitat furniture counterpointed by pieces from thrift stores.
Habitat branches began to appear in towns and cities throughout Britain.
In 1977 the design critic Stephen Bayley credited Conran with doing more to promote “good design” than any academics.

## 21.34 Habitat catalog, 1977. The cover of an early catalog that illustrated the Habitat ae
sthetic.
Modernistic elements—a chair, a coffee table, and floor lamp—sit in front of a retro wooden kitchen dresser with shelves to exhibit crockery and suggest an ironica respect for tradition.
The bentwood hat and coat stand was a popular catalog purchase for buyers keen to demonstrate in their entrance halls an enthusiasm for Habitat style.

## Domestic
Experiments Max Clendinning (1924–2020) made his name with chairs assembled from four interlocking plywood components.
Each had cutouts and corners with generous quadrants that were inspired by an early computer font.
Interior-design commissions followed from wealthy clients but it was in serial reworkings of the house he shared with the painter and theater designer Ralph Adron (b.
1937) that he most effectively demonstrated how modernist principles could evolve in the Georgian and Victorian row houses that were the essential components of British towns and cities.
An early foray, in 1967, was unrelentingly white, with white floors, walls, and ceilings.
He was subtler in 1969 when he introduced tonal variations on a buff–gray base.
Long cushions snaked across a floor of painted plywood squares and around a tall papier-mâché tulip light by Adron.
Sprawling on floor cushions was endemic in the 1960s (21.35).
21.35 Max Clendinning, living room, London, 1969.
The monochrome interior and the cloud seating scattered across the floor are typical of the time.
The enormous tulip lamp is by theater designer Ralph Adron.
Clendinning conducted a different experiment in the dining room (21.36).
The flat plywood back and sides of his Maxima furniture range were cut away as far as structural stability allowed.
The ceiling and joinery details were white but walls were dusty green with bands of strong colors that bent round corners and seemed to disappear behind the cornice to reappear on the ceiling.
It was, he said, a way to “destroy the corner.” It was a first glimpse of the even more colorful painting with which Clendinning would transform his home in a major revamp of 1973.
He brought the same deep and diverse color palette to his later commissioned work and counterpointed matt and gloss paint finishes.
Traditional decorators were known through society magazines such as House and Garden and Country Life but Clendinning featured regularly in style magazines and was the first radical interior designer with a significant public profile.
Max Clendinning, dining room, 1969.
Elements no longer fuse, strong color replaces monochrome, moldings are picked out in white but subsumed in curvaceous stripes that overwhelm corners.
The chairs are from Clendinning’s Maxima range.
In the 1960s change was driven by youthful whim.
A psychedelic counterculture emerged among the hippie community in California in which drugs were valued for their capacity to “expand consciousness” which, in turn, induced artistic aspirations that led to the painting of walls, ceilings, and, sometimes, floors with swirls of bright colors.
Such motifs briefly reshaped graphic design—and may have prompted Clendinning’s dining-room stripes.

## Hospitality
French restaurants occupied the culinary high ground in Britain but were too formal for the 1960s and were supplanted by the Italian trattoria.
The Neapolitan immigrant Vincenzo “Enzo” Apicella (1922–2018) defined Italian restaurant design with tiled floors, decorative modern art prints on white walls, downlighters, gingham tablecloths, and wooden chairs with woven cane seats.
His hard finishes introduced cacophony to the restaurant experience, an aural metaphor for Italian conviviality.
He created more than one hundred and fifty restaurants.
On the Champs Elysées in Paris, Le Drugstore was a small department store selling records, food, and pharmaceuticals.
Parisians were excited by the reference to American culture but, apart from the name, there was little to consolidate the reference.
It was the glamor of Paris that prompted the opening of the Chelsea Drugstore on the King’s Road in Chelsea, London in 1968.
Designed by the architectural firm Garnett Cloughley Blakemore, its brushed-steel interior and exterior, with tall quadrant-cornered windows, seemed to anticipate things to come (21.37).
It opened in the same year as the groundbreaking science-fiction movie 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Garnett Cloughley Blakemore, Chelsea Drugstore, London, 1968.
21.37 The store was futuristic with its curves and circles, and aluminum-clad interior and exterior.
The three-story store included a pharmacy, bar, and hangout, and successfully connected retail with pop culture.
It was so fashionable it is referred to in the Rolling Stones song “You Can’t Always Get What You Want” (1969) and features as a record store in the film A Clockwork Orange (1971).

## Office
Design British-born architect Frank Duffy (b.
1940) studied postgraduate architecture at Princeton in the United States and worked in New York for a space-planning company before returning to London.
Early on, he recognized the impact that information technology would have in the workplace and understood that existing office stock was not ready for the digital upheaval on the horizon.
He rejected space planners’ mechanistic layouts of bleak cubicles, and praised Germany, the Netherlands, and Scandinavia for pioneering Bürolandschaft (office landscaping) informal layouts subdivided by strategically placed plants with an emphasis on democratic control of the working environment.
He encouraged designers and clients to collaborate in evolving designs.
In his essay “An Escape from Banality” (1983) he attacked the mundane interiors produced for commercial clients and asked, “When was the last time anyone wanted a suspended ceiling because it moved the heart?” He praised architects, such as the Victorian practitioner Richard Norman Shaw (see here), who designed “rooms that looked like rooms,” and Louis Sullivan and Frank Lloyd Wright for creating humane, multistoried, multioccupancy office buildings.
He accused Mies of being “totally uninterested in what went on inside his buildings.” He identified four factors that would transform office design: digital information technology, social change with workers given more control over their environments, the need to conserve energy which would change the shape and section of buildings, and the rise of “facilities managers” who, he hoped, would thwart architects’ diktats.
In 1973 Centraal Beheer, a Dutch insurance company, employed Herman Hertzberger (b.
1932) a leading Dutch architect to design an office building in Apeldoorn in the Netherlands that seemed to meet Duffy’s criteria (21.38).
It offered an empty matrix, multilayered both vertically and horizontally, and was intended as a solution to the impersonality of both open-plan and cellular office floors.
Workers would be responsible for fine-tuning their own working environment.
The concrete frame was infilled with concrete block walls to heights appropriate to the function behind them.
Complex plans and sections created distinctive spaces, often looking into internal voids, and workers personalized them with plants, photographs and artifacts.
It was a generous solution.
Far exceeding standard office-sector space allocation, the experiment paid off as productivity improved by 25 per cent.
Ten years later, employees were no longer happy with blockwork walls and concrete columns as backgrounds for the material they might chose to express themselves and, indeed, not all felt the need to express themselves.
Communal areas were neglected.
Employees had come to expect a good working environment without having to do it for themselves.
It is the perennial problem with interiors: one is necessarily intimate with one’s surroundings and, with time, they may lose their charms.

## 21.38 Herman Hertzberger, Centraal Beheer, Apeldoorn, the Netherlands, 1973. The Centraal
Beheer insurance company moved away from the open-plan office in favor of a more cellular organization.
Platforms or balconies at various levels were placed in a complex, constantly varied pattern.
More than a thousand office workers were each offered a unique location.
The cultural and social realignments that had marked the 1960s seeped through to the 1970s but were losing momentum.
In architecture and design there was a growing sense that modernism had lost its momentum and was fragmenting.

## INSIGHTS

## Interior
Design vs.
Architecture In May 1966, Architectural Review published Inscape, a consideration of the relationship between interior design and architecture.
It apologized for including “superficial, even flippant” content in the form of interior design but asked why it should not, for once, be frivolous.1 Hugh Casson was chief contributor.
His role as head of interior design at the Royal College of Art had caused him to consider the demarcation between interiors and architecture, and his seventy-five pages for Inscape were the most significant writings on the subject up to that time and, possibly, since.
He wrote about the connection between interior design and decoration and how functionalist machismo caused architects to shy away from the subjectivity needed to design interiors.
He argued that change of use in buildings meant that interiors need no longer take their stylistic cues from the exterior.
He listed “color, texture, scale, heat, light, sound, movement even perhaps smell”2 as components of an interior and suggested that interior design was a profession distinct from architecture, explaining how an interior designer “must start with that architectural anathema, a preconception . . . not a mystic personal revelation, but the disciplined and imaginative application of insight. . . .”3 He deprecated “whims of fashion” but cited the author Arthur Koestler’s argument that art is appreciated by personal judgment and awareness of contemporary society.4 Casson posited that interior design is best when it is democratic, and designer and user share expectations of how buildings should look and perform.
He argued that a good interior “not only looks right but feels right.”5 Journalist and design critic Alastair Best worked at the British Design Council in the 1960s and remembered the council’s dismay when the “anarchy of Carnaby Street”6 called into question the council’s modernist criteria for awarding its certificates of merit.
He suggested that the upheaval had not been led by academics or critics but by “a synthesis of all the most fertile minds of the mid-sixties, the entrepreneurs, art-school educated musicians, fashion photographers, magazine designers and advertising men.
Architecture was just too slow on its feet.”7 1.
Architectural Review, vol.
139, issue 831, 1966, p.
330.
2.
Hugh Casson, Inscape, Architectural Review vol.
139, issue 831, 1966, p.
332; 3.
Ibid; 4.
Ibid; 5.
Ibid; 6.
Alastair Best, “The ‘60s Remembered: The Best of Times, the Worst of Times,” Designers Journal, issue 37, 1988, p.
55; 7.
Ibid CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO POSTMODERNISM Philippe Starck, hotel lobby, Royalton Hotel, New York, 1984.
Intimate small spaces, with bespoke furniture by Starck, made the Royalton Hotel lobby the preferred haunt of New York’s fashionistas.
For all its dominance in world popular culture, and its apparent progressiveness, Britain in the 1960s had looked back, embracing Art Nouveau and Art Deco.
Modernism in interior design and architecture seemed to have lost conviction; there were tentative changes of direction but both were in suspended animation.
It needed something outrageous to set it in a new direction and that—postmodernism—would come from the United States.

## UNITED
STATES

## Venturi
and Others In 1966 the American architect Robert Venturi (1925–2018) published Complexity and Contradiction in Architecture in which he argued for architecture’s “difficult whole.” He included decoration and what he called “honky-tonk” elements—those that broke accepted aesthetic rules.
He advocated “messy vitality” and counterpointed Ludwig Mies van der Rohe’s “less is more” with “less is a bore.” He designed a small house for his mother completed in 1964 in which the front elevation was treated as a broken classical pediment but built in the timber-framed construction techniques of North American suburbia.
Its painted exterior, even its pediment, had similarities to its neighbors’ gables but it was challengingly unfamiliar.
The interior was comparatively conventional, dependent on a few angled walls around the stair (22.2, 22.3, and 22.4).

## 22.2 Robert Venturi, Vanna Venturi House, Philadelphia, 1964. The front elevation could be
seen as a timber-boarded gable of a timber-framed suburban house but the symmetry, the central slot above the entrance that suggests a broken pediment, and the square openings all suggest, perhaps subliminally, something Neoclassical.
Venturi added complexities and contradictions to his plan.
Walls are angled, corners cut off rooms, the central entrance requires a sharp turn to reach the front door, and the stairway widens and is then suddenly awkwardly narrowed.

## 22.3 Robert Venturi, ground-floor plan, Vanna Venturi House, 1964. 22.4 Robert Venturi, in
terior, Vanna Venturi House, 1964.
The consequences of Venturi’s angled planning show in the stair and fireplace/chimney element.
In 1977 Venturi, with Denise Scott Brown (b.
1931) and Steven Izenour (1940–2001), published Learning from Las Vegas in which they denounced the sterility of corporate architecture and praised the populist vigor of Las Vegas.
They argued that symbolism and decoration were crucial in making popular architecture and suggested that inspiration for both might be found in pre-modernist styles, singling out classicism for attention, which particularly annoyed modernists for whom it represented social and political repression.
Postmodern classicism was itself honky-tonk enough to earn the affectionate abbreviation of “PoMo.” Its essence was effectively demonstrated in a series of chairs, in which Venturi and Scott Brown made molded plywood “cartoons” of work by the great eighteenth-century English designers—and painted them with bright random dots (22.5).
The inspiration came as much from Disney as Chippendale.
Modernism was no longer modern.
Robert Venturi, Chippendale chair, 1978.
The molded plywood back has cutouts that allude to eighteenth-century Chippendale furniture with cartoonish simplification.
In 1977 the critic and architectural historian Charles Jencks (1939–2019) published The Language of Post-Modern Architecture suggesting that variations on the theme of modernism could counter its aridity.
He identified five postmodernist sub-sects: the Historic, the Neo-Vernacular, the Adhoc, the Metaphorical, and the Metaphysical.
In 1980 he complained that postmodernism had become synonymous with PoMo, which had eclipsed the other categories.
He was more of an advocate for Metaphorical and Metaphysical.
When in 1977 the magazine Architectural Design asked the New York Times’ architectural critic Paul Goldberger to explain postmodernism it really meant PoMo.
Goldberger defined modernism as “puritan austerity” and postmodernism as “indulgent complexity.” Architects took advantage of the sheltering shells of the buildings they were converting to design what were, in effect, buildings within buildings.
In 1979–81 George Ranalli (b.
1946) converted a listed schoolhouse in Newport, Rhode Island, to six self-contained condominiums on three levels, grouped around communal spaces that were the equivalent of squares and streets (22.6).
Between 1979 and 1984, in Frankfurt in Germany, Oswald Mathias Ungers (1926–2007) converted a large house into the Deutsches Architekturmuseum (German Architecture Museum) and installed a structurally independent diagrammatic house at its core which rose through the four stories of the existing building.
Both projects were seen as opportunities to design buildings that were not compromised by the need for weatherproofing and security (22.7).
George Ranalli, Callender School renovation, Newport, Rhode Island, 1979–81.
The conversion of a small two-story former school building into six self-contained apartments.
The whole is conceived as a small town with dwellings accessed from a central shared public square flanked by diagrammatic house façades.
Oswald Mathias Ungers, German Architecture Museum, Frankfurt, 1979–84.
The conversion of a large house to an architectural museum with a structurally independent house at its core that rose through four floors of the existing building.
In 1978 Jencks, in collaboration with Britain’s leading PoMo architect Sir Terry Farrell (b.1938), began the five-year transformation of his Victorian villa in London to what he called The Cosmic House (22.8).
The new interior had fragmented forms, architectural quotations, changes of level, and views across areas into others.
The foundation that administers the house describes it as “a synthesis of ideas about science and the arts . . . a true PoMo Gesamtkunstwerk.” Jencks invited leading postmodernists to contribute elements to the whole.
Michael Graves designed fireplaces, Piers Gough, who had designed Knitwit in 1968 Campbell, Zogolovitch, Wilkinson and Gough (see here), created a sauna.
A first design for the Spring Room was rejected as insufficiently symbolic.
Charles Jencks and Michael Graves, Spring Room, The Cosmic House, London, 1978–83.
Jencks, the author of The Language of Post-Modern Architecture, worked with, among others, the United States foremost postmodern architect, Michael Graves, to convert his Victorian villa using his cosmic theories, which he then used in landscaping projects.
In 1979 Lance Wright, an architectural and design journalist, complained in Architectural Review that twentieth-century buildings were designed to process people efficiently and that, when interiors were treated as extensions of exteriors, they charmed few and offended most.
He suggested that function should not eliminate fantasy and wondered if it might be possible “to accept the practical advantages of modernity without rejecting aesthetic traditions as the Victorians had done.” In 1981 critic Ada Louise Huxtable wrote in The New York Review of Books, “whatever comes next will be the product or inheritor of modernism . . .
It will have at its heart the twentiethcentury revolution that we call modern architecture.” The following year, Robert Jensen, an academic, and Patricia Conway, an architect, interior designer and academic, published Ornamentalism: The New Decorativeness in Architecture and Design.
Jensen and Conway wrote of the impulse to decorate as fundamental to the human condition, a way of identifying buildings and the cultures that create them, and that ornamental detail gave a building scale.
In the foreword, Goldberger described ornamenting as a radical act in defiance of prevailing articles of faith imposed on architects and designers.

## Graves
The great American exponent of PoMo was Michael Graves (1934–2015).
With the Hanselmann House (1967–71) and the Snyderman House (1972; destroyed 2002) in Fort Wayne, Indiana, he had displayed his frustration with the limitations of the modernist formula.
He took enthusiastically to PoMo.
His work is distinguished by distortion of the proportions of classical elements and strong color.
In 1979 he designed a series of showrooms for the Sunar Furniture Company, across the United States and in London, which experimented with the column and capital but avoided the more literal interpretations that Venturi had used to make his polemical points (22.9).
Michael Graves, Sunar Furniture Company showroom, Houston, Texas, 1979.
Paired columns sharing a diagrammatic capital that contains uplighters and the use of strong secondary colors makes a quintessential postmodern classical interior.
As awareness of PoMo grew, Graves was commissioned to design large new buildings in which he evolved an architectural language that did not imitate any particular style but succeeded in matching the richness of form, color, and materials of pre-modernist architecture.
His buildings had a subliminal familiarity and for each project he provided a complementary interior with appropriate adjustments of scale and visual complexity.
He evolved a language that was uniquely his.
It was humane and could be compared with Art Deco, for its visual richness and popular appeal.
Architects and designers still committed to modernist principles were disturbed that he was getting such commissions from major corporations, of which, the headquarters of the Humana Corporation in Louisville, Kentucky, in 1982 was one of the most spectacular (22.10).
22.10 Michael Graves, Humana Building, Louisville, Kentucky, 1982–5.
This interior doorway makes no direct allusions but clearly suggests that it belongs philosophically—if ambiguously—to a long architectural tradition.
Such was the excitement around postmodernism that in the early 1980s Graves and other prominent postmodernists were commissioned by the Alessi company in Italy and departmentstore chain J.
C.
Penney in the United States to design household objects.
He contributed kettles, coffee pots, and pepper mills.
He also designed furniture that could be mistaken for Art Deco.
Postmodernism found a following, among designers and non-designers in Europe and beyond, much more quickly than modernism had done.
It was due to the excitement caused by the first extraordinary examples—which were conceived to give pleasure to those who used them.

## AUSTRIA

## Hollein
In Austria, Hans Hollein (1934–2014) was another pioneer in the search for a more palatable modern architecture.
He had studied engineering and architecture in Vienna and in 1963 began his career by rejecting the principle of “form follows function.” He became the most accomplished practitioner of European postmodernism.
Jencks described him as a product of finde-siècle Vienna and his work as “much funnier and with more consummate details than the American postmodernists were producing. . . .” In 1985 he won the prestigious Pritzker Architecture Prize and pronounced that architecture was an art “not primarily the solution of a problem, but the making of a statement.” In 1965–6, as Venturi was publishing his first polemic, Hollein designed the little Retti candle store in Vienna.
Its aluminum façade, in which the thin entrance slot may be seen as a pictogram of a candle, an Ionic column—or a phallus—generated controversy among architects and the seemingly gratuitous imagery led to its being described by architects—dismissively—as the work of a designer.
He designed two jewelry stores for the Schullin company in Vienna, both small but with dramatically ambiguous frontages.
The first (1972–6) offered a grid of terrazzo panels split by a seam that metaphorically dripped gold to make an irregularly shaped door.
In the second store (1981–2) a door flanked by thin columns supporting an elliptical pediment seemed to allude to classicism (22.11).
Hans Hollein, Schullin II jewelry store, Vienna, 1981–2.
Hollein accepts the components of a classical façade and evolves them until they belong to a different, unfamiliar language.
In his Österreichisches Verkehrsbüro (Austrian Travel Agency) in Vienna (1976–9), Hollein scattered a golden domed kiosk, chromed and gilded palm trees, and a chromed cylinder that rose from the core of the fluted bass of a classical column (22.12).
Two stuffed eagles hovered beneath a glazed barrel vault inspired by that in the city’s Austrian Postal Savings Bank created by Otto Wagner in the early twentieth century (see here).
Hans Hollein, Austrian Travel Agency, Vienna, 1976–9.
A collection of references to foreign places and different times, all under a ceiling inspired by Otto Wagner’s work on the Austrian Postal Savings Bank (see here).
At the Venice Biennale in 1980, Hollein was one of twenty leading postmodernist designers chosen to contribute a façade to the Strada Novissima (Newest Street) and his contribution was provocative and not the most beautiful (22.13).
Under a pediment that had a passing resemblance to that for his second Schullin store, he created six columns, the symbol of classical architecture, which represented the new and the worn, the relationship between natural and humanmade materials, the natural origin of the column and the strange imagination of his Austrian predecessor, Adolf Loos (see here).
Hans Hollein, Strada Novissima, Venice Biennale, 1980.
Leading postmodernists were invited to contribute a façade to the Strada Novissima.
Hollein presented variations on the theme of the column.

## BRITAIN
In Britain established practices followed the lead of architects and designers in the United States.
Fitch & Co used PoMo in stores, DEGW used it in offices.
A few young architects and designers also sensed that the rules of modernism had been dismantled.
They were uninterested in pastiches of classicisms but set out in other directions that would soon influence the way commercial interior design would evolve.
All had individual styles and needed clients who wanted extraordinary interiors.
They found them among their contemporaries: the fledgling entrepreneurs in fashion and pop music.
These game-changers were in their mid-teens during the 1960s, when norms were usurped and they were encouraged to break free from the modernist past.
Three of them, David Connor, Julian Powell-Tuck and Ben Kelly, trained in provincial art schools and were more influenced by art movements than architectural dogma.
Their ideas matured on the interior course at the Royal College of Art in London, which gave them a portal to a metropolitan world.
They had three years to develop their creativity in a challenging environment, time in which to develop the confidence to challenge orthodoxies.

## Connor
David Connor (b.
1950) was excited by German Expressionist cinema and the work of Max Clendinning (see here) but thought his generation’s responsibility was to move on from modernist orthodoxies.
He cooperated with musician and clothes designer Malcolm McLaren and fashion designer Vivienne Westwood, the doyens of British punk, to create the store Seditionaries on the King’s Road in Chelsea, London, to sell punk clothes in the former premises of Granny Takes A Trip (see here).
The interior was dominated by photomontages of the German city of Dresden after its destruction by Allied bombers during World War II and an inverted image of London’s tourist hub, Piccadilly Circus.
In 2013 its long-vanished interior was recreated in the Museum of Modern Art in New York.
In 1980 the New Romantic pop singer Adam Ant, who was then at the zenith of his fame and managed by McLaren, commissioned Connor to design his apartment in London.
Connor gave him a stage set.
Marbling, a paint technique that replicates the appearance of the stone was applied to all hard surfaces by specialist painter, David Campion.
Armchairs were overstuffed and draped in bespoke fabric, as if to protect them in the unexplained absence of the owner.
Drapes were too long and spilled across the floor.
An empty picture frame leant against a wall.
The apartment was moodily melancholic, which was very New Romantic and postmodern (22.14).
David Connor, interior, Adam Ant Apartment, London, 1981.
The walls, ceilings, and all hard surfaces were transfigured with a faux-marble paint finish.
Fabrics were designed and printed to harmonize.
Connor’s next project, in 1981, was the large entrance area of another London apartment for another musician, Marco Pirroni, but instead of faux-marble precision, walls were daubed with abstract slashes of paint made with unequivocal decorative intent by Madeleine Palme, a Swedish painter.
It was German Expressionist punk and contradicted perspective: doors were twisted out of shape, tops of base boards sloped sharply, and radiators were hung askew (22.15).
22.15 David Connor, Marco Pirroni Apartment, London, 1982.
Rather than craft finish, there are abstract paint daubs by Madeleine Palme on all the surfaces, including the recycled chairs that Connor claimed were upholstered with dog fur.
His admiration for German Expressionist cinema inspired the distorted doors, the sloping base boards that contradicted perspective, and the radiator hung at an angle.
Young designers and students were shocked and delighted by these two projects which seemed to be the antithesis of the sensible, problem-solving modernism they had been taught.
Imaginations and creative ambitions were unlocked.
A few years after they had graduated from the Royal College of Art Connor drifted into a professional partnership in the late 1970s with Julian Powell-Tuck who described it as a “mutual arrangement . . . we collaborated when the work was there . . . there was no business plan . . . it was basically just dealing with stuff that presented itself.” With that attitude and concentration on creative output, they were the most influential practice in London in the first half of the 1980s.

## Powell-Tuck
Julian Powell-Tuck (b.
1950), in collaboration with the architect Pierre d’Avoine (b.
1951), maintained his practice’s commitment to applied decoration.
In an office for Research Recordings, a video-editing company, they invited the textile designer, Sally Greaves-Lord (b.
1957), another Royal College graduate, to decorate the reception area.
She painted walls with intricate abstractions and designed the patterns cut into the linoleum floor (22.17).
The outcome, with its precise changes of scale and strategic inserts of sharp color, was as extraordinary as the faux marble in the Adam Ant apartment or the expressionistic gestures in the Marco Pirroni apartment.
It was made to be beautiful.
22.17 Powell-Tuck, Connor Orefelt & D’Avoine (design), Sally Greaves Lord (wall painting and chair fabric in the main double height reception), Research Recordings, London, 1984.
In the reception area of this modestly sized project, Greaves-Lord demonstrated that foursquare functional solids could be transformed by precisely detailed decoration in an inspired rebuttal of white walls that gave the project its identity and success.
Powell-Tuck created his own masterwork at the end of the 1980s, with the conversion of a lofty bus depot in London to a recording studio.
He split the volume on its long axis to make a fullheight atrium that was dominated by a twisting steel stair.
Two floors of studios and recreational rooms presented a canted plywood-clad façade to the atrium.
Concrete walls, cast in situ, provided sound-deadening mass.
Studios were splayed on plan and section in accordance with acoustic principles and surface detailing dealt with reverberation (22.16).
Powell-Tuck, Connor & Orefelt, interior, Metropolis Recording Studios, London, 1989.
The mezzanine café for breaks between recording sessions overlooking the atrium.
The plywood panels at the upper level clads the studios.

## Kelly
Ben Kelly (b.
1949) cited artists Marcel Duchamp and Andy Warhol as influences, both of whom elevated the mundane to the extraordinary.
He brought the ideas of creative recycling and repurposing to interior design and demonstrated how to apply them in the design of a clothes store in central London for the retailer Paul Howie in 1977 (22.18) and to The Haçienda, a nightclub in the northern industrial city of Manchester, in 1982 (22.19).
The club inhabited an abandoned warehouse, of which Manchester had many.
The building’s brick exterior enclosed a huge volume under a glazed roof, and Kelly hyped a few strategic elements.
He painted cast-iron columns with diagonal stripes and the edges of the wooden dance floor were marked by black and white bollards.
Balcony supports were clad in sheets of plywood, sometimes painted, sometimes not.
Newsweek magazine called it the most famous club in the world in the 1990s.
Kelly continues to retune existing elements and make the mundane glamorous.
He describes his projects as installations, maintaining that, in interior design, art is more important than architecture.

## 22.18 Ben Kelly, Howie store, London, 1977. In the spirit of French artist Marcel Duchamp,
Kelly’s found materials and gadgets make a rough and robust proto High-tech interior.
22.19 Ben Kelly, The Haçienda, Manchester, England, 1982.
Paint and pattern pick out and elevate existing elements in the nightclub.
The black and red painted cladding to the mezzanine structure was one of a series of totems that were variations on the color theme.

## Jiricna
Eva Jiricna (b.
1939) trained as an architect and engineer in her native Czechoslovakia but relocated to London in 1968 as a political refugee and built her reputation as a High-tech designer.
She worked with the architect Lord Richard Rogers on the interiors of his Lloyd’s Building in London (completed in 1986) while establishing her own practice—in partnership with Australian interior designer Kathy Kerr until 1987—and beginning a long series of store interiors for the Moroccan-born fashion retailer Joseph Ettedgui giving him white walls, smooth-tiled floors and black and chrome furniture, which established his brand and complemented his fashion collections.
These established her national and international reputations and her meticulous detailing attracted commissions for jewelry stores and museums.
Her early training in engineering has driven the series of increasingly delicate stairs that have become her signature pieces.
They are the spectacular center pieces that elevate the Joseph stores above the minimalism that prevails in high-end fashion stores and, in ancient buildings, their alien presence complements and is complemented by the old walls that contain them (22.20 and 22.21).
Eva Jiricna, Somerset House, London, 2015.
In this arts complex, Jiricna’s stair configuration was inspired by the building’s existing eighteenth-century stair.
The sculpted treads, of a composite material, reflect the stone treads of the original.
22.21 Eva Jiricna, Joseph, London, 1988.
For this fashion-store interior, Jiricna made a spectacular, disturbingly minimal stair with a structure of chromed tension wires and connection pieces supporting glass treads.
As her work has developed, she has progressively eroded elements.

## Pawson
John Pawson (b.
1949) is the quintessential exponent of minimalism, which he describes as ‘‘the perfection an artifact achieves when it is no longer possible to improve it by subtraction.” He suggests that simplicity has a moral dimension that is shared across cultures.
His walls and ceilings are white and devoid of moldings, floors are wide wooden planks or square tile grids, natural light may be filtered through translucent glass, artificial light sources wash across perfectly flat white surfaces, and his stair treads and risers meet in right angles and are squeezed into narrow, high-walled slots.
Objects are stored in cupboards that lack obvious means of opening (22.22).
22.22 John Pawson, interior, own home, London, 1996–9.
The ground-floor living area exemplifies Pawson’s aesthetic.
The floor is honey-colored limestone, which is also used for stairs, wall benches, worktops, baths, and basins.
A narrow shadow-gap recess separates hypersmooth white walls and floor.
Utilitarian objects are stored in a wall of floor-to-ceiling cupboards that also conceals the narrow stair connecting the four levels of the house.
The oak-framed, white-upholstered bench conforms to prevailing orthogona principles.
Pawson made his name with austere dwellings but his stripped-back aesthetic works well for fashion stores.
In 1993–5 he designed the Calvin Klein Collections Store in New York, filling the interior with lofty white towers (22.23).
For the Jigsaw chain of fashion stores in London he subdivided floors with sheets of translucent glass that filter daylight and blur the untidiness of clothing racks.
His work is assumed to have a spirituality that has brought commissions from religious bodies.
He has designed an installation in St.
Paul’s Cathedral in London, in 2011, and an abbey in Bohemia (1999–2004), but his status as the begetter of fashionable minimalism has also led to his designing kitchenware.
John Pawson, interior, Calvin Klein Collections Store, New York, 1993–5.
The tall windows on two sides of the store made the control of natural light difficult but the enormous piers that sit in orderly fashion throughout the space give new surfaces to provide light and shadow—and give order.

## Coates
Nigel Coates (b.
1949) admired the Festival of Britain’s “clunky but kind of dynamic fusion of art, science and narrative” and thought postmodernism a call to arms.
His London apartment, with high ceilings, generous moldings, and exotic artifacts, among unpainted pink plaster walls and doors partially stripped to reveal successive layers of ancient paints, was published in a Japanese lifestyle magazine and he was asked to design a Tokyo restaurant, Metropole, in 1985.
He responded with an assemblage of European artifacts: columns with capitals of twisted-steel reinforcing bars, black armchairs under a chandelier in front of a marble fireplace.
It was entered through a proscenium arch and its walls were hung with antique casts and mirrors that stretched it to infinity.
Café Bongo opened in 1986 on Tokyo’s busiest pedestrian corner.
Its collage of hanging draperies, painted ceilings, and trashy objects sealed in acrylic floors evoked European decadence (22.24).
A stretched facsimile of an airplane wing curved around the room providing a plinth for classical statues before bursting through the façade to become an entrance canopy.
This quasicatastrophic collision of tradition and technology astonished other designers, who could only wonder both at Coates’s nerve and that there was a client who would build his design.
22.24 Nigel Coates, Café Bongo, Tokyo, 1986.
The antidote to Japanese minimalism, Café Bongo is an ironic collage of European culture.
An airplane wing wraps around the room before it crashes through the façade to become a canopy above the entrance.
It is supported on raked columns that suggest harps and acts as a plinth for facsimiles of classical sculptures.
The ceiling painting would not be out of place in an Italian palazzo.
Coates’s tsunami of Japanese projects brought him British projects.
He challenged fashion retailing’s commitment to sparse white rooms.
In 1986 Lord Norman Foster (b.
1935) gave the fashion designer Katharine Hamnett a top-lit store in London with white walls, towering mirrors, and racks of clothes distributed casually across the concrete floor.
A few years later Coates’s interior for Hamnett, in a conventional store unit, was a conundrum of draped fabrics, etched glass, abstract floor patterns and fish tanks, which was much more to Hamnett’s taste (22.25).
Foster gave her a magnificently definitive Foster, a hard-edged empty room; Coates gave her something ephemeral, of its moment, like fashion itself—and complex enough to take seasonal tuning without losing its character.
At first glance, Coates’s interiors seemed to be overloaded, with elements and incidents, an aesthetic tension that made them compelling.
22.25 Nigel Coates, Katharine Hamnett store, London, 1988.
The starting point here is Art Deco, or perhaps 1950s haute-couture salon, yet there is no doubt that it belongs to the late 1980s because the mix is too rich, the motifs too flamboyant, and the lighting and the fish tanks are too incongruous.

## Collins
David Collins (1955–2013) was another architectural scion for whom modernism was simply another style that he added to his mix when appropriate.
A Dubliner, he was not part of London’s inner architectural circle but in the mid 1980s his pronounced social skills brought him rich and adventurous clients for whom he created sumptuous interiors that were ignored by professional publications but welcomed in fashion magazines.
When his house for an art collector, in an expensive and fashionable area in London, was published a stream of commissions for grand private houses followed (22.26).
At first glance, the various elements are conventional but then the fine-tuning becomes clear.
The marble that frames the fireplace stretches beyond the edges of the chimney breast, the flat, plain cornice is acutely angled, everything has been tweaked.
If it had to be labeled, it is closest to Art Deco.
David Collins, interior, apartment, London, 2008.
His other forte was designing smart restaurants but he was equally successful creating sandwich bars.
He designed restaurant chains that aimed to satisfy the aspirations of the modestly affluent to have better food in better places, where atmosphere was more important than cuisine.
He knew how to plan and decorate to make every restaurant table desirable and to create the appropriate atmosphere.
His strategic planning and superficially retrospective detailing perfectly supported twenty-first-century informalities and taste.
His highly tuned aesthetic worked for haute-couture fashion designers, giving them a lush elegance that complemented their creative bravado.
His design vocabulary was broad and could evoke a period that one could never be sure what that period was, as in the ambiguous nostalgia of The Wolseley brasserie in London (2003).
His studio continues after his death, creating spaces such as Alexander McQueen’s Aoyama flagship store Tokyo (2014; 22.27).
David Collins Studio, Alexander McQueen Aoyama, Tokyo, 2014.
22.27 The intricacy of the white-on-white plaster molding in this flagship store matches the spirit of McQueen’s exotic fashion designs.

## INSIGHTS

## Finding
an Audience In Britain, the projects of the radical new interior designers revolutionized interior-design practice and inspired young practitioners and students.
They also excited a lay public who found their extraordinary images in glamorous magazines.
In 1982 the journalist Min Hogg (1938–2019) founded World of Interiors, the first of many such magazines and newspaper supplements that followed.
The first edition featured an apartment created in London by interior designer Nicky Haslam (b.
1939) for the pop singer Bryan Ferry, an art-school graduate, whose studied elegance intrigued his fans.
They, Hogg rightly anticipated, would boost sales of the magazine.
Haslam gave Ferry a miniature stately home with pediments on book cases, ruched drapes, two kinds of chintz and blue and white china.
A classical cornice separated the formal layout of period furniture from crude timber roof trusses.
The design was postmodern but free of the self-conscious distortions other designers introduced to signal that they were not entirely serious.a

## FRANCE

## Putman
Andrée Putman (1925–2013) abandoned her studies at the Conservatoire de Paris (Paris Conservatory) to work on fashion magazines before becoming editor of L’Oeil du Décorateur (The Eye of the Decorator) in 1960.
From 1958 to 1967 she worked as a stylist for Prisunic, the ubiquitous French chain store, and introduced inexpensive, well-designed furniture, tableware, and fabrics.
She was enthusiastic about French furniture of the 1930s and, in 1978, founded Ecart to sell pieces by, among others, Eileen Gray (see here) and Robert Mallet-Stevens (see here).
Buyers often asked her to advise on appropriate contexts for their purchases and she became an interior designer by default.
Her first commercial interior project, in 1985, was for YSL Rive Gauche stores in the United States and she designed for other fashion designers keen to move on from the tradition of flowery, frilly haute-couture stores.
In 1984 she designed Morgans Hotel in Manhattan (22.28), generally acknowledged to be the first boutique hotel, for Ian Schrager and Steve Rubell, owners of the notoriously decadent Studio 54 nightclub in New York.
Morgans was famous for black and white checkerboard tile patterns in its bathrooms but, while black and white details in furniture and fabric recurred throughout, other rooms favored pale grays and taupes.

## 22.28 Andrée Putman, bathroom, Morgans Hotel, New York, 1984. To upgrade a downtown hotel,
Putman employed an uncompromising black and white scheme, here applied in a bathroom where chrome fittings both reflect and are camouflaged by the pattern.
Philippe Starck, Café Costes, Paris, 1984 (no longer in existence).
She offered well-orchestrated simplicity, restraint and subtle color, in contrast to the prevailing Louis XVI decoration of luxury hotels, and many hotel designs followed.
In 1993, she designed the interior of the Concorde supersonic jet.

## Starck
Philippe Starck (b.
1949) is an indefatigable designer of interiors, exteriors, furniture, shoes, scents, a yacht, a motorcycle, a lemon squeezer, a toothbrush—an estimated 10,000 projects.
He changed the perceptions of fellow designers and the public for whom they work.
After local success in France, Starck made his international impact in 1984 with Café Costes in Paris (22.29).
He declared it was inspired by the “poignancy” of Prague railroad station and it confirmed that an interior could be poetic.
He has said that an interior is not just about appearance but the emotion it evokes.
Costes was demolished to make way for an unimpressive clothes store, which is the way of the commercial world in which interior design works.
It was a place of dark woods and a terrazzo floor with a wide tapering stair rising to a 6 1/2-foot (2-m) high clock and lavatories of perplexing originality.
With the chair he designed for Costes he demonstrated that something as familiar as a chair could be provocatively reinterpreted.
22.29 The stair and terrazzo floor pattern that contradicted perspective, and a clock that contradicted logic confronted customers when they had pushed aside the heavy drape that hung at the entrance.
Starck designed the tables and chairs for the project.
The French government was subsidizing radical design and Starck had pieces in production so that his newfound international audience was able to satisfy the urge to own the brand.
He followed Costes with a battery of cafés and hotels, which were all distinct, sharing only the marks of the Starck imagination.
In an old Madrid theater he created Teatriz (1991), a lofty restaurant with heavy drapes, a monumental stair, and a bar of back-lit onyx.
In 1984 Schrager and Rubell asked Starck to design the Royalton Hotel in New York (22.1).
The existing building gave no opportunities for grand gestures but he transformed its existing spaces with bespoke furniture and details that were without precedent.
In 1988–9 Schrager called on him again to design the Paramount Hotel, a budget Royalton a few blocks away (22.30).
Bedrooms were small, each dominated by a reproduction of a female head sampled from an Old Master painting on bedheads (a Starck pun).
If the bedrooms were small, the lofty lobby, dominated by a monumental stair cantilevered from a precariously sloping wall, was spacious and filled with oversized furniture.
22.30 Philippe Starck, Paramount Hotel, New York, 1988–9.
The Paramount had small bedrooms but an enormous lobby dominated by a tapering stair against a rakishly angled wall.
The oversized furniture was designed in sympathy with the space and ignored the convention of matching pieces neatly laid out.
He designed two buildings without architectural precedents in Tokyo.
Nani Nani (1987) is Japanese for “what is it?” and is an apt name for what is a curvaceous copper-clad office building that rears up from the street like a surfacing whale.
It has been described as non-functional and non-modern.
Flamme d’Or (1989) is a beer hall for the Asahi Brewery (22.31).
An enormous golden structure resembling a flame was fabricated using submarine construction techniques to sit on top of glossy black walls that splay outwards and are pierced by little lights.
The interior is at least as spectacular, with splayed walls and columns that are variations on the rooftop flame.
In the twenty-first century, the Starck studio is necessarily large but it maintains the extraordinary standards he set in the 1980s and his staff have grown up in the world he created.

## 22.31 Philippe Starck, Flamme d’Or, Tokyo, 1989. The outward sloping interior walls reflec
t the angles of the external walls and the enormous columns are variations on the golden flame sculptural element that decorates the top of the brewery.

## ITALY

## Sottsass
and the Memphis Group Ettore Sottsass (1917–2007) made his reputation designing office furniture and equipment.
While working with Italian office-equipment manufacturer Olivetti, he began to develop complex, highly colored objects that anticipated the work of the Memphis Group that he founded in 1980.
Memphis was a multinational collective of young designers drawn to Milan by its reputation as a creative hub.
They produced brightly colored, boldly patterned, wantonly nonfunctional objects that could only find a place in museums or as trophies for rich collectors.
If American postmodernists looked at European classicism for inspiration, then Memphis looked at more recent Italian precedents, particularly the plastic laminates and terrazzo floors in the cafés that were the egalitarian heart of Italy’s daily life.
Memphis confirmed the potency of color and pattern (22.32).

## 22.32 Ettore Sottsass, Carlton bookcase, wood, polychrome printed laminate, Italy, 1981. A
defining work from the Memphis Group, the obviously dysfunctional configuration and whimsical coloration reject modernist rationality.

## Mendini
After the end of World War II, when architects and designers were trying to understand and get to grips with evolving modern design, the Italian architecture and design magazine Domus provided a compendium of the most progressive work across Europe.
It was produced in Milan, the Italian city least in thrall to its past and a gathering place for radical Italian designers.
Alessandro Mendini (1931–2019) edited Domus from 1979 to 1985 and was consequentially influential in the evolution of European postmodernism.
He considered that the human instinct was to decorate and that a designer should draw on precedents from all historical periods.
His Proust armchair of 1978 was an early, and among the most memorable, of postmodernist provocations (22.33).
It was called “Proust” because French writer Marcel Proust wrote the modernist novel A la Recherche du Temps Perdu (Remembrance of Things Past, 1913–27).

## 22.33 Alessandro Mendini, Proust armchair, carved and hand-painted wood and fabric, Italy,
1978.
Designed when Mendini was a member of the avant-garde Studio Alchimia, the chair plays with a classic form, tweaking concepts of modernist good taste.

## Branzi
Andrea Branzi (b.
1938) was a close associate of Sottsass and the Memphis Group.
He designed his Animali Domestici (Pets) series of furniture in $\scriptstyle 1 9 8 4 ,$ in what he described as Neo-Primitive style.
It was a polemical collection of objects that resembled chairs, with sides and backs of twigs on smooth, foursquare bases (22.34).
It suggested that furniture, and by extension, the other elements in an interior have an intimate relationship, like pets, with those who own and use them and whose lives are, or should be, enriched by them.
Nicoletta Morozzi (b.
1948), a designer of limited-edition art clothing, who was also married to Branzi, created complementary quasiprimitive garments.

## 22.34 Andrea Branzi, bench, Pets collection, Milan, 1984. A polemical collection by a conf
irmed theoretician, all were a combination of the precision machine-made wooden base and the pristine natural forms of twigs and branches.

## Aulenti
Gae Aulenti (1927–2012) designed interiors, furniture, exhibitions, stage sets, and products.
She set up practice in 1954 and joined the Neo-Liberty movement, which accepted the modernist legacy while respecting historical precedents, pointing towards postmodernism.
In 1981 she converted a Beaux-Arts railroad station in Paris into the Musée d’Orsay (22.35).
Under the original glazed barrel-vaulted roof, she created a wide promenade that ran the length of the station, flanked by walls that suggested something of ancient Egypt, and which were punctuated by entrances to side galleries above which mezzanines displayed sculpture and gave access to smaller galleries.
Old and new were complementary.
Gae Aulenti, Musée d’Orsay, Paris, 1981.
Within the Beaux-Arts shell of an old railroad station, the central concourse might be a platform and the separate structures along its length might be carriages, if the architecture of each unit did not suggest an ancient Egyptian building.
After the success of Musée d’Orsay, Aulenti was appointed to solve the problem of displaying paintings in the Centre Pompidou, Paris, the apogee of 1970s High-tech.
The architects’ original intention, to hang paintings on movable partitions, lacked gravitas.
Aulenti again proposed long promenades with smaller side rooms.
Her flat white walls were simpler than those in the Musée d’Orsay, and her new ceiling did not entirely obscure the building’s notoriously visible service ducts (22.36).
Gae Aulenti, Centre Pompidou, Paris, 1983.
Walls are flat and white, marking the central circulation route, with small rooms off on either side.
The more complicated ceiling structure does not obscure the building’s exposed ductwork.
